AI.result: Across three knowledge-injection settings, six retention benchmarks, multiple baselines, and multiple base models, RoCo-ACE achieves the best injected-knowledge accuracy while keeping retention close to the base model.
AI.conclusion: RoCo-ACE effectively injects new knowledge into MLLMs with superior accuracy and minimal retention drift.

title: CodeNib: A Multi-View Data System for Serving Repository Context to Coding Agents
summary:
Coding agents repeatedly search, navigate, and retain context from evolving repositories, but disconnected indexes, language servers, and task-local histories force repeated discovery and obscure lifecycle costs. CodeNib builds reusable lexical, dense, and structural views per repository commit, maps outputs to repository-relative source ranges, maintains selected views across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through one runtime.
  Across 100 snapshots, we map quality-cost frontiers across the repository-context lifecycle. When outputs match an independent rebuild, graph and vector updates are $8.7\times$ and $25.4\times$ faster at the median. On the static-navigation subset matching normalized live-server locations (63% of 1,000 requests), the median per-request live/static latency ratio is $4.7\times$. Across five models, selected context policies preserve localization with 50--87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read. Together, these results support multi-view repository-context serving with explicit, operation-specific validity boundaries.

AI.tldr: CodeNib builds reusable multi-view repository context (lexical, dense, structural) per commit, enabling faster graph/vector updates (8.7×/25.4×), lower latency than live servers (4.7× median), and 50–87% fewer trajectory tokens across five models.
AI.motivation: Coding agents repeatedly search, navigate, and retain context from evolving repositories, but disconnected indexes, language servers, and task-local histories force repeated discovery and obscure lifecycle costs.
AI.method: CodeNib builds reusable lexical, dense, and structural views per repository commit, maps outputs to repository-relative source ranges, maintains selected views across edits, and serves ranked search, symbol navigation, and bounded context through one runtime.
AI.result: Across 100 snapshots, graph and vector updates are 8.7× and 25.4× faster at median when outputs match independent rebuild. On static navigation (63% of 1,000 requests), median live/static latency ratio is 4.7×. Across five models, context policies preserve localization with 50–87% fewer trajectory tokens than paired grep/read.
AI.conclusion: Results support multi-view repository-context serving with explicit, operation-specific validity boundaries.

title: IMPRINT: Image-Conditioned Query Enrichment for Long-Tail Object Goal Navigation
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Project page: https://github.com/JelinR/IMPRINT
summary: Embodied AI increasingly relies on queryable semantic maps built from pre-trained vision-language models to enable zero-shot Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav). However, existing approaches typically depend on text-only queries, which become less reliable as semantic specificity increases toward fine-grained object categories. We introduce IMPRINT, a zero-shot plug-and-play framework that enriches textual object queries with web-sourced images to improve grounding in queryable maps. Retrieved images are encoded using a vision-language model, matched against the semantic map to produce similarity maps, and aggregated to yield context-aware localization. Notably, this requires no training or modification of the underlying navigation policy. To explicitly evaluate long-tail behavior, we present HSSD-rare, a new ObjectNav benchmark built on Habitat Synthetic Scenes and featuring semantically specific subcategories. Across both OVON and HSSD-rare, image-conditioned queries consistently improve object grounding and yield end-to-end navigation gains. Further analysis reveals that translating localization gains to navigation performance depends critically on downstream detection quality, highlighting a key systems bottleneck in long-tail embodied navigation.

AI.tldr: IMPRINT is a zero-shot, plug-and-play framework that enriches textual object queries with web-sourced images to improve Object Goal Navigation using queryable semantic maps, achieving consistent gains without training, especially on fine-grained categories.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot ObjectNav approaches rely on text-only queries, which degrade in performance as object categories become more fine-grained and semantically specific. This limits their effectiveness for long-tail object grounding in embodied AI.
AI.method: IMPRINT retrieves web-sourced images for each object category, encodes them via a vision-language model, matches against a pre-built semantic map to produce similarity maps, and aggregates them for context-aware localization. It operates as a zero-shot plug-and-play module requiring no training or modification to the underlying navigation policy.
AI.result: Image-conditioned queries consistently improve object grounding and end-to-end navigation performance on both OVON and the new HSSD-rare benchmark. However, translating localization gains into navigation improvements critically depends on downstream detection quality, revealing a systems bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Enriching textual queries with web-sourced images is an effective zero-shot strategy for improving fine-grained ObjectNav, but downstream detection quality remains a key bottleneck for long-tail embodied navigation.

title: Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization
summary: Generative models are increasingly adopted in distributionally robust optimization (DRO), but existing approaches trade off model compatibility and adversarial structure: methods that accept arbitrary samplers do not restrict worst-case laws to a generator family, while generator-parameterized adversaries rely on model-specific access such as likelihoods, scores, or training data. We propose Generative Distributionally Robust Optimization (GDRO), a principled framework that accepts any sampleable conditional generator as the nominal model and restricts worst-case laws to a chosen conditional generator family. The key is the sampler-Sinkhorn pairing: samplers represent the conditional laws exactly, while Sinkhorn divergence compares their induced distributions without likelihood access and can be estimated from samples alone. The resulting population problem admits a direct finite-sample approximation and differentiable primal-dual implementation at the active decision context. For Lipschitz losses, the population Sinkhorn radius bounds downstream degradation. Across explicit and implicit generators, our method reduces rare-context inventory regret by 60% and SocialGAN navigation collisions by 50% relative to nominal decisions.

AI.tldr: GDRO is a DRO framework that accepts any sampleable conditional generator as nominal model, uses Sinkhorn divergence to restrict worst-case laws to a chosen conditional generator family without likelihood access, and demonstrates 50-60% improvements in inventory and navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing DRO approaches either accept arbitrary samplers but fail to restrict worst-case laws to a generator family, or rely on generator-parameterized adversaries with model-specific access (likelihoods, scores, training data), creating a trade-off between model compatibility and adversarial structure.
AI.method: Proposes GDRO using a sampler-Sinkhorn pairing: samplers represent conditional laws exactly, Sinkhorn divergence compares induced distributions without likelihood access. Enables finite-sample approximation and differentiable primal-dual implementation at the active decision context.
AI.result: For Lipschitz losses, the population Sinkhorn radius bounds downstream degradation. Reduces rare-context inventory regret by 60% and SocialGAN navigation collisions by 50% relative to nominal decisions.
AI.conclusion: GDRO provides a principled, widely compatible framework for DRO that works with any sampleable conditional generator and demonstrates significant practical improvements across both explicit and implicit generative models.

title: RSMeM: Knowledge-Enhanced Memory Evolution for Remote Sensing Agents with Systematic Evaluation
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. Code: https://github.com/AI9Stars/RSMeM
summary: Geoscience research requires complex analysis and domain expertise, with remote sensing (RS) observations as a key foundation. However, existing RS agents built on general-purpose LLMs remain largely domain-agnostic, resulting in brittle and error-prone workflows. Moreover, these failures are seldom consolidated into a reusable experience for subsequent analyses. To address this issue, we introduce RSMeM, a knowledge-enhanced memory evolution mechanism that bootstraps RS agents with pre-distilled domain knowledge and iteratively integrates online experience for robust multi-step tool execution. RSMeM is composed of two components: (i) Hierarchical Knowledge Grounding, which performs taxonomy-aware retrieval over a hierarchical domain corpus to guide planning and tool selection; and (ii) Failure-Aware Experience Refinement, which distills failure-annotated tool-use traces into reusable constraints for next-round tool execution. By iteratively employing these two processes, RS agents can evolve to absorb task-level domain knowledge and effectively translate it into instance-level execution experience. Extensive experiments on EarthBench demonstrate that RSMeM consistently improves tool-use performance and end-to-end answer across a diverse set of LLM backbones. Notably, RSMeM achieves a 6% accuracy improvement on DeepSeek-V3.2 with less than 1% additional experience tokens, demonstrating the strong knowledge density of our distilled experience. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/RSMeM

AI.tldr: RSMeM introduces a knowledge-enhanced memory evolution mechanism for remote sensing agents, combining hierarchical knowledge grounding with failure-aware experience refinement to improve multi-step tool execution. It achieves 6% accuracy improvement on DeepSeek-V3.2 with minimal additional tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing RS agents built on general-purpose LLMs are domain-agnostic, leading to brittle and error-prone workflows, and failures are not consolidated into reusable experience for subsequent analyses.
AI.method: RSMeM consists of two components: (i) Hierarchical Knowledge Grounding - taxonomy-aware retrieval over a hierarchical domain corpus for planning and tool selection; (ii) Failure-Aware Experience Refinement - distilling failure-annotated tool-use traces into reusable constraints for next-round execution. These processes are iteratively employed for agent evolution.
AI.result: Consistent improvement in tool-use performance and end-to-end answer across diverse LLM backbones on EarthBench. Specifically, 6% accuracy improvement on DeepSeek-V3.2 with less than 1% additional experience tokens.
AI.conclusion: RSMeM effectively bootstraps RS agents with pre-distilled domain knowledge and iteratively integrates online experience for robust multi-step tool execution, achieving strong knowledge density with minimal token overhead.

title: Repositories, Contributors, and Continuity: An Empirical Study of Foundational Quantum Software
summary: Driven by contributions from academia, industry, and open-source communities, the quantum software ecosystem is rapidly growing. Across this ecosystem, new concepts often emerge through software artefacts accompanying scientific publications as well as through sustained development in larger communities. However, many repositories receive development efforts only over a limited period of time, raising the question whether their concepts persist beyond individual repositories. In this paper, we apply established empirical software engineering techniques to analyse a set of foundational quantum software repositories. We combine cross-repository activity with contributor relationships to study the evolution of communities. Our analysis provides empirical evidence of contributor migration patterns and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. We observe multiple development paths: projects may evolve into sustained communities, contributors may integrate concepts into established ecosystems, or activity may continue through new and follow-up software artefacts. Our observations provide an initial empirical perspective on how concepts and influence persist across repository boundaries in quantum software ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes quantum software repositories using empirical software engineering techniques to study contributor migration patterns, knowledge transfer, and how concepts persist across repository boundaries, finding that projects may evolve into sustained communities, integrate into established ecosystems, or continue through new software artefacts.
AI.motivation: To understand how concepts and influence persist beyond individual repositories in the rapidly growing quantum software ecosystem, given that many repositories receive only limited development effort over time.
AI.method: Applied established empirical software engineering techniques to analyze foundational quantum software repositories by combining cross-repository activity data with contributor relationship analysis to study community evolution.
AI.result: Provided empirical evidence of contributor migration patterns and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. Identified multiple development paths: evolution into sustained communities, integration into established ecosystems, or continuation through new and follow-up software artefacts.
AI.conclusion: Concepts and influence persist across repository boundaries in quantum software ecosystems through various development paths, offering an initial empirical perspective on community evolution in this domain.

title: OPERA: Offline Policy-guided Expert Routing and Adaptation for Universal Biomedical Image Analysis
summary: Biomedical image analysis spans diverse modalities and tasks, yet real-world deployment is hindered by severe distribution shifts across scanners, protocols, and patient populations. High-performing models consequently require repeated domain-specific fine-tuning, which is a costly cycle that becomes impractical when labels are scarce or privacy constraints limit data sharing. We propose OPERA (Offline Policy-guided Expert Routing and Adaptation), a multi-agent ensemble framework that addresses this deployment bottleneck by treating expert weight assignment as an offline policy learning problem: a routing policy is learned from a small validation set without gradient updates to any expert agent, then deployed with test-time adaptation to handle distribution shift. OPERA coordinates heterogeneous specialist agents through complementary mechanisms. The expert profiling module learns selection policies offline, enabling informed allocation of expertise. Each agent undergoes confidence calibration through temperature adjustment, ensuring more reliable probabilistic outputs. OPERA also incorporates distribution aware adaptation, where class weights are dynamically adjusted at the batch level using statistics derived from unlabeled test data. Instance level routing assigns each sample to the most suitable expert by leveraging inter model agreement and predictive entropy. We evaluate OPERA on 9 datasets covering fundus photography, chest X-ray, CT, MRI, and multimodal diagnostic benchmarks, comparing against 30+ baselines across classification, segmentation, and multimodal settings. OPERA consistently improves performance and calibration quality, demonstrating that offline policy-guided expert agents coordination is a practical path to deployable biomedical AI without retraining. Code is on \href{https://github.com/HUANGLIZI/OPERA}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: OPERA is a multi-agent ensemble framework that uses offline policy learning to route biomedical images to specialized expert models, enabling deployment without retraining across diverse imaging modalities and distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Biomedical image analysis faces severe distribution shifts across scanners, protocols, and populations, making high-performing models require repeated domain-specific fine-tuning that is costly, impractical with scarce labels, and constrained by privacy limitations.
AI.method: OPERA treats expert weight assignment as offline policy learning: a routing policy learned from a small validation set without gradient updates to experts. It includes expert profiling (offline selection policy learning), confidence calibration via temperature adjustment, distribution-aware adaptation (dynamic class weight adjustment at batch level), and instance-level routing using inter-model agreement and predictive entropy.
AI.result: Evaluated on 9 datasets (fundus photography, chest X-ray, CT, MRI, multimodal) against 30+ baselines across classification, segmentation, and multimodal settings, OPERA consistently improves performance and calibration quality.
AI.conclusion: Offline policy-guided expert agent coordination is a practical path to deployable biomedical AI without retraining.

title: Calibrated Partial Resets: Preventing Policy Collapse in Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Neural networks are hindered by accumulating dormant neurons and loss of expressivity throughout training, particularly in non-stationary data settings, such as continual supervised and reinforcement learning. Recently, neuron resets have been used to maintain gradient flow and restore plasticity. However, full unit reinitialization often sacrifices peak performance and can destabilize training, leading to policy collapse.
  To preserve plasticity without destabilizing training, we propose Calibrated Partial Resets (CPR), an optimizer that periodically pulls low-utility neurons toward their initialization, with pull strength scaled by each neuron's utility. Unlike binary reset methods, partial resets avoid brittleness; unlike uniform decay, calibrated utility-scaling concentrates adjustment on the units that need it most.
  Among compared methods, only CPR avoids policy collapse over 400M training steps in SlipperyAnt, and it outperforms prior decay and reset-based methods on Continual MetaWorld and Continual MinAtar benchmarks. Ablations reveal a tunable trade-off between plasticity and peak performance, highlighting utility-scaled reinitialization as a promising direction for continual learning.

AI.tldr: Calibrated Partial Resets (CPR) periodically pulls low-utility neurons toward initialization with utility-scaled strength, preserving plasticity without the destabilization of full resets, and avoids policy collapse over 400M steps while outperforming prior methods on continual learning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Neural networks lose expressivity due to dormant neurons in non-stationary settings (continual learning, RL). Existing fixes like full neuron resets maintain gradient flow but sacrifice peak performance and risk policy collapse.
AI.method: CPR is an optimizer that periodically pulls low-utility neurons toward their initialization, with pull strength scaled by each neuron's utility, avoiding the brittleness of binary resets and focusing adjustment on the most affected units.
AI.result: Only CPR avoids policy collapse over 400M training steps in SlipperyAnt; outperforms prior decay and reset-based methods on Continual MetaWorld and Continual MinAtar; ablations show a tunable trade-off between plasticity and peak performance.
AI.conclusion: Utility-scaled reinitialization is a promising direction for continual learning, offering a tunable balance between maintaining plasticity and preserving peak performance.

title: Right-sizing Recommendations (RSR): Cloud Workload Conformal Prediction for Virtual Machines in Data Center Operations
comment: 10 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2025 IEEE/WIC International Conference on Web Intelligence and Intelligent Agent Technology (WI-IAT 2025). Author Accepted Manuscript
summary:
Managing cloud infrastructure efficiently, especially in environments of large cloud providers or hyperscalers, requires optimizing the use of physical resources to minimize costs and maximize performance. Selecting the right virtual machine (VM) sizes is crucial to achieving cost efficiency in these dynamic environments. However, traditional VM allocation and scheduling approaches often fail to account for the fluctuating and unpredictable nature of VM utilization, leading to inefficiencies such as over- or under-provisioning of resources. High-quality interval prediction helps accurately capture uncertainty in cloud resource demand and supports cloud operators in efficient instance provisioning.
  As an effective and reliable framework for constructing prediction intervals (PIs), conformal prediction (CP) is used for mid- and long-term forecasting tasks in cloud computing environments. This study proposes a new data-driven PI construction approach using bootstrapping conformal prediction for modern, dynamic, data-driven Right-sizing Recommendations (RSR) to enhance provisioning for diverse application workloads on hyperscalers. By learning workload utilization patterns, identifying correlations across multiple time series, and predicting medium- to long-term utilization trends, this research seeks to improve the efficiency of cloud and data center operations through an AI/ML-based provisioning pipeline.
  Our study demonstrates that AI-driven models, powered by machine learning regression techniques and evaluated using backtesting, achieve promising forecasting results for cloud resource utilization. Additionally, we rank the selected models to identify top-performing approaches for long-life VM candidates. The proposed framework enhances right-sizing recommendations and supports more cost-effective resource allocation in dynamic cloud environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a data-driven prediction interval construction approach using bootstrapping conformal prediction for VM right-sizing recommendations in hyperscale cloud environments, aiming to improve resource provisioning efficiency by capturing utilization uncertainty through AI/ML-based forecasting.
AI.motivation: Traditional VM allocation and scheduling approaches fail to account for fluctuating and unpredictable VM utilization, causing over- or under-provisioning. High-quality interval prediction is needed to capture uncertainty in cloud resource demand for efficient instance provisioning.
AI.method: The study uses bootstrapping conformal prediction (CP) to construct prediction intervals for mid- and long-term forecasting. It employs AI/ML regression techniques with backtesting, learning workload utilization patterns, identifying cross-time-series correlations, and predicting utilization trends to generate right-sizing recommendations (RSR).
AI.result: AI-driven regression models evaluated via backtesting achieve promising forecasting results for cloud resource utilization. Selected models are ranked to identify top-performing approaches for long-life VM candidates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enhances right-sizing recommendations and supports more cost-effective resource allocation in dynamic cloud environments by leveraging conformal prediction for uncertainty-aware provisioning.

title: Input Relation Prompting for Metamorphic Testing on Query-Based Systems
summary: Testing query-based systems (QBSs) presents significant challenges due to the absence of ground truth for validation and the extensive time and effort required for manual testing. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing an approach that assists testers in identifying metamorphic relations (MRs) for metamorphic testing (MT) instead of solely and exhaustively relying on prerequisite domain knowledge. MT is an approach rising in popularity employed to alleviate the oracle problem by applying input transformation rules (MRs) to a program. The proposed approach helps the tester by prompting MRs that describe the relationships between inputs and outputs, enabling fault detection when the expected relationship is not met. Unlike traditional testing approaches, this approach does not rely on pre-defined test cases or concrete ground truth, making it suitable for the testing of real-world QBSs. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be combined with other testing methods such as combinatorial testing and fuzz testing, expanding the possibilities for QBS testing. A conducted case study of a real-world web application demonstrates the applicability and potential of the proposed approach. Overall, this research contributes to advancing the field of metamorphic testing and provides a valuable tool for QBS testers to enhance their testing efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an approach to help testers identify metamorphic relations (MRs) for metamorphic testing (MT) of query-based systems (QBSs), addressing the oracle problem without requiring ground truth. A case study on a real-world web application demonstrates its applicability and potential.
AI.motivation: Testing QBSs is challenging due to the lack of ground truth and the high cost of manual testing. Existing MT approaches rely heavily on domain knowledge to define MRs, which is a bottleneck.
AI.method: The approach assists testers in identifying MRs for MT by prompting input-output relationships, rather than exhaustively relying on domain knowledge. It can be combined with combinatorial testing and fuzz testing.
AI.result: A case study on a real-world web application demonstrates the applicability and potential of the proposed approach for QBS testing.
AI.conclusion: The approach advances MT by reducing reliance on domain knowledge for MR identification, providing a valuable tool to enhance testing efficiency for query-based systems.

title: LENS: Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Zooming for Keyframe Sampling in Long-Form Videos
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project page: https://zhangce01.github.io/LENS/
summary: Despite rapid progress in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), understanding long-form videos is still bottlenecked by limited context windows. While recent keyframe sampling methods attempt to mitigate this by distilling video inputs into a compact set of query-relevant frames, navigating the vast spatio-temporal search space remains challenging, as spatial detail and temporal coverage often conflict. To address this, we introduce LENS, a training-free keyframe sampling framework that dynamically decides when to zoom in for fine-grained details and when to zoom out for broader context based on the text query. Concretely, LENS adaptively allocates a limited frame budget between spatial zoom-ins, which highlight query-relevant regions within individual frames, and temporal zoom-outs, which expand the temporal scope through multi-frame aggregation, enabling the model to reason across multiple granularities while capturing both high-fidelity details and long-range context. Across diverse long-form video benchmarks, LENS consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art keyframe sampling methods and delivers substantial gains over uniform sampling, improving Video-MME accuracy from 53.3% to 60.7% with Qwen2.5-VL.Code is available at https://github.com/zhangce01/LENS.

AI.tldr: LENS is a training-free keyframe sampling framework for MLLMs that dynamically allocates a limited frame budget between spatial zoom-ins (query-relevant regions within frames) and temporal zoom-outs (multi-frame aggregation for broader context), outperforming prior methods and improving Video-MME accuracy from 53.3% to 60.7% with Qwen2.5-VL.
AI.motivation: Long-form video understanding in MLLMs is bottlenecked by limited context windows. Keyframe sampling methods must navigate the conflict between spatial detail and temporal coverage when distilling videos into query-relevant frames.
AI.method: LENS is a training-free framework that dynamically decides between spatial zoom-ins (highlighting query-relevant regions within individual frames) and temporal zoom-outs (expanding temporal scope via multi-frame aggregation), adaptively allocating a limited frame budget across granularities to capture both fine-grained details and long-range context.
AI.result: LENS consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art keyframe sampling methods across diverse long-form video benchmarks, and delivers substantial gains over uniform sampling, improving Video-MME accuracy from 53.3% to 60.7% with Qwen2.5-VL.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive spatial-temporal allocation in keyframe sampling effectively resolves the conflict between detail and coverage, enabling training-free improvements in long-form video understanding with MLLMs.

title: Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference
summary: Large language model (LLM) cascades reduce inference cost by routing easy queries to a small model and deferring hard queries to a larger one. Production cascades govern this deferral through a confidence threshold, but LLM confidence scores are miscalibrated, the threshold must be tuned per model pair and per domain, and no setting yields a formal bound on cascade accuracy. We introduce \textbf{Conformal Cascade} (CC), a multi-tier inference framework that uses conformal prediction set size as the deferral rule: accept when the calibrated set collapses to a single answer, defer otherwise. The procedure delivers a distribution-free, finite-sample accuracy guarantee. By a per-tier union bound, the prediction set at the accepting tier covers the correct answer with probability at least $1 - Kα$ for any user-specified $α$; under a selection-preservation condition (consistent with, but not strictly implied by, our marginal coverage results), the bound tightens to $1 - α$. We further characterise expected cascade cost as an explicit function of $α$ and the calibration-set acceptance rate. Across 18 multiple-choice benchmarks spanning science, medicine, commonsense, and standardized exams, evaluated on two-tier cascades drawn from four open-weight model families, CC strictly improves over the strongest calibration-tuned heuristic cascade on the majority of family--benchmark pairs, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks where majority vote is unreliable; on easier benchmarks the cascade commits the vast majority of queries to the small model at no accuracy cost. Extension to open-ended generation requires an answer-clustering step that we leave for future work. The method requires no model training and only black-box API access.

AI.tldr: Conformal Cascade (CC) is a multi-tier LLM inference framework that uses conformal prediction set size as a deferral rule, providing distribution-free, finite-sample accuracy guarantees while reducing inference cost. It outperforms calibration-tuned heuristic cascades across 18 multiple-choice benchmarks using four model families.
AI.motivation: LLM cascades reduce inference cost but suffer from miscalibrated confidence scores, requiring per-model-pair and per-domain threshold tuning, and offer no formal accuracy bound.
AI.method: Conformal Cascade uses conformal prediction set size as the deferral rule: accept when the calibrated prediction set collapses to a single answer, defer otherwise. It provides a per-tier union bound guaranteeing coverage of at least 1-Kα, with a tighter 1-α bound under selection-preservation condition.
AI.result: CC strictly outperforms strongest calibration-tuned heuristic cascades on most model-benchmark pairs across 18 multiple-choice benchmarks and four model families, with largest gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks. On easier benchmarks, most queries are committed to the small model with no accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: Conformal Cascade delivers distribution-free accuracy guarantees with reduced inference cost, requires no model training, and only black-box API access. Extension to open-ended generation requires future work on answer clustering.

title: Atmospheric Diffusion-Guided Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Nuclear Radiation Forecasting
summary: Nuclear radiation, the energy released during atomic decay, poses persistent risks to public health and the environment, and concerns have only grown since the Fukushima accident and the recent commencement of treated-water discharge. Modern monitoring networks now record radiation levels and accompanying weather conditions at thousands of stations, opening the door to nationwide forecasting that can inform emergency response, agricultural advisories, and routine public-safety decisions. However, turning this abundance of monitoring data into reliable forecasts is difficult for three reasons. First, the time series at each station are highly non-stationary, shaped by radioactive decay, weather variability, and irregular human interventions. Second, monitoring stations are severely unevenly distributed in space. Roughly 78% of Japan's stations sit in less than 6% of the country, clustered near Fukushima, which breaks the assumptions of standard graph-based models. Third, radiation co-evolves with heterogeneous context such as wind, temperature, and humidity through atmospheric transport processes that purely data-driven models struggle to capture from observations alone. In this study, we introduce NRFormer+, a spatio-temporal Transformer for nationwide nuclear radiation forecasting. NRFormer+ couples non-stationary temporal attention and density-adaptive spatial attention with a new atmospheric diffusion module that estimates how meteorology drives radiation dispersion and injects this physical signal into the network as an architectural prior. NRFormer+ delivers state-of-the-art accuracy on both datasets across all 13 baselines, reducing sudden-change MAE by up to 19.1% over the strongest baseline at comparable inference latency. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/tfeilyu/NRFormer_Plus.

AI.tldr: NRFormer+ is a spatio-temporal Transformer for nationwide nuclear radiation forecasting that addresses non-stationary time series, uneven station distribution, and physics-coupled atmospheric transport, achieving state-of-the-art results with up to 19.1% reduction in sudden-change MAE.
AI.motivation: Nuclear radiation poses persistent risks to public health and the environment, especially post-Fukushima. While modern monitoring networks generate abundant data, reliable nationwide forecasting remains challenging due to non-stationary time series, severely uneven spatial distribution of stations (78% in <6% of Japan), and complex atmospheric transport processes that pure data-driven models fail to capture.
AI.method: NRFormer+ is a spatio-temporal Transformer that couples (1) non-stationary temporal attention to handle shifting time series dynamics, (2) density-adaptive spatial attention to address uneven station distribution, and (3) an atmospheric diffusion module that estimates meteorology-driven radiation dispersion and injects physical signals as architectural priors.
AI.result: NRFormer+ achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on all 13 baselines across two datasets, reducing sudden-change MAE by up to 19.1% over the strongest baseline with comparable inference latency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed physically-informed Transformer architecture effectively addresses the key challenges in nationwide nuclear radiation forecasting, demonstrating that coupling domain-specific physical priors (atmospheric diffusion) with adaptive attention mechanisms yields superior forecasting performance.

title: SkillGate: Cost Efficient Runtime Malicious Skill File Detection in Coding Agents
summary: Software engineering teams now deploy AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) as first-class productivity tools, installing domain-specific skill files to tailor agent behavior to project APIs, framework conventions, and organizational workflows. These complex Markdown files are easily downloaded from public registries with a single npx skills add command and no real security screening, representing a novel supply-chain attack surface: a malicious skill file can silently reprogram agent behavior, exfiltrating credentials, injecting backdoors into generated code, or redirecting agent actions to attacker-controlled endpoints. The threat is not hypothetical: recent reports document hundreds of malicious skill packages in public registries, including organized campaigns that distributed credential-stealing infostealers via fake productivity skills. No systematic toolchain defense exists for this attack surface. We present SkillGate, a deployable security gateway that screens AI skill packages before coding agent installation. SkillGate uses a hybrid regex-prefilter + LLM-judge pipeline: safe-signal files bypass the LLM entirely (skip savings); flagged files have only their matched snippet windows sent to the judge, not the full content (snippet savings). We answer four research questions covering detection effectiveness, screening cost, runtime overhead, and false positive behavior on the SkillsBench benchmark against two existing tools. On SkillsBench (n=1,650, 9.1% malicious), SkillGate achieves F1=0.817, FPR=1.13% while reducing LLM input tokens by 77% vs. full-file screening, and outperforming existing tools by 5-6x on threshold-independent AUPRC (0.830 vs. 0.144/0.162).

AI.tldr: SkillGate is a security gateway that screens AI coding agent skill packages (Markdown files) before installation, using a hybrid regex-prefilter + LLM-judge pipeline. It achieves F1=0.817, FPR=1.13% on SkillsBench (n=1,650, 9.1% malicious), reducing LLM input tokens by 77% vs. full-file screening and outperforming existing tools by 5-6x on AUPRC.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot) now install domain-specific skill Markdown files from public registries with minimal security screening. This creates a novel supply-chain attack surface where malicious skill files can silently reprogram agent behavior to exfiltrate credentials, inject backdoors, or redirect to attacker-controlled endpoints, with hundreds of malicious packages already documented in the wild.
AI.method: SkillGate uses a hybrid regex-prefilter + LLM-judge pipeline. Safe-signal files bypass the LLM entirely (skip savings), while flagged files have only matched snippet windows sent to the judge (snippet savings), reducing LLM input tokens by 77% vs. full-file screening.
AI.result: On SkillsBench (n=1,650, 9.1% malicious), SkillGate achieves F1=0.817, FPR=1.13%, reduces LLM input tokens by 77%, and outperforms existing tools by 5-6x on AUPRC (0.830 vs. 0.144/0.162).
AI.conclusion: No systematic toolchain defense existed for this novel attack surface prior to SkillGate. The results demonstrate effective detection with low false positive rates and substantial cost savings via the hybrid screening pipeline.

title: FIDAC: An Easy-to-use Pipeline to Extract and Interpret Interpersonal Distance From Video
summary: The distance between persons reveals significant information about their perception of each other. However, such information is not easily extractable and interpretable from video input. We developed an open-sourced library, Facial Interpersonal Distance Analysis and Coding (FIDAC) that transforms facial detection results into actionable data about location and interpersonal distance. This tool merges data from multiple open-source facial detection models, strategically compensating for gaps in any individual model. In addition, we include methods for more accurate tracking, such as a pipeline for human coding of the selection of faces and a benchmarking tool to reduce depth distortion. For next steps, we plan on building upon FIDAC by evaluating its effectiveness at measuring interpersonal distance at various depths and orientations while further integrating features of proxemic analysis such as synchrony into its software.

AI.tldr: FIDAC is an open-source library that transforms facial detection data into actionable interpersonal distance information by merging multiple detection models and providing human coding and benchmarking tools.
AI.motivation: Interpersonal distance reveals significant information about perception, but is difficult to extract and interpret from video input.
AI.method: The library merges data from multiple open-source facial detection models to compensate for individual model gaps, includes human coding pipelines for accurate tracking, and provides a benchmarking tool to reduce depth distortion.
AI.result: Developed FIDAC, an open-sourced library that transforms facial detection results into actionable location and interpersonal distance data.
AI.conclusion: Future work includes evaluating effectiveness at various depths and orientations and integrating proxemic analysis features such as synchrony.

title: Lantern: Conflict-Aware Gradient Blending for Physics-Guided Diffusion Models in Calorimeter Simulation
summary: Monte Carlo simulation of calorimeter showers is a principal bottleneck for the High-Luminosity LHC, and diffusion models have emerged as fast, high-fidelity surrogates. Their denoising objective is purely statistical, however: a model can minimize it while placing the physics wrong. Existing physics-informed generative methods cannot close this gap, because they assume a closed-form law, a governing PDE residual or a hard per-sample constraint, that a shower does not supply: no per-sample PDE governs a stochastic cascade, and energy conservation fixes only one scalar per shower. Standard metrics ignore the correlation structure across calorimeter layers and voxels, comparing showers only in a physics feature space. We address both gaps. We introduce the Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD), a single normalized score for correlation fidelity at layer-wise and voxel-wise scales. We then encode the soft per-sample structure available in a shower as two physics-aware auxiliary losses: a variance-stabilized voxel residual loss grounded in counting statistics, and a graph Laplacian loss over the detector geometry. We combine both with denoising through GradBlend, which anchors the step magnitude to the denoising gradient while letting the auxiliary steer its direction, yielding Lantern, a physics-guided diffusion surrogate. On CaloChallenge Dataset 2, injecting the physics losses through task-symmetric rules such as PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, and ConFIG inflates FPD by 2-100x relative to denoising alone, whereas GradBlend admits the same signal without regression and, with the Laplacian loss, Lantern improves both FPD and CFD. Our ablation on the auxiliary loss scheduler shows that the voxel residual loss, whose gradient conflicts with denoising, requires a terminal denoising-only phase to preserve shower fidelity, whereas the non-conflicting Laplacian loss is insensitive to the schedule.

AI.tldr: Lantern is a physics-guided diffusion model for calorimeter shower simulation that uses GradBlend (combining denoising with auxiliary physics losses) and introduces the Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD) metric. It outperforms standard multi-task balancing methods on CaloChallenge Dataset 2, achieving better FPD and CFD by using a graph Laplacian loss and a carefully scheduled voxel residual loss.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo simulation of calorimeter showers is a bottleneck for High-Luminosity LHC. Diffusion models offer fast surrogates but their denoising objective is purely statistical and can place physics incorrectly. Existing physics-informed methods assume closed-form laws or PDE residuals not applicable to stochastic showers. Standard metrics also ignore correlation structure across layers and voxels.
AI.method: Introduces Correlation Frobenius Distance (CFD) for evaluating correlation fidelity. Proposes two physics-aware auxiliary losses: (1) variance-stabilized voxel residual loss based on counting statistics, (2) graph Laplacian loss over detector geometry. Combines these with denoising via GradBlend, which anchors step magnitude to denoising gradient while steering direction with auxiliary losses. Compares against PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, and ConFIG on CaloChallenge Dataset 2.
AI.result: Standard multi-task methods (PCGrad, GradNorm, IMTL-G, ConFIG) inflate FPD by 2-100x when injecting physics losses. GradBlend avoids this regression. With the Laplacian loss, Lantern improves both FPD and CFD. The voxel residual loss requires a terminal denoising-only phase due to gradient conflict, while the non-conflicting Laplacian loss is schedule-insensitive.
AI.conclusion: GradBlend enables effective physics guidance for diffusion models in domains lacking per-sample PDE constraints. The CFD metric and physics-aware losses (especially graph Laplacian) improve correlation fidelity without sacrificing generative quality, with careful scheduling needed for conflicting auxiliary objectives.

title: Steering topology distributions for unified generative design of architected metamaterials
summary: Architected metamaterials derive their functions from structure, creating vast opportunities to program physical responses through topology design. However, existing design methods are often tailored to individual design problems, making limited use of topology knowledge for effective and broadly applicable design as objectives, constraints, and physical functions change. Here we introduce Generative Topology Optimization (GenTO), a unified framework that turns a learned topology prior into a reusable design engine. GenTO trains a diffusion model on a large full-order topology dataset and then iteratively steers the resulting topology distribution toward task-specific high-performing regions using user-defined physical objectives and constraints. This shifts the object of optimization from a single structure to a task-adapted topology distribution. Across topology design problems spanning thermal extremization, multi-objective morphology control, property-targeted auxetic design, and vibration transmission design, GenTO reuses pretrained topology priors for heterogeneous tasks, preserves structural diversity, and reaches high-performing solutions supported by numerical benchmarks and experimental validation. These results establish reusable topology knowledge as a unified principle for effective and scalable architected metamaterial design.

AI.tldr: GenTO is a unified framework that trains a diffusion model on topology data and steers it toward task-specific high-performing designs, enabling reusable topology knowledge across diverse metamaterial design problems.
AI.motivation: Existing topology optimization methods are tailored to individual design problems, lacking reusability and broad applicability when objectives, constraints, or physical functions change.
AI.method: GenTO trains a diffusion model on large full-order topology datasets, then iteratively steers the learned topology distribution toward task-specific high-performing regions using user-defined physical objectives and constraints, shifting optimization from a single structure to a task-adapted topology distribution.
AI.result: Across thermal extremization, multi-objective morphology control, property-targeted auxetic design, and vibration transmission, GenTO reuses pretrained priors, preserves structural diversity, and achieves high-performing solutions validated by benchmarks and experiments.
AI.conclusion: Reusable topology knowledge serves as a unified principle for effective and scalable architected metamaterial design.

title: An Empirical Study of Model Context Protocol Applications
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how large language model applications communicate with external tools, but leaves the application side unspecified: unlike traditional dependencies resolved through package managers, developers integrating MCP servers face no conventions for configuration, communication, or human oversight. This ecosystem is also under-researched, with existing work focused on servers rather than the applications consuming them. We conduct a large-scale study of 1,723 MCPApps mined from GitHub. We first derive MCPAppTax from a representative sample, then use an LLM-assisted pipeline to apply it across the full dataset, characterizing server integration across configuration, SDK use, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms. Our results show that the ecosystem has converged on some practices but not others: most MCPApps configure servers using files (85.2%) and use an official SDK (81.1%) to communicate with servers, yet no naming convention has emerged for configuration files. Human oversight diverges most, logging (90.8%) and enable/disable controls (77.2%) are common, but only 37.2% gate tool execution behind a blocking approval step, leaving the LLM able to invoke any enabled tool unconditionally in most MCPApps.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 1,723 MCPApps from GitHub to characterize how LLM applications integrate external tools via the Model Context Protocol. It finds convergence on some practices (85.2% use config files, 81.1% use official SDKs) but divergence on others (no naming conventions, only 37.2% implement blocking approval for tool execution).
AI.motivation: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes communication between LLM applications and external tools but leaves the application side unspecified—no conventions exist for configuration, communication, or human oversight. The ecosystem is under-researched, with prior work focusing on servers rather than consuming applications.
AI.method: Large-scale empirical study of 1,723 MCPApps mined from GitHub. First derived MCPAppTax from a representative sample, then applied an LLM-assisted pipeline to classify the full dataset across three dimensions: configuration, SDK use, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms.
AI.result: Most MCPApps configure servers via files (85.2%) and use official SDKs (81.1%). No naming convention exists for config files. Human oversight is highly variable: 90.8% log events, 77.2% have enable/disable controls, but only 37.2% gate tool execution behind a blocking approval step, meaning most apps allow unconditional LLM-triggered tool invocation.
AI.conclusion: The MCP ecosystem has converged on some practices but not others. The lack of blocking approval in the majority of MCPApps raises security and control concerns, suggesting a need for better design conventions for human-in-the-loop mechanisms in LLM tool-use applications.

title: OpenPVMapper: A Multi-source, Nationwide Database of Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems in France
summary: Rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems account for the vast majority of PV grid connections, yet no open, comprehensive, installation-level dataset of these systems exists: public registries aggregate data only above a capacity threshold, and remote sensing-based detection efforts, while extensive, are typically confined to a single method, a limited geographic scope, or a single point in time. We introduce OpenPVMapper, a nationwide, multi-source database of rooftop PV installations in mainland France, built by aggregating and reconciling complementary sources: a deep learning-based detection pipeline deployed on nationwide aerial imagery, OpenStreetMap and a probabilistic building-level detection dataset. The resulting database contains 1,135,850 installations, totaling approximately 15.01~GWp of installed capacity, each documented with its provenance, detection method, and, where available, a manual validation flag. Manual review of a stratified sample of 1,862 installations places the database's overall precision at approximately 74--75\%, with corroboration across independent sources bringing a substantial, quantified precision gain. By aggregating independent sources rather than relying on any single detection method, OpenPVMapper reaches a level of confidence beyond what any one source could provide on its own, while remaining extensible to further sources as they become available. It is released under an open (CC-BY) license alongside the full source code used to build it.

AI.tldr: OpenPVMapper is a nationwide, multi-source database of rooftop PV installations in mainland France, built by aggregating deep learning-based aerial imagery detection, OpenStreetMap, and probabilistic building-level detection. It contains 1,135,850 installations (~15.01 GWp) with ~74-75% precision, released under CC-BY license with full source code.
AI.motivation: No open, comprehensive, installation-level dataset of rooftop PV systems exists; public registries are threshold-limited and remote sensing efforts are typically confined to a single method, limited geographic scope, or single point in time.
AI.method: Aggregation and reconciliation of complementary sources: a deep learning-based detection pipeline on nationwide aerial imagery, OpenStreetMap, and a probabilistic building-level detection dataset, with manual validation flags and provenance tracking.
AI.result: Database contains 1,135,850 installations totaling ~15.01 GWp; overall precision ~74-75% based on stratified manual review of 1,862 installations; corroboration across independent sources provides quantified precision gains.
AI.conclusion: Aggregating independent sources achieves confidence beyond any single detection method, and the framework remains extensible to further sources. OpenPVMapper is released as open data (CC-BY) with full source code.

title: Score-Based Stabilization for Time-Dependent Problems
summary: We propose a score-based stabilization framework for numerical simulation of partial differential equations, in which a learned score model defines a stabilization operator applied to provisional numerical updates. This operator augments standard time-stepping schemes by enforcing structure and physical consistency through a correction that drives iterates toward the manifold of admissible states. We show that the stabilization operator acts as a contraction toward this manifold, yielding a correction mechanism with basin-conditional stability. Numerical experiments on Advection, Korteweg-de Vries (KdV), Nonlinear Schrodinger (NLS), and Burgers' equations demonstrate improved robustness, suppression of nonphysical instabilities, and preservation of qualitative dynamics.

AI.tldr: A score-based stabilization framework that uses learned score models to enforce physical consistency in numerical PDE solvers, demonstrating improved stability and robustness across multiple equations.
AI.motivation: Numerical simulations of PDEs often suffer from nonphysical instabilities and drift away from admissible state manifolds, requiring stabilization techniques that preserve physical structure and dynamics.
AI.method: The framework integrates a learned score model as a stabilization operator that corrects provisional numerical updates, contracting iterates toward the manifold of admissible states within time-stepping schemes.
AI.result: Experiments on Advection, KdV, NLS, and Burgers' equations show improved robustness, suppression of nonphysical instabilities, and preservation of qualitative dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The score-based stabilization operator provides basin-conditional stability and effectively enforces physical consistency, offering a promising approach for robust PDE simulation.

title: HOBA: Hierarchical On-Policy Bidding Agents for Adaptive Online Advertising
summary: Online advertising bidding systems typically deploy multiple offline-trained expert models (e.g., PID controllers, model predictive control, offline RL policies) but face two critical limitations: lack of online adaptability to non-stationary auction markets, and reliance on costly manual tuning of hyperparameters such as bid bounds and budget pacing constraints. We propose HOBA (Hierarchical On-policy Bidding Agents), a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that decouples strategic reasoning, model selection, and bid execution across three time scales. At the high level, a large language model infers hyperparameters from contextual signals through a Think-Act-Observe-Reflect loop with historical experience retrieval. At the mid level, a SARSA agent dynamically selects among expert models, incorporating causal adjustment to eliminate selection bias. At the low level, a dynamic expert pool (PID, MPC, IQL, Decision Transformer) executes bids under high-level constraints. This design confines online learning to discrete expert selection rather than continuous bid optimization, significantly reducing exploration risk while maintaining adaptability. Experiments on the AuctionNet benchmark and a large-scale A/B test demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. In a large-scale online deployment, HOBA delivered substantial business value, achieving a +3.6\% increase in target cost, proving the effectiveness of our hierarchical multi-agent bidding paradigm.

AI.tldr: HOBA is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that uses a three-level architecture (LLM hyperparameter tuning, SARSA expert selection, dynamic expert pool) to enable online adaptability in advertising bidding systems, achieving +3.6% target cost improvement in large-scale deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing offline-trained bidding models (PID, MPC, RL) lack online adaptability to non-stationary auction markets and require costly manual hyperparameter tuning.
AI.method: Three-level hierarchy: (1) High-level LLM infers hyperparameters via Think-Act-Observe-Reflect with retrieval; (2) Mid-level SARSA agent selects experts with causal adjustment for bias elimination; (3) Low-level dynamic expert pool (PID, MPC, IQL, Decision Transformer) executes bids under constraints. Online learning confined to discrete expert selection to reduce exploration risk.
AI.result: Outperforms SOTA baselines on AuctionNet benchmark and large-scale A/B test; +3.6% target cost increase in online deployment.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical multi-agent bidding paradigm proves effective for real-world advertising systems, balancing adaptability with safe exploration through discrete expert selection.

title: KQFuzz: Knowledge-Guided Fuzzing for Quantum Libraries via Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering. 17 pages, 9 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: As quantum computing continually improves, ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum libraries has become increasingly critical. To this end, many LLM-based fuzzing approaches towards quantum libraries have been proposed to uncover potential bugs. However, these methods still suffer from limitations such as insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, which hinder the progress of the quantum computing field. To address these challenges, we propose KQFuzz, a novel knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries. It leverages comprehensive codebase knowledge to ground LLM-based test generation, synergizing this with fitness-guided evaluation and two-level mutations to explore complex execution paths and trigger potential bugs. Firstly, KQFuzz introduces a novel prompting scheme tailored to quantum programs, which strategically incorporates knowledge of the codebase to efficiently generate high-quality quantum seed programs. Moreover, we develop evaluation and mutation strategies to handle the generated seed programs, facilitating efficient fuzzing execution while further enriching the diversity of the resulting test cases. We implement KQFuzz and conduct fuzzing on three popular quantum libraries, including Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, with coverage improved by up to 18.44%. During the development of KQFuzz, we discovered 13 bugs, all of which have been confirmed and 12 have already been fixed by the developers.

AI.tldr: KQFuzz is a knowledge-guided fuzzer for quantum libraries that uses LLMs with codebase knowledge and fitness-guided mutation to generate test programs, improving coverage by up to 18.44% and finding 13 confirmed bugs in Qiskit, PennyLane, and Cirq.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based fuzzing approaches for quantum libraries suffer from insufficient flexibility and low efficiency, hindering progress in ensuring quantum library reliability.
AI.method: KQFuzz combines (1) a novel prompting scheme incorporating codebase knowledge to generate high-quality quantum seed programs, (2) fitness-guided evaluation, and (3) two-level mutation strategies to explore complex execution paths and trigger bugs.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods with coverage improved by up to 18.44%; discovered 13 bugs (12 fixed).
AI.conclusion: KQFuzz demonstrates that knowledge-guided LLM-based fuzzing with tailored prompting and mutation strategies effectively improves test coverage and bug discovery in quantum libraries.

title: OrganLens: Organ-Specific Representation Learning for CT Foundation Models
summary: A CT examination captures multiple organs, but many biomedical questions concern abnormalities, prognosis, or longitudinal change in a specific organ. These questions require a separate representation for each organ within the same CT volume. Existing CT foundation models commonly produce a single volume-level representation, while recent anatomy-aware methods either encode pre-separated organ volumes or explicitly disentangle images into organ token groups. The former may remove clinically relevant surrounding context, while the latter does not condition a shared encoder on a selected organ before its features are formed. We introduce OrganLens for organ-specific representation learning through self-supervision. An organ identity conditions a shared CT encoder, while organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision shape features for anatomy-weighted pooling into organ-specific representations. At inference, the shared model produces 11 organ-specific representations without external segmentation masks. We evaluate OrganLens on CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT, INSPECT, and NLST across diverse acquisitions and downstream evaluations. Relative to CT-pretrained DINOv2, heart representations raise CT-RATE cardiomegaly AUROC from 0.910 to 0.953, while lung representations improve the Harrell C-index for NLST lung-cancer mortality by 14.2\%. The global representation reaches INSPECT Recall@10 of 33.09\% and 32.04\% for text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval, respectively. Across organ-related tasks, anatomically matched representations provide stronger task-relevant signal, while the global representation retains broad utility. OrganLens offers a scalable approach to organ-specific CT representation learning with a shared encoder. More broadly, it provides the medical research community with a reusable framework for studying organ-specific disease across cohorts and clinical endpoints.

AI.tldr: OrganLens learns organ-specific CT representations via self-supervision using a shared encoder conditioned on organ identity, enabling 11 organ-specific representations without external segmentation masks at inference, outperforming global representations on organ-specific tasks while retaining broad utility.
AI.motivation: Existing CT foundation models produce single volume-level representations unsuited for organ-specific questions, while anatomy-aware methods either remove clinical context by pre-separating organs or fail to condition the encoder on a selected organ before feature formation.
AI.method: A shared CT encoder is conditioned on organ identity; organ-specific distillation and anatomy-mask supervision shape features for anatomy-weighted pooling into organ-specific representations. At inference, 11 organ-specific representations are produced without external segmentation masks.
AI.result: Heart representations improve CT-RATE cardiomegaly AUROC from 0.910 to 0.953; lung representations improve NLST lung-cancer mortality Harrell C-index by 14.2%; global representation achieves INSPECT Recall@10 of 33.09% (text-to-image) and 32.04% (image-to-text).
AI.conclusion: OrganLens provides a scalable, reusable framework for organ-specific CT representation learning with a shared encoder, offering stronger task-relevant signal for organ-specific tasks while maintaining global representation utility.

title: Semantic Space Search Trajectory Networks
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, submitted to EA 2026: 17th Biennal International Conference on Artificial Evolution
summary: Search Trajectory Networks (STNs) are a graph-based tool for visualizing and characterizing the behavior of optimization algorithms. STNs' reliance on discretization of the search space has largely confined them to low-dimensional or combinatorial settings. We introduce a methodology for constructing STNs in semantic spaces, defined as the space of a model's predictions on a fixed sample set. Our approach discretizes semantic vectors and aggregates them into network nodes via agglomerative clustering with complete linkage under a normalized Hamming distance. Since any predictor can be summarized by its semantic vector, this method enables comparison of learning dynamics across otherwise incomparable algorithm families. We apply semantic space STNs to classification and regression tasks solved using different machine learning algorithms, recovering known qualitative differences between them. Additionally, we use semantic space STNs to study neural network generalization by contrasting standard training with the label randomization regime of Zhang et al. (2017). The resulting STNs exhibit consistent structural differences, training on real labels produces denser, more efficient and more centralized graphs than training on shuffled labels. Together, our results show that semantic space STNs capture functional training dynamics arising from the interaction between learning algorithms and data, providing a tool for analyzing and comparing learning dynamics across machine learning models and training regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Search Trajectory Networks (STNs) from low-dimensional/combinatorial spaces to semantic spaces (model predictions on fixed samples), using discretization and agglomerative clustering under normalized Hamming distance. This enables comparison of learning dynamics across diverse ML algorithms. Experiments on classification/regression and neural network training with real vs. shuffled labels show STNs capture functional training dynamics, with real labels producing denser, more efficient, and more centralized graphs.
AI.motivation: STNs are limited to low-dimensional or combinatorial settings due to their reliance on search space discretization. The authors aim to generalize STNs to arbitrary model classes by operating in semantic space (prediction space), enabling cross-algorithm comparison of learning dynamics.
AI.method: Semantic vectors (model predictions on a fixed sample set) are discretized and aggregated into network nodes via agglomerative clustering with complete linkage under normalized Hamming distance. The resulting STNs are constructed for classification and regression tasks across different ML algorithms, and for studying neural network generalization under standard vs. label randomization training.
AI.result: Semantic space STNs recover known qualitative differences between ML algorithms. In the generalization study, real-label training produces denser, more efficient, and more centralized STNs compared to shuffled-label training, revealing consistent structural differences.
AI.conclusion: Semantic space STNs capture functional training dynamics arising from the interaction between learning algorithms and data, providing a general tool for analyzing and comparing learning dynamics across diverse machine learning models and training regimes.

title: LivingArena: Do LLMs Know What Other LLMs Don't? Peer-Probing as Scalable Evaluation
summary: Evaluating frontier LLMs is challenging: static benchmarks suffer from contamination and saturation -- leaving users unable to distinguish top models and developers blind to specific failure modes -- while human preference is subjective. In this paper, our question is: \emph{Do LLMs know what other LLMs don't? And can we leverage this dynamic for evaluation?} We present \textbf{LivingArena}, an automated, contamination-resistant evaluation framework. In this framework, models take turns proposing questions, aiming to pose items that opponents cannot answer correctly. Questioners are encouraged to actively identify and exploit opponents' knowledge boundaries, receiving rewards when the answerer fails, while the answerer is rewarded otherwise. To ensure questions contain objectively verifiable answers, a judge panel of strong models validates them, penalizing questioners if validation fails. Evaluating ten frontier LLMs, LivingArena yields a stable Elo leaderboard. Our behavioral analyses show that models identify and exploit their peers' cognitive boundaries: self-play and tournament logs indicate that they localize and double down on opponents' weak dimensions. Beyond static knowledge recall, peer probing measures factual rigor and the higher-order ability to probe an opponent's weaknesses, correlating only weakly with human preference and offering a scalable, low-cost approach to continuous evaluation.

AI.tldr: LivingArena is an automated, contamination-resistant evaluation framework where LLMs take turns posing questions to probe each other's knowledge boundaries, yielding stable Elo rankings of frontier models.
AI.motivation: Static benchmarks suffer from contamination and saturation, while human preference evaluation is subjective; there is a need for a dynamic, scalable, and objective evaluation method for frontier LLMs.
AI.method: Models take turns as questioners and answerers; questioners propose items exploiting opponents' knowledge boundaries and receive rewards when opponents fail; a judge panel of strong models validates answerability, penalizing invalid questions. Evaluated via self-play and tournament among ten frontier LLMs with Elo scoring.
AI.result: LivingArena produces a stable Elo leaderboard; behavioral analysis shows models identify and exploit peers' cognitive boundaries by localizing and doubling down on weak dimensions; peer probing correlates weakly with human preference.
AI.conclusion: Peer probing measures factual rigor and higher-order probing ability beyond static knowledge recall, offering a scalable, low-cost, contamination-resistant approach to continuous LLM evaluation.

title: Delta Debugging for Cyber-Physical Systems with Flaky Test Executions
summary: Simulation-based testing is widely used to validate Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs), yet modern CPS simulators frequently exhibit non-deterministic (flaky) behavior, making failures difficult to reproduce and debug. Although delta debugging has proven effective for deterministic systems, its underlying assumptions do not hold in stochastic environments. This paper presents three delta debugging algorithms that combine statistical failure analysis, repeated executions, and environment-aware reduction to isolate minimal failure-inducing test inputs for stochastic CPSs. We evaluate the proposed techniques on two complementary case study systems: an industrial elevator dispatching system employing stochastic optimization and an autonomous mobile robot exhibiting simulator-induced non-determinism. The results show that the proposed approaches substantially reduce debugging time while preserving the original failure behavior. More importantly, we observe that minimizing failure-inducing test inputs frequently increases failure reproducibility compared with the original executions. By eliminating execution segments that introduce incidental stochastic effects, the reduced test inputs isolate the causal conditions of the failure and consistently reproduce it with higher probability. These findings suggest that delta debugging not only simplifies failure analysis but also mitigates execution flakiness, providing a practical foundation for debugging CPSs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces three delta debugging algorithms adapted for stochastic Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) that combine statistical failure analysis, repeated executions, and environment-aware reduction to isolate minimal failure-inducing test inputs. Evaluated on an industrial elevator system and an autonomous mobile robot, the approaches reduce debugging time and unexpectedly increase failure reproducibility by eliminating incidental stochastic effects.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based testing of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) suffers from non-deterministic (flaky) behavior that makes failures difficult to reproduce and debug. Existing delta debugging techniques assume deterministic environments and thus fail in stochastic CPS contexts.
AI.method: Three delta debugging algorithms are proposed that integrate statistical failure analysis, repeated execution runs, and environment-aware reduction to handle non-determinism in CPS simulators, enabling minimal failure-inducing input isolation under stochastic conditions.
AI.result: The approaches substantially reduce debugging time while preserving original failure behavior. Notably, minimizing failure-inducing inputs increases failure reproducibility compared to original executions by removing incidental stochastic effects that obscure causal conditions.
AI.conclusion: Delta debugging can be effectively extended to stochastic CPSs, and the reduction process not only simplifies failure analysis but also mitigates execution flakiness, providing a practical foundation for CPS debugging.

title: LGFNet: A CTC-Guided Local-Global Fusion Framework for Single-Channel Sleep Staging
summary: Sleep staging remains challenging due to long-range temporal dependencies, ambiguous stage transitions-particularly in N1-and substantial distribution shifts across subjects, sampling rates, and EEG montages. These difficulties are further amplified in single-channel, low-latency scenarios required by wearable and real-world applications. To address these issues, we propose LGFNet, a CTC-guided sequence-to-sequence framework for robust sleep staging. LGFNet introduces a Local-Global Fusion encoder that jointly models fine-grained temporal dynamics and long-range sleep structure, overcoming the limitations of conventional serial hybrid architectures. A CTC-Attention joint training paradigm is adopted to unify temporal alignment with context-dependent modeling, enabling more accurate recognition of stage boundaries and transitions. Furthermore, a three-stage decoding strategy is devised, leveraging CTC-guided decoding and Viterbi-based smoothing to reduce error accumulation and enforce physiological consistency. Extensive cross-dataset evaluations on five public benchmarks demonstrate that LGFNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-channel methods. In particular, on Sleep-EDF-78, LGFNet surpasses DMIN by +1.27% accuracy, +1.74% macro-F1, and +1.93% kappa, with pronounced gains on N1 and transition segments, highlighting its robustness and strong generalization across diverse sampling rates, montages, and recording environments.

AI.tldr: LGFNet is a CTC-guided sequence-to-sequence framework for robust single-channel sleep staging, featuring a Local-Global Fusion encoder, CTC-Attention joint training, and three-stage decoding. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across five public benchmarks, with notable gains on N1 and transition segments.
AI.motivation: Sleep staging is challenged by long-range temporal dependencies, ambiguous stage transitions (especially N1), and distribution shifts across subjects, sampling rates, and EEG montages—problems amplified in single-channel, low-latency wearable scenarios.
AI.method: LGFNet proposes: (1) a Local-Global Fusion encoder jointly modeling fine-grained temporal dynamics and long-range sleep structure; (2) CTC-Attention joint training unifying temporal alignment with context-dependent modeling; (3) a three-stage decoding strategy using CTC-guided decoding and Viterbi-based smoothing to reduce error accumulation and enforce physiological consistency.
AI.result: On Sleep-EDF-78, LGFNet outperforms DMIN by +1.27% accuracy, +1.74% macro-F1, and +1.93% kappa, with pronounced gains on N1 and transition segments. Consistent SOTA results across five public benchmarks under diverse sampling rates, montages, and recording environments.
AI.conclusion: LGFNet demonstrates robust generalization and strong performance for single-channel sleep staging, effectively addressing long-range dependencies, transition ambiguity, and cross-dataset distribution shifts.

title: Endpoint Replay: Compressing the Recency Buffer in Deep Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at the Reinforcement Learning Conference (RLC) 2026, to appear in the Reinforcement Learning Journal (RLJ)
summary: Experience replay remains one of the most practical and useful algorithmic tools in the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) toolbox. Aside from the limited success of prioritized replay and specialized approaches for large asynchronous systems, most DRL algorithms make use of a large, uniformly sampled recency buffer---even the size, one million, remains unchanged. Could we store less data, reduce redundancy, or more effectively chain experience together to speed up value propagation and still retain the performance of large buffers? In this paper, we investigate a simple compression approach that stores representative transitions derived from the end-points of a chain of connected $n$-step sequences. By curating these end-points in a smaller recency buffer, our method maintains an effective memory horizon comparable to a standard large buffer while requiring an order of magnitude less storage. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that this approach prevents the systematic bias inherent in naive compression strategies and matches the performance of traditional large buffers in the Pinball environment and the Atari 2600 benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a compression method for experience replay in deep reinforcement learning that stores representative transitions from the end-points of n-step sequence chains, reducing storage by an order of magnitude while matching the performance of standard large buffers (1M transitions) on Pinball and Atari 2600 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard experience replay buffers in DRL typically require large storage (e.g., 1 million transitions) and are sampled uniformly. The authors investigate whether we can store less data, reduce redundancy, and more effectively chain experiences to speed up value propagation while retaining large-buffer performance.
AI.method: The approach stores representative transitions derived from the end-points of a chain of connected n-step sequences. These end-points are curated in a smaller recency buffer, maintaining an effective memory horizon comparable to a standard large buffer but requiring an order of magnitude less storage.
AI.result: The compression approach prevents systematic bias inherent in naive compression strategies and matches the performance of traditional large buffers in the Pinball environment and the Atari 2600 benchmark.
