Existing inverse-rendering and reflection-aware Gaussian-splatting methods require full 360-degree coverage and fail under incomplete views.
AI.method: PanoLess uses surface-aligned 2D Gaussian splats with deferred shading to recover per-pixel normals and reflection cues, which are fused into a neural cubemap representation of the environment. It also produces a visibility map indicating which environment regions are supported by partial reflective observations.
AI.result: PanoLess achieves high-fidelity and geometrically consistent environment reconstruction, outperforming reflection-aware baselines on custom synthetic benchmarks and public datasets, and demonstrating generalization to real-world reflective captures.
AI.conclusion: PanoLess enables consistent, physically grounded illumination estimation from partial-view input, unlike existing approaches that require full 360-degree coverage, making it effective for real-world scenarios with limited reflective observations.

title: Breaking the Periodicity Assumption: Robust Tensorial Multi-View Clustering via Graph-Spectral Low-Rank Learning
summary: Tensorial multi-view clustering (TMC) has achieved strong performance due to its ability to capture high-order correlations across multiple views. Most existing t-SVD-based TMC frameworks apply the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) along the sample mode to impose frequency-domain low-rank constraints. However, we reveal that this widely adopted design critically relies on an implicit ``periodicity assumption'' induced by the sample arrangement. When samples are ordered by class, neighboring indices tend to be semantically similar, creating artificial local continuity along the sample mode and a favorable spectral structure for FFT-based low-rank regularization. Once this ordering is removed by random permutation, existing t-SVD-based TMC methods suffer severe performance degradation. This strong sensitivity to class ordering conflicts with the permutation-invariant nature of clustering and indicates that part of the reported performance may be attributed to a privileged sample arrangement rather than genuine high-order structure modeling. In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and its underlying algebraic and spectral mechanisms. To address this fundamental flaw, we further propose a graph-spectral low-rank tensor learning framework based on the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT), which replaces the fixed Fourier basis along the sample mode with a data-driven graph spectral basis, thereby capturing the intrinsic manifold structure without relying on a particular sample ordering. Moreover, we develop an anchor-based variant to address large-scale datasets efficiently. Extensive experiments on various benchmarks validate our findings and demonstrate the competitive or superior performance of the proposed methods compared with state-of-the-art TMC approaches.

AI.tldr: Existing t-SVD-based tensorial multi-view clustering (TMC) methods suffer from a hidden periodicity assumption that makes them highly sensitive to sample ordering, leading to performance drops when class-based order is removed. The paper proposes a Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)-based low-rank tensor learning framework that uses data-driven graph spectral bases to capture intrinsic manifold structure without relying on privileged sample ordering.
AI.motivation: To reveal and address the overlooked "periodicity assumption" in t-SVD-based multi-view clustering, where performance gains come from class-ordered sample arrangement rather than genuine high-order structure modeling, which contradicts the permutation-invariant nature of clustering.
AI.method: Systematic analysis of the spectral mechanism behind FFT-based low-rank constraints in TMC; proposal of a Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)-based low-rank tensor learning framework that replaces the fixed Fourier basis with a data-driven graph spectral basis along the sample mode; an anchor-based variant for large-scale scalability.
AI.result: Demonstrates severe performance degradation of existing t-SVD-based TMC methods under random permutation; the proposed GFT-based method achieves competitive or superior performance on various benchmarks while being permutation-invariant.
AI.conclusion: The implicit periodicity assumption in FFT-based TMC is a fundamental flaw; the GFT-based framework effectively removes this dependency by leveraging intrinsic manifold structure, providing a more principled and robust approach to multi-view clustering.

title: Leak-Free Cross-Validated Stacking with Per-Architecture Calibration for Sand-Boil Segmentation in Earthen Levees
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures, 14 tables. Supported by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under Contract No. W912HZ-23-2-0004
summary: Sand boils, points where water seeping beneath an earthen levee re-emerges at the surface, are early warnings of internal erosion, and deep segmentation networks are increasingly used to find them in inspection photographs. Annotated examples are scarce, and two common ways of working around that scarcity quietly inflate reported accuracy: tuning ensemble weights on the same images later used to score them, and training on synthetic images derived from the very photographs held out for testing. We present a sand-boil segmentation framework that closes both loopholes. Every synthetic image carries a pointer to its real parent, and a per-fold filter excludes any image whose parent is held out; five encoder-decoder backbones are trained under five-fold cross-validation, calibrated by one temperature scalar each, and combined by a per-pixel meta-learner fitted only on out-of-fold predictions. On the held-out test set the proposed Updated SandBoilNet reaches an intersection-over-union of 0.707 over three seeds, against 0.608 for the published original re-evaluated on the same split. Under the stacking protocol the calibrated stack reaches 0.681 against 0.694 for the strongest fold-averaged member, so it does not improve on the best single model; eight meta-learner families reproduce that outcome, which we trace to a mean pairwise error correlation of 0.894 among members. A synthetic pool filtered for label fidelity lifts the champion to 0.718 over three seeds against a 0.707 control. We also introduce a mask-conditioned synthesis route that makes the conditioning mask the label by construction, giving labelled training images at zero annotation cost.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two common methodological loopholes that inflate segmentation accuracy in sand-boil detection (tuning ensemble weights on test data and training on synthetic images derived from test-set parents) and proposes Updated SandBoilNet, a framework that closes both loopholes via per-fold parent filtering, calibrated stacking, and mask-conditioned synthesis, achieving 0.707 IoU vs. 0.608 for the original, though stacking does not improve over the best single model due to high error correlation (0.894).
AI.motivation: Sand boils are early warnings of internal erosion in levees, and deep segmentation models are used for automated detection, but annotated examples are scarce. The authors identify that common practices for working around data scarcity—tuning ensemble weights on test images and training on synthetic images derived from test-set parents—inflate reported accuracy, so they aim to close both loopholes to produce honest performance estimates.
AI.method: The framework uses five encoder-decoder backbones trained under five-fold cross-validation, each calibrated by one temperature scalar, combined via a per-pixel meta-learner fitted only on out-of-fold predictions. A per-fold filter excludes any synthetic image whose real parent image is held out. A mask-conditioned synthesis route produces labelled training images at zero annotation cost by making the conditioning mask the label by construction.
AI.result: Updated SandBoilNet achieves 0.707 IoU vs. 0.608 for the original on the same split. The calibrated stack reaches 0.681 vs. 0.694 for the best single model, showing stacking does not improve over the best member due to mean pairwise error correlation of 0.894. A synthetic pool filtered for label fidelity lifts the champion to 0.718 over three seeds against a 0.707 control.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully closes both identified loopholes and provides honest accuracy estimates. However, stacking does not outperform the best single model due to high inter-member error correlation. Mask-conditioned synthesis enables zero-cost labelled data generation, offering a practical path forward for data-scarce segmentation tasks.

title: Zhinv: Real-time hub-height wind field reconstruction using only local sparse observations
summary: The high proportion of wind power connected to the grid places higher demands on fine-grained knowledge of regional wind fields. Since the wind information directly obtainable in actual operations is mostly sparse, discrete, and irregularly distributed local observations, it is difficult to directly meet the needs of tasks such as wind power regulation, wind resource assessment, and low-altitude environmental perception of continuous regional wind fields. Therefore, we propose Zhinv, an end-to-end reconstruction framework that directly weaves sparse and irregular observations into a fine-grid wind field at hub-height. Experiments in Northeast China, Europe, and Southeast Asia demonstrate that Zhinv can accurately, robustly, and efficiently reconstruct fine-grid wind fields from sparse observations, reducing the error by about 66% compared with Kriging. With local wind-power observations as input, Zhinv enables wind power centers to bypass NWP and complex assimilation processes, supporting direct and real-time wind resource assessment from locally available data.

AI.tldr: Zhinv is an end-to-end reconstruction framework that weaves sparse, irregular wind observations into fine-grid hub-height wind fields, reducing error by ~66% over Kriging across three diverse regions.
AI.motivation: High wind power penetration demands fine-grained regional wind field knowledge, but operational wind data is sparse, discrete, and irregular, which is insufficient for tasks like wind power regulation, resource assessment, and low-altitude environmental perception.
AI.method: An end-to-end reconstruction framework (Zhinv) that directly transforms sparse and irregular local wind observations into a continuous, fine-grid wind field at hub-height without requiring NWP or complex data assimilation.
AI.result: Experiments in Northeast China, Europe, and Southeast Asia show Zhinv reconstructs fine-grid wind fields accurately, robustly, and efficiently, reducing error by approximately 66% compared to Kriging interpolation.
AI.conclusion: Zhinv enables wind power centers to bypass NWP and complex assimilation, supporting direct and real-time wind resource assessment from locally available data alone.

title: Hyperspectral Intrinsic Decomposition: Joint Recovery of Reflectance and Photometric Components for Non-Lambertian Scenes
summary: Hyperspectral intrinsic decomposition (HID) aims to disentangle material-related spectral properties and photometric effects in hyperspectral images (HSIs), which is essential for understanding real-world imaging processes and benefits a variety of downstream applications. Most existing HID studies have been developed under Lambertian or near-Lambertian assumptions. The few prior non-Lambertian efforts rely on simplified specular assumptions insufficient to handle diverse real-world specularity, and typically require auxiliary inputs or recover only a subset of the coupled reflectance and photometric components, hindering complete and blind decomposition. In this paper, we revisit the dichromatic reflection model (DRM) and develop a unified inversion paradigm that reformulates the recovery of four coupled reflectance and photometric components as the estimation of two spectral--spatial target variables. Building on this reformulation, we propose a dual-scale decomposition scheme to handle non-Lambertian effects with distinct spatial characteristics. At the global scale, photometrically invariant descriptors serve as edge priors for high-fidelity intrinsic boundary preservation; at the local scale, specularity-guided attention directs refinement with emphasis on specularity-dominated regions, including those affected by clipping distortion. To facilitate future research, we establish CITE, the first public real-world HID dataset for non-Lambertian objects, and develop a Physically-faithful Intrinsic Set Generator (PISG) for controllable data synthesis. Extensive ablation studies and experiments on the CITE and additional HSIs demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its robustness across diverse scenes.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified inversion paradigm for hyperspectral intrinsic decomposition (HID) under non-Lambertian conditions by reformulating the dichromatic reflection model into a two-variable estimation problem with a dual-scale decomposition scheme, and introduces CITE, the first public real-world HID dataset for non-Lambertian objects, along with a Physically-faithful Intrinsic Set Generator (PISG) for controllable data synthesis.
AI.motivation: Existing HID methods mostly rely on Lambertian or near-Lambertian assumptions, while the few non-Lambertian efforts use simplified specular assumptions that cannot handle diverse real-world specularity, often requiring auxiliary inputs or recovering only a subset of reflectance/photometric components, preventing complete and blind decomposition.
AI.method: The method revisits the dichromatic reflection model (DRM) to reformulate the recovery of four coupled reflectance and photometric components as estimation of two spectral-spatial target variables. A dual-scale decomposition scheme is proposed: global scale uses photometrically invariant descriptors as edge priors for boundary preservation; local scale uses specularity-guided attention for refinement in specularity-dominated regions, including those with clipping distortion.
AI.result: Extensive ablation studies and experiments on the newly introduced CITE dataset and additional HSIs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and its robustness across diverse scenes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reformulation of DRM and dual-scale decomposition scheme enables effective blind hyperspectral intrinsic decomposition under non-Lambertian conditions, supported by the new CITE dataset and PISG for future research.

title: Retraction-Free Optimization over the Stiefel Manifold for the LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Optimization over the Stiefel manifold plays a significant role in various machine learning tasks. Existing methods either use the retraction operators, requiring costly orthonormalization for large-scale matrices, or employ landing methods that rely on careful step size selection and penalty parameter tuning. To address these challenges, we propose a retraction-free and penalty parameter-free algorithm that directly lands on the manifold. By leveraging the strongly-convex-like property of the quadratic penalty function and the proximal smoothness of the Stiefel manifold, we establish global convergence guarantees with the best-known iteration complexities under both constant and diminishing step sizes. Then, we reformulate the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning problem for large language models as a manifold optimization problem, introducing Manifold-LoRA for geometry-accelerated adaptation. This approach employs the proposed landing technique and a carefully designed step size strategy to accelerate the training process. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficiency and strong downstream performance of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A retraction-free and penalty parameter-free landing algorithm for optimization over the Stiefel manifold is proposed, with global convergence guarantees and application to LoRA fine-tuning for LLMs via Manifold-LoRA, demonstrating efficiency on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing Stiefel manifold optimization methods suffer from costly orthonormalization (retraction-based) or require careful step size/penalty parameter tuning (landing methods). The goal is to develop a more efficient and less sensitive algorithm.
AI.method: Proposes a retraction-free and penalty parameter-free landing algorithm that directly lands on the Stiefel manifold. Leverages the strongly-convex-like property of the quadratic penalty function and proximal smoothness of the Stiefel manifold. Reformulates LoRA fine-tuning as a manifold optimization problem (Manifold-LoRA) with a designed step size strategy.
AI.result: Establishes global convergence guarantees with the best-known iteration complexities under both constant and diminishing step sizes. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate efficiency and strong downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method eliminates the need for retractions and penalty parameter tuning while achieving strong theoretical guarantees and practical performance, particularly for LLM fine-tuning via Manifold-LoRA.

title: CogEEGAgent: Toward Autonomous Cognitive EEG Analysis with Grounded Execution and Selection-Aware Verification
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, and 16 tables. The supplementary material is included in the same PDF
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis in cognitive studies requires specialized expertise and involves many defensible choices over contrasts, channels, time windows, and statistical tests. LLM agents can translate varied natural-language questions into analysis choices, offering a flexible interface for automation. Yet fluent reports alone cannot establish that an agent selected the requested analysis or evaluated a confirmatory claim independently of adaptive search. We present CogEEGAgent, a cognitive-EEG analysis agent grounded in MNE-Python. Its EEG-specific scientific harness separates semantic from scientific authority. The LLM interprets intent and proposes registered analyses, while deterministic components validate typed contracts, control confirmation access, and authorize evidence-bound release. On a prespecified routing benchmark, CogEEGAgent maps language to registered analyses more accurately than a matched deterministic router, while matched preflight makes both systems abstain whenever required. In an externally model-authored, outcome-blind campaign, the complete system releases supported analyses with participant-disjoint confirmation and blocks prespecified capability hazards and lifecycle-reuse requests. Policy stress testing shows that held-out confirmation curbs false positives from uncorrected adaptive search. Together, these studies establish bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows. More broadly, they show how scientific agents can combine flexible language understanding with fail-closed control over inference and release.

AI.tldr: CogEEGAgent is a grounded cognitive-EEG analysis agent that uses LLMs for flexible language interpretation while enforcing deterministic validation, confirmation access control, and evidence-bound release to ensure scientific integrity and bounded autonomy.
AI.motivation: EEG analysis in cognitive studies requires specialized expertise and involves many defensible choices. LLM agents offer flexible automation but fluent reports alone cannot guarantee that the agent selected the requested analysis or evaluated claims independently of adaptive search.
AI.method: CogEEGAgent separates semantic from scientific authority: LLM interprets intent and proposes registered analyses, while deterministic components validate typed contracts, control confirmation access, and authorize evidence-bound release. The system is grounded in MNE-Python.
AI.result: On a routing benchmark, CogEEGAgent maps language to registered analyses more accurately than a matched deterministic router. In an outcome-blind campaign, it blocks prespecified capability hazards and lifecycle-reuse requests. Policy stress testing shows held-out confirmation curbs false positives from uncorrected adaptive search.
AI.conclusion: The system establishes bounded autonomy and an auditable automation framework for cognitive-EEG workflows, showing how scientific agents can combine flexible language understanding with fail-closed control over inference and release.

title: Guiding Posterior Exploration with Optimizer-Derived Geometry
comment: Accepted for presentation at the OPTIMAL Workshop at AISTATS 2026
summary: Sampling-based methods offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification in Bayesian neural networks. Their practical use, however, is often challenged by the computational cost of exploring high-dimensional and multimodal posterior distributions. To overcome these difficulties, Bayesian Deep Ensembles, i.e., warmstarting the sampling from several optimized solutions, have proven to be an effective strategy. In this paper, we demonstrate that curvature estimates computed during the warmstart as a byproduct in adaptive optimizers such as AdamW can inform the sampling phase at negligible additional cost. Specifically, our proposed preconditioned sampling strategy based on optimizer-derived geometries can substantially reduce or even eliminate the need for a lengthy sampling burn-in phase and leads to greater numerical stability. This approach consistently maintains or improves predictive performance and uncertainty quantification without any additional computational costs. We confirm the consistency of our findings across various datasets and network architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a preconditioned sampling strategy for Bayesian neural networks that leverages curvature estimates from adaptive optimizers (like AdamW) to warmstart sampling, reducing or eliminating burn-in phases without extra computational cost, while maintaining or improving predictive performance and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based Bayesian neural networks are computationally expensive due to high-dimensional, multimodal posteriors. Bayesian Deep Ensembles (warmstarting from optimized solutions) help, but still require costly burn-in phases. The authors aim to reduce this cost by reusing curvature information already computed during optimization.
AI.method: The authors use curvature estimates obtained as a byproduct from adaptive optimizers (e.g., AdamW) during warmstart optimization to precondition the sampling phase. This preconditioning is incorporated into the sampler, leveraging optimizer-derived geometries to guide exploration more efficiently.
AI.result: The proposed preconditioned sampling strategy substantially reduces or eliminates the need for a lengthy sampling burn-in phase, improves numerical stability, and consistently maintains or improves predictive performance and uncertainty quantification—all without additional computational cost. Results are consistent across multiple datasets and network architectures.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging curvature estimates from adaptive optimizers for preconditioning is an effective, zero-cost way to improve sampling efficiency in Bayesian neural networks, making Bayesian Deep Ensembles more practical and scalable.

title: Psychological Influences of Conversational AI: Research and Design Directions for Reducing Harm and Promoting Well-Being
summary: As conversational AI systems become increasingly integrated into daily life, their potential effects on user well-being require ongoing attention. While consumer-facing generalist models can provide benefits, including improved access to information, learning, productivity, self-reflection, and companionship, they also introduce risks, such as emotional entanglement, unhealthy dependence, and the amplification of psychological vulnerabilities. Drawing on prior research and empirical observations of AI chatbot behavior, we propose a set of aspirational directions for guiding the behavior of general-purpose AI systems in ways that may reduce potential psychological harms and support user well-being. We acknowledge the difficulty of systematically assessing the long-term impacts of AI chatbot use and frame these directions as hypotheses for studying how AI behavior may influence users across general interactions, role-playing scenarios, and contexts that could be characterized as providing psychological support. While some proposed directions are supported by existing research and expert insights, others identify open questions and areas requiring deeper study. We hope that this formulation and these hypotheses encourage further discussion, empirical investigation, and exploration of interactive design approaches aimed at better accommodating users' psychological needs and promoting their well-being.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes aspirational behavioral directions for general-purpose conversational AI to reduce psychological harms and support user well-being, while acknowledging the difficulty of assessing long-term impacts and framing these as hypotheses for future empirical investigation.
AI.motivation: As conversational AI becomes widely integrated into daily life, there is a need to address potential negative effects on user well-being, such as emotional entanglement, unhealthy dependence, and amplification of psychological vulnerabilities, while still enabling benefits like information access, learning, and companionship.
AI.method: Drawing on prior research and empirical observations of AI chatbot behavior, the authors propose aspirational directions for guiding AI system behavior, framed as testable hypotheses for studying how AI behavior influences users across general interactions, role-playing scenarios, and psychologically supportive contexts.
AI.result: A set of aspirational behavioral directions is proposed, with some supported by existing research and expert insights, while others identify open questions requiring deeper study to reduce potential psychological harms and support user well-being.
AI.conclusion: The authors hope these formulations and hypotheses encourage further discussion, empirical investigation, and exploration of interactive design approaches to better accommodate users' psychological needs and promote well-being in general-purpose AI systems.

title: HOME: Robust Hough-space Matching Method for Structured and Textureless Videos
summary: Visual front-ends for robotic localization typically rely on point-based features such as Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF (ORB), which frequently fail in structured environments dominated by strong linear structures or textureless surfaces. While line-based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems mitigate this by utilizing line segments, conventional line extraction and description algorithms are computationally prohibitive for real-time edge robotics. To address this fundamental bottleneck, we propose HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema), an ultra-lightweight, training-free feature matching framework. HOME transforms images into Hough space, mapping global linear structures to stable local extrema, which serve as keypoints, thereby reformulating complex line matching into highly efficient one-dimensional point matching. The proposed 1D radial descriptor mathematically guarantees rotational and translational invariance without the overhead of explicit orientation estimation. As a proof of concept to validate the matching accuracy and efficiency of HOME, this paper focuses on homography estimation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that HOME achieves robust registration in challenging scenarios where point-based methods fail, operating at a much faster speed than existing line-based methods. Extending this robust matching engine to full 3D pose estimation remains a highly promising future direction.

AI.tldr: HOME is an ultra-lightweight, training-free line feature matching framework that transforms images into Hough space to map global linear structures to stable local extrema, reformulating complex line matching into efficient 1D point matching with mathematically guaranteed invariance, validated through homography estimation.
AI.motivation: Point-based features (e.g., ORB) fail in structured environments with strong linear structures or textureless surfaces, while existing line-based SLAM systems are computationally too expensive for real-time edge robotics.
AI.method: HOME transforms images into Hough space, maps linear structures to local extrema as keypoints, uses a 1D radial descriptor with mathematically guaranteed rotational and translational invariance, and reformulates line matching as 1D point matching.
AI.result: HOME achieves robust registration in challenging scenarios where point-based methods fail, operating at significantly faster speeds than existing line-based methods.
AI.conclusion: HOME provides an efficient, training-free solution for line matching; extending it to full 3D pose estimation is a promising future direction.

title: Explainable AI for Chronic Kidney Disease Prediction Using Simulated Federated Learning
summary: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), characterized by the gradual loss of kidney function, remains a significant public health challenge. Early detection is crucial for preventing severe complications and enhancing patient outcomes. In this study, Federated Learning (FL) with a VotingClassifier was used to predict CKD using a clinical dataset, where Random Forest, AdaBoost, and XGBoost were utilized to compare and identify the best-fitting model for the global server. Additionally, GridSearchCV was applied to optimize the models' performance on the client's side. To enhance model transparency and trustworthiness, explainable AI (XAI) techniques were incorporated to interpret the prediction mechanisms. The global model's average accuracy was 99%, highlighting the potential of interpretable FL models in supporting early CKD diagnosis and advancing data-driven healthcare solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Federated Learning framework with VotingClassifier (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) and GridSearchCV optimization for early Chronic Kidney Disease prediction, achieving 99% global model accuracy with explainable AI integration for model interpretability.
AI.motivation: Chronic Kidney Disease is a significant public health challenge, and early detection is critical for preventing severe complications and improving patient outcomes. The study aims to leverage Federated Learning and ensemble methods to enable privacy-preserving, accurate CKD prediction.
AI.method: Federated Learning with VotingClassifier combining Random Forest, AdaBoost, and XGBoost; GridSearchCV for client-side hyperparameter optimization; explainable AI (XAI) techniques for model interpretability.
AI.result: The global FL model achieved an average accuracy of 99% for CKD prediction.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable Federated Learning models show strong potential for supporting early CKD diagnosis and advancing privacy-preserving, data-driven healthcare solutions.

title: Similar Models Learn Differently: Final-Window Pretraining Shapes Post-Training Beyond SFT
summary: Developers judge a model checkpoint by how it behaves. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), two checkpoints that perform about the same across relevant benchmarks are treated as interchangeable, equally ready for the next alignment stage, typically preference optimization. We ask whether this judgment misses a pretraining imprint: a difference that no post-SFT benchmark reveals, yet that decides how each checkpoint responds to further training. To find out, we run a controlled experiment on the final window of pretraining, the last data trained on before instruction tuning. Six branches fork from one partially pretrained checkpoint and differ only in this window: 500 million tokens, 0.1% to 1% of the tokens that precede it. Each branch trains its window on a single data source: generic web text, filtered web text, normative discourse, safety text, mathematical text, or synthetic educational text. SFT and post-training are then identical. After SFT the branches behave near-identically, within about one point on instruction following, refusal, and capability, yet the same post-training carries them to very different endpoints, under both a direct preference optimization update and a reinforcement learning update with a verifiable reward. We measure this deviation through refusal of harmful requests: when post-training begins the safety text branch refuses no more than the web text branch, yet by the end it has lost far less of its refusal. The other four branches gain little or no protection, so the effect is selective to what the window contained. The protection requires the safety text to arrive last rather than earlier in pretraining, and it reproduces on a second model family. What a model is pretrained on last shapes how it reacts to alignment. Therefore, a checkpoint should not be evaluated by its post-SFT behavior alone, and what it was trained on last should be reported with it.

AI.tldr: The final pretraining data (last 500M tokens) has a selective, lasting effect on how a model responds to post-training (preference optimization/RL), even though post-SFT benchmarks show near-identical performance across branches trained on different data sources. Safety text in the final window protects against refusal loss during alignment, but only when it arrives last in pretraining.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the commonly held assumption that checkpoints with similar post-SFT benchmark performance are interchangeable for subsequent alignment stages misses a "pretraining imprint"—a latent difference from the final pretraining data that only manifests during post-training.
AI.method: Controlled experiment: fork six branches from one partially pretrained checkpoint, each differing only in the final 500M tokens (0.1–1% of total), trained on a single source (generic web, filtered web, normative discourse, safety text, math, synthetic educational text). All branches undergo identical SFT and post-training (DPO and RL with verifiable reward). Behavior is measured via instruction following, refusal, and capability benchmarks.
AI.result: After SFT, all six branches perform near-identically (within ~1 point). However, post-training leads to divergent endpoints: the safety-text branch retains significantly more refusal of harmful requests compared to the web-text branch, while other branches gain little/no protection. This effect is specific to the final window and does not occur when safety text appears earlier in pretraining. The result replicates on a second model family.
AI.conclusion: A model checkpoint should not be evaluated solely by its post-SFT behavior; the content of the final pretraining data significantly influences how the model responds to alignment. The last data trained on should be reported alongside standard benchmarks.

title: Noise-Free One-Step LoRA for Task-Driven Image Restoration with Diffusion Priors
summary: Degraded images not only reduce visual quality but also impair downstream high-level vision tasks. Task-driven image restoration (TDIR) addresses this issue by jointly optimizing restoration quality and task performance. Recent works show that pretrained diffusion priors benefit TDIR, yet diffusion-based restoration is inherently stochastic, as the sampling process depends on a random noise term, which can undermine task consistency. In this paper, we show that a deterministic, noise-free one-step forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors can substantially improve TDIR, but the benefit critically depends on the adaptation module: LoRA yields consistent gains, whereas ControlNet-style conditioning does not. This enables one-step forwarding that surpasses conventional multi-step diffusion TDIR baselines. Furthermore, we introduce a task-preserving GAN training strategy that improves perceptual quality without sacrificing task performance. Extensive experiments on classification, segmentation, and detection demonstrate consistent gains over prior TDIR methods, and we further validate generalization on real-world degraded images and OCR.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deterministic, noise-free one-step forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors for task-driven image restoration, showing LoRA adaptation is critical and introducing a task-preserving GAN training strategy to improve perceptual quality without harming task performance, achieving consistent gains over prior methods on classification, segmentation, detection, and real-world degradations.
AI.motivation: Degraded images impair both visual quality and downstream high-level vision tasks. Existing task-driven image restoration (TDIR) methods using diffusion priors suffer from inherent stochasticity (random noise) that undermines task consistency.
AI.method: (1) A deterministic, noise-free one-step forward pass with pretrained diffusion priors; (2) Key finding that LoRA adaptation yields consistent gains while ControlNet-style conditioning does not; (3) A task-preserving GAN training strategy that enhances perceptual quality without sacrificing task performance.
AI.result: Outperforms conventional multi-step diffusion TDIR baselines; consistent gains on classification, segmentation, and detection; validated on real-world degraded images and OCR.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic one-step diffusion prior with LoRA adaptation and task-preserving GAN training effectively addresses TDIR, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple vision tasks.

title: Raven: High-Recall Sequence Modeling with Sparse Memory Routing
summary: Long-context recall in linear-time sequence models highlights a tradeoff in how they write to memory. State-based linear models, such as state-space models (SSMs) and linear Transformers, write densely, updating the entire state for each newly arrived token, which leads to interference and makes specific past tokens hard to recover. Sliding-window attention (SWA) exhibits the opposite behavior: it writes sparsely by storing explicit token representations, but only within a fixed window, so recall drops once the relevant token is evicted. Interpolating between these models, we introduce Raven, a linear-time sequence model that maintains a fixed set of memory slots and, at each step, decays and updates only a selected subset via learned, input-dependent routing. This lets Raven mitigate SWA's position-based overwriting and hard eviction while reducing interference from dense state updates in SSMs, thereby preserving long-range content much more effectively. Across recall-intensive benchmarks, Raven is competitive with or outperforms prior linear-time baselines, achieving strong long-context recall where both SWA and SSMs sharply degrade. It remains effective when extrapolating to context lengths as large as 16x its training length, with similar gains in hybrid architectures.

AI.tldr: Raven introduces a linear-time sequence model with fixed memory slots that uses learned, input-dependent routing to selectively decay and update memory, balancing dense state updates (SSMs) and sparse sliding-window attention (SWA) to achieve strong long-context recall.
AI.motivation: Long-context recall in linear-time models suffers from a tradeoff: state-based models (SSMs, linear Transformers) write densely causing interference, while sliding-window attention writes sparsely but suffers from hard eviction. The goal is to mitigate both problems for better long-range content preservation.
AI.method: Raven maintains a fixed set of memory slots; at each step, it decays and updates only a selected subset via learned, input-dependent routing, interpolating between dense state updates and sparse explicit token storage.
AI.result: Raven is competitive with or outperforms prior linear-time baselines on recall-intensive benchmarks, achieves strong long-context recall where both SWA and SSMs degrade, and extrapolates to 16x training context length effectively.
AI.conclusion: Raven effectively balances the tradeoff between interference from dense updates and hard eviction from sparse windows, preserving long-context content more effectively and showing similar gains in hybrid architectures.

title: Addressable Recall Compaction for Long Context-Window Control in AI Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that can eventually exceed a model's fixed context window. Existing compaction methods address this limitation by discarding, summarizing, or retrieving earlier information, but they may remove task-critical details or fail to recover them reliably. We propose ARC (Addressable Recall Compaction), a context-management framework that separates archival storage from active-context presentation. ARC stores tool observations in an append-only, ID-addressable log and replaces older observations with compact citations when compaction is required. The agent can subsequently use these identifiers to request stored content without re-executing the corresponding tools or depending solely on similarity-based retrieval. We evaluate ARC using Qwen3-8B with a 16k context window and Qwen3-32B with a 32k context window. On the Needle-in-a-Haystack evaluation, ARC achieves an average exact-answer accuracy of 99.40%, compared with 88.12% for the best-performing baseline in our evaluation. ARC also reduces estimated serving time and HBM traffic under our hardware-cost model. On the LongBench-v2 Hard subset, ARC obtains an average accuracy of 29.97%, compared with 28.25% for the best-performing baseline. These results indicate that explicit, address-based recall can improve information retention and serving efficiency relative to the evaluated context-management baselines under the tested settings.

AI.tldr: ARC (Addressable Recall Compaction) is a context-management framework that separates archival storage from active-context presentation, using ID-addressable logs and compact citations to manage long-horizon LLM agent contexts, achieving 99.40% accuracy on Needle-in-a-Haystack and reducing serving costs.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents generate reasoning traces, actions, and tool observations that exceed fixed context windows. Existing compaction methods (discarding, summarizing, retrieving) risk losing task-critical details or fail to reliably recover them.
AI.method: ARC separates archival storage from active-context presentation by storing tool observations in an append-only, ID-addressable log. When compaction is needed, older observations are replaced with compact citations. Agents use these identifiers to request stored content without re-executing tools or relying solely on similarity-based retrieval.
AI.result: On Needle-in-a-Haystack, ARC achieves 99.40% exact-answer accuracy vs. 88.12% for the best baseline. On LongBench-v2 Hard, ARC achieves 29.97% vs. 28.25% for the best baseline. ARC also reduces estimated serving time and HBM traffic under the hardware-cost model.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, address-based recall improves information retention and serving efficiency relative to evaluated context-management baselines under tested settings.

title: RDVSv2: A Large-scale Benchmark for RGB-D Video Salient Object Detection
summary: We introduce RDVSv2, a large-scale benchmark for RGB-D video salient object detection (RGB-D VSOD) with dense frame-level annotations. Existing datasets in this emerging field are often limited in scale and annotation quality, while also relying on less geometry-consistent depth cues. To address these limitations, RDVSv2 is built from publicly accessible stereoscopic online videos and contains 249 video sequences with 29,077 annotated frames. It includes depth maps derived from stereoscopic videos, together with frame-wise salient object masks annotated with eye-tracking guidance. Compared with existing datasets, RDVSv2 is much larger in scale and covers more diverse and challenging scenarios. In addition, we establish a strong baseline for RGB-D VSOD based on Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2). Specifically, we employ a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy to adapt the SAM2 encoder to jointly encode RGB, depth, and optical flow cues. Extensive experiments show that RDVSv2 is substantially more challenging for existing RGB-D VSOD methods. Meanwhile, the proposed baseline achieves state-of-the-art results on RDVSv2 and existing RGB-D VSOD benchmarks. We hope that RDVSv2 and the provided baseline will serve as useful resources for future research on RGB-D VSOD and related multi-modal video understanding tasks. Our dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/ltynick/RDVSv2.

AI.tldr: RDVSv2 is a large-scale RGB-D video salient object detection benchmark with 249 videos and 29,077 annotated frames, using stereoscopic depth and eye-tracking-guided masks. It also proposes a SAM2-based baseline with parameter-efficient fine-tuning that achieves state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing RGB-D VSOD datasets are limited in scale, annotation quality, and rely on less geometry-consistent depth cues. RDVSv2 aims to address these gaps.
AI.method: Built from stereoscopic online videos with dense frame-level annotations, depth maps from stereoscopic cues, and eye-tracking-guided mask annotation. Baseline uses SAM2 with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to jointly encode RGB, depth, and optical flow.
AI.result: RDVSv2 is more challenging for existing methods. The proposed SAM2-based baseline achieves state-of-the-art results on both RDVSv2 and existing RGB-D VSOD benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: RDVSv2 and the baseline provide useful resources for future RGB-D VSOD and multi-modal video understanding research.

title: Rethinking Likelihood distributions: Student's t Likelihood Boosts Bayesian Neural Network Performance
summary: In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), variational inference is a widely adopted framework for modeling uncertainty in a distributional way, with the evidence lower bound (ELBO) serving as the standard objective function. Several distributions contribute to the ELBO loss, such as the prior, approximated posterior, and likelihood distribution. Typically, these distributions are all approximated by a Gaussian distribution, since it is easy to compute, allows for reparameterized gradients, and provides a closed-form loss for training. However, several works have highlighted that this assumption may not generally hold, posing the risk of model misspecification. Alternative distributions have been proposed for the prior specifically, while the effect of distribution choice on the likelihood distribution remains unexplored. In this work, our aim is to close this gap by investigating whether alternative assumptions for the likelihood distribution can outperform the commonly used Gaussian. We compare several likelihood distribution assumptions, such as skewed or heavy-tailed, across regression tasks on both artificial and real-world datasets using standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Our findings demonstrate that Student's t yields better predictive performance than a Gaussian likelihood distribution, independent of the data distribution and MLP architecture (depth and width). In some cases, Student's t can also lead to shorter training times, while still being easy to implement.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether alternative likelihood distributions (like Student's t) can outperform the standard Gaussian likelihood in Bayesian neural networks trained with variational inference, finding that Student's t consistently yields better predictive performance across regression tasks regardless of data distribution or MLP architecture.
AI.motivation: While variational inference in BNNs commonly assumes Gaussian distributions for prior, posterior, and likelihood for computational convenience, recent work has questioned this assumption due to model misspecification risk. However, the effect of alternative likelihood distribution choices remains unexplored — this gap motivates the study.
AI.method: The authors compare several likelihood distribution assumptions (e.g., skewed, heavy-tailed) against the standard Gaussian likelihood in regression tasks. They evaluate across artificial and real-world datasets using standard MLPs with varying depths and widths, under a variational inference framework.
AI.result: Student's t distribution consistently outperforms Gaussian likelihood in predictive performance across all tested settings, independent of data distribution and MLP architecture (depth and width). In some cases, Student's t also leads to shorter training times while remaining easy to implement.
AI.conclusion: The commonly used Gaussian likelihood assumption in BNNs can be suboptimal; Student's t is a simple, effective alternative that improves predictive performance and sometimes training efficiency, closing a gap in the literature on likelihood distribution choice.

title: How Often Should a Recommender Call an LLM? Value-Weighted Routing, Monitoring, and Seasonal Robustness
summary: Routing decisions between a cheap heuristic and an expensive large language model (LLM) are typically framed as a difficulty problem: send the hard cases to the expensive path. We argue this framing is incomplete because difficulty and business value are distinct axes - a difficult cheap item and a difficult costly item do not have the same cost of error. We present Value Router, a fully synthetic simulation of a retail merchandising pipeline that routes items using only estimated difficulty and estimated value, never ground truth. The study has three stages. First, a value-weighted threshold router is compared with a difficulty-only and a random baseline on a synthetic catalog with an inverse correlation between category volume and value. Value-weighting matches the difficulty-only baseline's recall of true high-value items (60%) while achieving substantially higher precision (98.3% vs. 94.3%). Second, a decision logger and monitor expose a failure mode hidden by aggregate metrics showing that the aggregate result is driven almost entirely by between-category differences rather than per-item discrimination. Third, a simulated Black Friday demand surge (2.5 volume with a shift toward higher-value categories) compares a static router, a seasonally tuned router, and two slow-path budget policies. All results are from a controlled synthetic simulation with experimenter-defined ground truth and illustrate design principles for cost-aware routing systems rather than validated real-world claims.

AI.tldr: Value Router proposes a cost-aware routing framework that uses both estimated difficulty and estimated business value to route items between a cheap heuristic and an expensive LLM. In synthetic retail simulations, value-weighted threshold routing matches recall (60%) of difficulty-only baselines while achieving higher precision (98.3% vs 94.3%) for high-value items, and reveals hidden failure modes in aggregate metrics.
AI.motivation: Current routing decisions between cheap heuristics and expensive LLMs are framed solely as a difficulty problem, ignoring that errors on high-value items are costlier than errors on low-value items. The paper argues that difficulty and business value are distinct axes, motivating a value-aware routing approach.
AI.method: A fully synthetic simulation of a retail merchandising pipeline using estimated difficulty and estimated value (no ground truth). Three stages: (1) value-weighted threshold router vs difficulty-only and random baselines on a synthetic catalog with inverse correlation between category volume and value; (2) decision logger/monitor to expose per-category vs per-item discrimination; (3) simulated Black Friday demand surge testing static router, seasonally tuned router, and two slow-path budget policies.
AI.result: Value-weighting matches difficulty-only baseline's recall of true high-value items (60%) while achieving substantially higher precision (98.3% vs 94.3%). Aggregate results are driven almost entirely by between-category differences rather than per-item discrimination, a failure mode hidden by aggregate metrics.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates design principles for cost-aware routing systems, showing that incorporating value into routing decisions improves precision on high-value items without sacrificing recall, and that aggregate metrics can mask important category-level dynamics.

title: Towards Reliable Stain Transfer: An Iterative Data-Model Co-Optimization Framework Based on Multimodal Expert-Guided Assessment
comment: 10 pages, accepted by ACMMM2026 Main Track
summary: Histopathological examination primarily relies on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining. Although IHC provides critical molecular information, it is costly and requires specialized expertise. Stain transfer provides an efficient alternative by computationally generating IHC from H&E images, but remains challenged by unified and interpretable modeling for heterogeneous biomarkers under pixel-unaligned supervision. We propose DMCoStain, a novel Data-Model Co-optimization framework for Stain transfer. It iteratively co-refines training data and model capability, improving staining accuracy and interpretability in both pathological and structural consistency. To refine training data in a clinically meaningful manner, it incorporates the Multimodal Expert-Guided Finer Selection (MEGFS) strategy, built upon a pioneering IHC-positive-expression (IPE) vision-language model (VLM) that emulates pathologist reasoning. To support MEGFS, we construct ImmunoInstruction, the first large-scale IPE instruction-following dataset with 150K VQA samples. Extensive experiments on multiple tissues and biomarkers demonstrate that DMCoStain achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy. This paradigm offers strong practical value, and MEGFS also functions as a specialized evaluation tool for future model development. Dataset, code, and more details are in https://github.com/SikangSHU/DMCoStain.

AI.tldr: DMCoStain is a data-model co-optimization framework for stain transfer that iteratively refines training data and model capability to generate IHC images from H&E, using a novel MEGFS strategy powered by an IPE vision-language model and the ImmunoInstruction dataset of 150K VQA samples, achieving SOTA accuracy across multiple tissues and biomarkers.
AI.motivation: IHC staining provides critical molecular information but is costly and requires specialized expertise; stain transfer offers an efficient computational alternative, but existing methods struggle with unified and interpretable modeling for heterogeneous biomarkers under pixel-unaligned supervision.
AI.method: A Data-Model Co-optimization (DMCoStain) framework that iteratively co-refines training data and model capability; incorporates the Multimodal Expert-Guided Finer Selection (MEGFS) strategy based on an IHC-positive-expression (IPE) vision-language model (VLM) that emulates pathologist reasoning; supported by ImmunoInstruction, the first large-scale IPE instruction-following dataset with 150K VQA samples.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) accuracy across multiple tissues and biomarkers in stain transfer.
AI.conclusion: DMCoStain offers strong practical value for stain transfer; the MEGFS strategy also functions as a specialized evaluation tool for future model development.

title: Learned, Relied Upon, or Necessary? Separating Checkpoint Dependence from Task-Level Value in Sheaf GNNs
summary: Learned restriction maps in sheaf graph neural networks are often treated as proof that the model has discovered useful edge geometry. That conclusion does not follow from parameter movement or from a post-hoc ablation: both can show how one checkpoint is organized while leaving open whether learned transport still helps after the rest of the model adapts. We separate these claims with two estimands. Checkpoint reliance intervenes on the maps of a fixed predictor; protocol-relative replacement retrains matched families that remove map capacity, edge variation, or persistent edge assignment. A task-null theorem shows why the claims can diverge: labels identify only the transported classifier directions, leaving $d^2-d$ invisible degrees of freedom in every full $d\times d$ map. An exact frame model then gives the boundary at which reliance becomes unreplaced task value. Label-only training realizes the predicted separation, while audits of public NSD, DNSD, and Directed Sheaf Neural Network (DSNN) implementations recover both replaceable and unreplaced transport regimes on real graphs. All five DNSD benchmarks exhibit fixed-checkpoint reliance. After retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover Full performance on four; Roman-Empire retains a $.0675$ advantage over continually resampled assignment and a $.0391$ advantage over a parameter-matched shared map across ten official splits. Thus, a learned map can govern a fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry. Claims of learned transport should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that learned restriction maps in sheaf graph neural networks can show checkpoint reliance (intervening on a fixed model) without being irreplaceable (surviving retraining with controls). The authors introduce two estimands—checkpoint reliance and protocol-relative replacement—and prove a task-null theorem showing that only transported classifier directions are label-identified, leaving d²-d invisible degrees of freedom. Using an exact frame model and audits of NSD, DNSD, and DSNN implementations, they find that all five DNSD benchmarks exhibit fixed-checkpoint reliance, but after retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover Full performance on four. Only Roman-Empire retains small advantages (0.0675 over resampled assignment, 0.0391 over shared map). The authors conclude that learned maps can govern fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry, and recommend pairing checkpoint interventions with matched retraining.
AI.motivation: To separate two conflated claims about learned restriction maps in sheaf GNNs: whether a map is relied upon in a fixed predictor (checkpoint reliance) versus whether it provides irreplaceable task value that cannot be recovered by retrained controls (protocol-relative replacement). The authors aim to show these claims can diverge and to establish rigorous methodology for testing learned transport.
AI.method: The paper defines two estimands: checkpoint reliance (intervening on maps of a fixed predictor) and protocol-relative replacement (retraining matched families that remove map capacity, edge variation, or persistent edge assignment). A task-null theorem is proved to show why claims can diverge (only d label-identified directions in d×d maps). An exact frame model gives the boundary between reliance and irreplaceable value. Label-only training and audits of public NSD, DNSD, and DSNN implementations are conducted.
AI.result: All five DNSD benchmarks show fixed-checkpoint reliance. After retraining, assignment-breaking or shared-map controls recover Full performance on four of five benchmarks. Roman-Empire retains a 0.0675 advantage over continually resampled assignment and a 0.0391 advantage over a parameter-matched shared map across ten official splits.
AI.conclusion: A learned restriction map can govern a fitted computation without constituting indispensable edge geometry. Claims of learned transport should pair checkpoint interventions with matched retraining to distinguish reliance from irreplaceable task value.

title: Towards an Agent Operating System - Lessons from Classical and Cloud OS
summary: Every major wave of platform software follows the same arc: an initial period of experimentation with competing frameworks and ad-hoc implementations, followed by the articulation of a small set of stable abstractions with well-defined semantics, and finally consolidation around those abstractions into a platform that applications can portably target. POSIX did this for classical operating systems; Kubernetes did it for the cloud. Agentic AI systems - autonomous, LLM-driven agents that plan, use tools, maintain memory, and collaborate - are currently in the experimentation phase of the third such wave. dozens of frameworks and protocols have emerged, but no community consensus exists on what the core abstractions are or what guarantees they carry. Without that consensus, agentic applications cannot be written portably, platforms cannot compose reliably, and the field cannot advance beyond prototype deployments. We argue that the path forward is to follow the prior-wave methodology: derive new agentic abstractions by extending classical OS and cloud OS primitives to stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution, specify their semantics precisely, and consolidate around them - just as POSIX and Kubernetes consolidated their respective waves.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that agentic AI systems are in an experimental phase similar to early OS and cloud platforms, and proposes consolidating around stable abstractions—extending classical OS/cloud primitives to stochastic, LLM-driven execution—to enable portable, composable, and reliable agentic applications.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems currently lack community consensus on core abstractions and semantics, preventing portable applications, reliable platform composition, and advancement beyond prototypes.
AI.method: Follow the methodology of prior waves (POSIX, Kubernetes): derive new agentic abstractions by extending classical OS and cloud OS primitives to stochastic, natural-language-mediated execution, and specify their semantics precisely.
AI.result: No empirical results presented; the paper provides a conceptual argument and roadmap for abstraction consolidation in agentic AI.
AI.conclusion: Consolidating around well-defined agentic abstractions—analogous to POSIX and Kubernetes—is necessary for the field to achieve portability, composability, and production-grade deployment.

title: ANFI: Rethinking Neighbor Feature Interaction in Person Re-ID
summary: In person re-identification, neighbor-based methods have achieved significant success by interacting with neighbor samples to obtain more robust representations. However, existing methods rely only on affinity relations, causing their success to depend heavily on the reliability of selected neighbors. We find that affinity-only interaction often fails in challenging scenarios due to the inevitable presence of noisy neighbors. To enable effective interactions under noisy neighborhoods, we revisit neighbor-based methods under distinct reliability conditions and propose a novel Adaptive Neighbor Feature Interaction (ANFI) method. The core idea of ANFI is to account for negative effects from noisy neighbors, allowing samples to remain distinguishable from false positive neighbors. Unlike existing methods, ANFI models not only affinity relations but also discrepancy relations, and employs sample-wise adaptive weighting for these two types of relations. Given that capturing negative effects from noisy neighbors differs significantly from traditional relation learning, we derive discrepancy relations from a new neighborhood similarity, which provides more information than pairwise similarity. In addition, we propose Noisy Relation Supervision (NRS) to train ANFI, gradually injecting robustness to noisy relations into the model. Extensive experiments conducted under standard, cross-modal, and cross-domain settings, including comparisons with neighbor-based methods and re-ranking methods, demonstrate the superiority of our method across various neighbor distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adaptive Neighbor Feature Interaction (ANFI), a method that improves person re-identification by modeling both affinity and discrepancy relations with adaptive weighting, along with Noisy Relation Supervision (NRS) to handle noisy neighbors effectively.
AI.motivation: Existing neighbor-based methods rely solely on affinity relations and fail in challenging scenarios due to noisy neighbors, making their success heavily dependent on neighbor reliability.
AI.method: ANFI models both affinity and discrepancy relations with sample-wise adaptive weighting, derives discrepancy relations from a new neighborhood similarity, and uses Noisy Relation Supervision (NRS) to train the model with robustness to noisy relations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments under standard, cross-modal, and cross-domain settings show superiority over existing neighbor-based and re-ranking methods across various neighbor distributions.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both affinity and discrepancy relations with adaptive weighting, guided by noise-aware supervision, enables effective neighbor-based feature interaction even under noisy neighborhood conditions.

title: TWICE: Two-Clock, Two-Window Learning for Long-Horizon Conversion Prediction in Online Advertising
summary:
Long-horizon conversion prediction under delayed feedback creates a two-clock, two-window learning problem in online advertising. A short base observation window releases recent clicks on the click clock before their outcomes mature, whereas conversions continue to arrive on the conversion clock throughout a longer target conversion window. The click clock provides timely but partially observed status supervision. The conversion clock reveals long-tail delays, but the delay composition within an arrival-time slice is weighted by historical click cohorts with different traffic volumes and target-window conversion rates.
  We present TWICE, a framework that factorizes long-horizon post-click conversion rate (CVR) into a target-window conversion probability and a grouped elapsed-delay cumulative distribution function (CDF). The two clocks provide complementary supervision. Click-clock records train the target-window CVR head through a current-status likelihood over the base observation window. Newly arrived conversions train the delay model on the conversion clock. To account for the cohort mixture, TWICE uses fixed click-time predicted CVR (pCVR) mass as cohort exposure in an arrival-conditioned likelihood. This accounts for differences in cohort traffic and conversion propensity. The resulting aggregate records are self-contained. A single learned CDF produces monotone predictions for all requested horizons up to the target conversion window. Serving requires neither historical lookup nor convolution. Experiments on a public benchmark and an industrial advertising dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of TWICE. In an online A/B test in Kwai's advertising system, TWICE increased expected revenue, revenue, and conversions by 2.486%, 1.858%, and 2.061%, respectively. It was subsequently deployed to full traffic.

AI.tldr: TWICE is a framework for long-horizon post-click conversion rate prediction under delayed feedback, using a two-clock (click and conversion) learning system. It factorizes CVR into a target-window conversion probability and a grouped elapsed-delay CDF, using click-clock records for current-status supervision and conversion-clock arrivals for delay modeling, with cohort-mixture weighting via fixed pCVR mass. It achieved significant revenue and conversion gains in an online A/B test at Kwai.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon conversion prediction under delayed feedback presents a two-clock, two-window learning problem: the click clock provides timely but partially observed supervision (via a short base observation window), while the conversion clock reveals long-tail delays but suffers from cohort mixture with varying traffic volumes and conversion rates. Existing methods struggle to jointly handle these two clocks effectively.
AI.method: TWICE factorizes post-click CVR into a target-window conversion probability (trained via click-clock records with a current-status likelihood) and a grouped elapsed-delay CDF (trained on conversion-clock arrivals). An arrival-conditioned likelihood uses fixed click-time pCVR mass as cohort exposure to account for differences in cohort traffic and conversion propensity. The learned CDF produces monotone predictions for all horizons up to the target window without requiring historical lookup or convolution.
AI.result: On a public benchmark and an industrial advertising dataset, TWICE outperformed baselines. In an online A/B test at Kwai's advertising system, it increased expected revenue by 2.486%, revenue by 1.858%, and conversions by 2.061%, and was subsequently deployed to full traffic.
AI.conclusion: TWICE effectively addresses the two-clock delayed feedback problem by factorizing CVR and using complementary supervision from both clocks with cohort-aware weighting. It produces monotonic horizon predictions and is practically deployable, as demonstrated by significant online gains and full deployment at Kwai.

title: PLATO: Pointer Learner for Agent and Task Openness
summary: Open agent systems (OASYS) are increasingly prevalent in real-world domains where the sets of agents and tasks change unpredictably over time. Such openness, including agent openness (AO) and task openness (TO), poses a fundamental challenge to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), which typically assumes fixed state and action spaces. Existing methods address openness only partially: padding and masking approaches introduce artificial bounds, while recent graph-based or hypergraph methods handle one dimension of openness but still depend on restrictive assumptions. In this paper, we introduce Pointer Learner for Agent and Task Openness (PLATO), a pointer-network-based actor combined with a centralized graph neural network (GNN) critic, trained with multi-agent proximal policy optimization under a centralized training and decentralized execution paradigm. Our pointer-based actor outputs distributions directly over the current task set. This directly supports changing action spaces without masking or retraining. Our GNN critic encodes agent-task interactions as a graph that changes shape with task and agent composition. Together, these components consider AO and TO without the boundedness of existing approaches. We formalize PLATO in a Task-and-Agent-Open Markov Game (TaAgO-MG), extending prior task-open formulations, and prove it is well-defined over the resulting unbounded state and action spaces. We evaluate PLATO with the Methods for Open Agent Systems Evaluation Initiative (MOASEI) wildfire suppression domain, an environment designed for open multi-agent system evaluation, and we demonstrate strong performance and more consistent zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art baselines in OASYS.

AI.tldr: PLATO is a pointer-network-based MARL method that handles both agent and task openness in open agent systems without the limitations of padding, masking, or other bounded approaches, achieving strong zero-shot generalization in wildfire suppression domains.
AI.motivation: Open agent systems have agents and tasks that change unpredictably, but existing MARL methods assume fixed state/action spaces and only partially address openness through artificial bounds or restrictive assumptions.
AI.method: PLATO uses a pointer-network-based actor that outputs distributions directly over current task sets, combined with a centralized GNN critic that encodes agent-task interactions as dynamic graphs, trained with MAPPO under CTDE.
AI.result: PLATO demonstrates strong performance and more consistent zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art baselines in the MOASEI wildfire suppression domain.
AI.conclusion: PLATO handles both agent and task openness without bounded assumptions, is well-defined over unbounded state/action spaces, and generalizes effectively to unseen open settings.

title: Bi-Level Collaborative Learning for Few-Shot Scribble-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Scribble annotations offer an efficient alternative to costly pixel-wise labeling for medical image segmentation, yet in real clinical scenarios, scribble-annotated samples are often still limited, imposing the dual challenges of sparse supervision and annotated sample scarcity. These compounded constraints severely deprive models of the structural evidence needed for complete region recovery and precise boundary delineation. To break this bottleneck, we propose a bi-level collaborative learning framework for few-shot scribble-supervised medical image segmentation. Specifically, an upper-level learnable superpixel model is introduced to provide region-structural priors for lower-level segmentation, while superpixel-based region-wise pseudo-label propagation and a spatial-prior-guided filtering strategy are performed to generate reliable dense pseudo-labels for segmentation learning. Meanwhile, the anatomical semantics learned by the lower-level segmentation model under the guidance of the current superpixels are fed back to the upper level, further driving it to learn region-structural representations better aligned with the segmentation task. Through bidirectional interaction and collaborative learning between the upper and lower levels, the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art scribble-supervised methods on the ACDC and Prostate datasets under the few-shot scribble-supervised setting.

AI.tldr: A bi-level collaborative learning framework for few-shot scribble-supervised medical image segmentation, where an upper-level superpixel model provides region-structural priors and the lower-level segmentation model feeds back anatomical semantics, achieving state-of-the-art results on ACDC and Prostate datasets.
AI.motivation: Scribble annotations reduce labeling cost but in real clinical scenarios, scribble-annotated samples are often limited, imposing dual challenges of sparse supervision and annotated sample scarcity, which deprive models of structural evidence for complete region recovery and precise boundary delineation.
AI.method: A bi-level collaborative learning framework with: (1) an upper-level learnable superpixel model providing region-structural priors; (2) superpixel-based region-wise pseudo-label propagation and spatial-prior-guided filtering for reliable dense pseudo-labels; (3) lower-level segmentation model feeding back anatomical semantics to the upper level for better alignment with the segmentation task through bidirectional interaction.
AI.result: Significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art scribble-supervised methods on ACDC and Prostate datasets under the few-shot scribble-supervised setting.
AI.conclusion: The bidirectional interaction and collaborative learning between upper and lower levels effectively breaks the bottleneck of sparse supervision and sample scarcity in few-shot scribble-supervised medical image segmentation.

title: SPARC Segmentation to Prediction via Affine Regression and Counterfactuals
summary: Transaction propensity prediction in B2B e commerce presents unique challenges distinct from B2C contexts, primarily due to the heterogeneous procurement behaviors of organizational entities, which violate SMOTE's implicit assumption of within class feature homogeneity. Specifically, B2B buyers exhibit multi modal procurement cycles that render linear interpolation between minority class samples structurally invalid, producing synthetic data that does not represent real purchasing behavior. This paper introduces a production deployed propensity modeling framework designed to address these complexities through two primary contributions. First, we replace conventional SMOTE based augmentation with a synthetic data generation approach leveraging Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE). This method produces minority class samples with superior distributional fidelity compared to SMOTE, as validated through quantitative proximity analysis and UMAP cluster visualization. Second, we adapt the PyPARC piecewise affine classification framework to generate calibrated propensity probabilities, facilitating the interpretable segmentation of customers into actionable risk tiers. Evaluated on two years of longitudinal data from a large scale B2B e commerce platform with a 1 to 9 class imbalance ratio, the proposed architecture achieves 93.1% precision at a decision threshold of 0.8, a 9.2 percentage point improvement over SMOTE based baselines at the same threshold (83.9%), and a 26.1 point improvement over SMOTE at threshold 0.7 (66.04%), demonstrating consistent superiority across operating points. These results demonstrate the framework's efficacy in enabling high precision marketing campaigns with significant improvements in customer activation and return on investment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a B2B transaction propensity prediction framework that replaces SMOTE with DiCE-based counterfactual synthetic data generation and adapts PyPARC for calibrated propensity scoring, achieving 93.1% precision (9.2 pp improvement over SMOTE) on a 1:9 imbalanced B2B e-commerce dataset.
AI.motivation: B2B transaction propensity prediction is fundamentally different from B2C due to heterogeneous organizational procurement behaviors and multi-modal purchasing cycles, which violate SMOTE's assumption of within-class feature homogeneity. Linear interpolation between minority class samples produces structurally invalid synthetic data that does not reflect real B2B buying patterns.
AI.method: (1) Replaces SMOTE-based augmentation with Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) for synthetic minority class generation, producing samples with higher distributional fidelity. (2) Adapts the PyPARC piecewise affine classification framework to generate calibrated propensity probabilities for interpretable customer risk tier segmentation.
AI.result: On a large-scale B2B platform dataset (2 years, 1:9 imbalance), the framework achieves 93.1% precision at threshold 0.8, outperforming SMOTE baselines by 9.2 pp (83.9%) at the same threshold and by 26.1 pp (66.04%) at threshold 0.7.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables high-precision B2B marketing campaigns with significant improvements in customer activation and ROI, demonstrating consistent superiority across operating points for production-deployed propensity modeling.

title: Matryoshka Agent: Unfolding Sub-Agents for Long-Horizon Machine Learning Engineering
summary: Machine learning engineering (MLE) tasks require long-horizon decision making over iterative solution debugging and refinement, under expensive and feedback-driven environment interactions. Developing and training a monolithic agent for such tasks is fundamentally challenging, as it must simultaneously manage extremely long and noisy contexts, explore vast solution spaces, and remain effective under limited model capacity and computational budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Matryoshka Agent, a unified hierarchical agent framework for complex long-horizon tasks. Matryoshka Agent decomposes agentic problem solving into a coordinated hierarchy of decision making and execution: a high-level Orchestrator maintains compact, long-horizon exploration states and issues strategic instructions, while lower-level Sub-Agents execute concrete solution attempts through direct environment interaction, mediated by standardized Tool interface.
