This design decouples strategic exploration from costly execution, substantially reducing the burden of long-context reasoning and enabling efficient iterative refinement. We further develop an efficient training paradigm for Matryoshka Agent. Experimental results on a broad range of MLE tasks with diverse model types and scales demonstrate that Matryoshka Agent is an effective and scalable paradigm for long-horizon MLE tasks and complex agentic problem solving. Notably, Matryoshka Agent enables Qwen3-4B-Instruct to reach Orchestrator performance comparable to o4-mini. Applying Matryoshka Agent to Qwen3-30B-Coder results in at most 36.7% relative performance gain.

AI.tldr: Matryoshka Agent is a hierarchical framework that decomposes complex long-horizon MLE tasks into a high-level Orchestrator (strategic planning) and low-level Sub-Agents (execution), enabling efficient iterative refinement under limited budgets. It achieves strong performance, e.g., Qwen3-4B-Instruct matches o4-mini, and Qwen3-30B-Coder gains up to 36.7%.
AI.motivation: Monolithic agents struggle with long-horizon MLE tasks due to noisy long contexts, vast solution spaces, and limited model capacity/compute. A new architecture is needed to decouple strategic exploration from costly execution.
AI.method: A unified hierarchical agent framework with an Orchestrator (maintains compact long-horizon states, issues strategic instructions) and Sub-Agents (execute concrete solutions via Tool interface). Includes an efficient training paradigm for this hierarchy.
AI.result: Matryoshka Agent enables Qwen3-4B-Instruct to match o4-mini's Orchestrator performance, and applying it to Qwen3-30B-Coder yields up to 36.7% relative improvement across diverse MLE tasks and model scales.
AI.conclusion: Matryoshka Agent is an effective and scalable paradigm for long-horizon MLE tasks and complex agentic problem solving, substantially reducing long-context reasoning burden while enabling efficient iterative refinement.

title: Reading Legends on Ancient Coins: An Object Detection Approach for Character Recognition on a Novel Roman Republican Dataset
summary: When it comes to the proper classification of ancient coins with respect to their time and issuer, the textual inscriptions on these coins, also known as legends, are of paramount importance. These legends consist of alphabets or characters still used in English. This paper addresses image based character recognition on ancient Roman Republican coins via a deep learning based object detection strategy. However, legends on these coins pose high variation due to non-uniform placement, primitive inscription techniques, and wear and tear. Additional challenges include inconsistent imaging conditions such as illumination, orientation, and scale. To accommodate these, we gathered a novel large-scale dataset of 5,654 Roman Republican coin images, manually annotated with 21 character labels, totaling 38,808 annotations. For recognition, we use You Only Look Once (YOLO) variants: YOLOv3, v4, v5, v7, and v8. YOLOv7-Large achieves the best mAP50 of 90.4%, followed by YOLOv7-Extended and YOLOv7-xl with 90.2% and 90.1%, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper uses YOLO-based object detection models (v3-v8) to recognize character inscriptions (legends) on ancient Roman Republican coins from a new dataset of 5,654 images with 38,808 annotations, achieving best mAP50 of 90.4% with YOLOv7-Large.
AI.motivation: Proper classification of ancient coins by time and issuer relies heavily on textual inscriptions (legends), but these legends are difficult to recognize due to non-uniform placement, primitive inscription techniques, wear and tear, and inconsistent imaging conditions.
AI.method: A deep learning-based object detection strategy using YOLO variants (v3, v4, v5, v7, v8) was employed on a novel dataset of 5,654 Roman Republican coin images with 21 character labels and 38,808 manual annotations.
AI.result: YOLOv7-Large achieved the best performance with mAP50 of 90.4%, followed by YOLOv7-Extended (90.2%) and YOLOv7-xl (90.1%).
AI.conclusion: YOLOv7 variants outperform other YOLO versions for character recognition on ancient Roman Republican coin legends, demonstrating the feasibility of deep learning-based object detection for this challenging task.

title: PIcsC: Partitioning-Induced Covariate Shift Correction
summary: Covariate shift across training-data partitions biases model selection and parameter estimation in cross-validation, lifelong learning, and federated learning. We propose \textit{Partition-Induced Covariate-shift Correction} (\texttt{PIcsC}), a Fisher information-based regularization framework that mitigates distribution mismatch between data partitions and a reference distribution. \texttt{PIcsC} approximates partition divergence using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and incorporates the resulting statistic as a regularizer during optimization. The same formulation applies to both centrally partitioned datasets (batches or cross-validation folds) and inherently distributed data (federated clients or decentralized nodes), requiring only partition-local gradient statistics rather than raw data. We further introduce a conditional adaptation mechanism that combines FIM shift with KL divergence to detect significant distribution shifts and activates regularization only when necessary. Experiments on more than 40 datasets demonstrate consistent improvements under both natural and synthetic covariate shift. On fragmented batch and fold settings, \texttt{PIcsC} reduces fragmentation-induced performance degradation by more than 20\% and 25\%, respectively. On seven federated learning benchmarks, it consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3 -5 percentage points without requiring client-specific personalization. These results demonstrate that Fisher information provides an effective and unified mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across both centralized and distributed learning.

AI.tldr: PIcsC is a Fisher information-based regularization framework that corrects covariate shift across data partitions in centralized and distributed learning, improving performance by over 20% in fragmented settings and 3-5% in federated learning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Covariate shift across training-data partitions biases model selection and parameter estimation in cross-validation, lifelong learning, and federated learning, necessitating a unified correction mechanism.
AI.method: Proposes PIcsC, which approximates partition divergence using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and incorporates it as a regularizer during optimization, with a conditional adaptation mechanism combining FIM shift with KL divergence to activate regularization only when necessary. Requires only partition-local gradient statistics rather than raw data.
AI.result: On over 40 datasets: reduces fragmentation-induced performance degradation by >20% in batch settings and >25% in fold settings; outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD by 3-5% on seven federated learning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Fisher information provides an effective and unified mechanism for mitigating partition-induced covariate shift across both centralized and distributed learning paradigms.

title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning for Small-Scale Language Model Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC), Bellevue, WA, USA
summary: The alignment of Small Language Models (SLMs) in the 70--500M parameter range using reinforcement learning is often considered unstable, though the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically investigated. In the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) research, fifteen (model, corpus) configurations were trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The experiments included Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M and SmolLM2-135M, 360M on the TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103 corpora. Three reproducible failure modes were identified in small-scale language models: silent LoRA parameter freezing in standard PEFT/TRL pipelines, numerical overflow in importance ratios when using bfloat16, and catastrophic policy collapse due to reward-model error. These issues were addressed using a merge-and-reinitialize adapter technique, float32 precision during PPO updates, and a three-layer safety mechanism comprising reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, and weight rollback. In this paper, a capacity-headroom hypothesis is proposed, which states that PPO performance at the SLM scale depends on both a fluent supervised model ($\text{PPL}<20$) and a discriminative reward signal, rather than on the number of model parameters. The proposed system converged stably in all experiments and improved preference win rate over the SFT baseline in configurations with a fluent prior and an informative reward signal. Furthermore, it outperformed instruction-tuned baselines while requiring significantly less training data. All checkpoints, preference datasets, and training scripts are publicly released$^§$.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates failure modes in reinforcement learning (PPO) for Small Language Models (70M-500M parameters), identifies three reproducible issues (silent LoRA freezing, numerical overflow in bfloat16, catastrophic policy collapse), proposes fixes (merge-and-reinitialize adapter, float32 precision, three-layer safety mechanism), and introduces a capacity-headroom hypothesis linking PPO success to fluent supervised models (PPL<20) and discriminative reward signals rather than parameter count.
AI.motivation: PPO-based alignment of SLMs (70M-500M) is considered unstable but the underlying failure mechanisms have not been systematically investigated.
AI.method: Trained 15 (model, corpus) configurations using PPO with Pythia-70M/160M/410M and SmolLM2-135M/360M on TinyStories, CNN/DailyMail, and Wikitext-103. Identified three failure modes and proposed fixes: merge-and-reinitialize adapter, float32 precision, three-layer safety mechanism (reward whitening, importance-ratio guarding, weight rollback). Proposed capacity-headroom hypothesis.
AI.result: Proposed system converged stably in all experiments, improved preference win rate over SFT baseline in configurations with fluent prior and informative reward signal, outperformed instruction-tuned baselines with less training data.
AI.conclusion: PPO performance at SLM scale depends on a fluent supervised model (PPL<20) and a discriminative reward signal, not on parameter count. All checkpoints, datasets, and scripts publicly released.

title: DensFiLM: Density-Conditioned Video Saliency for Crowd Scenes
summary: Video saliency models typically apply a single fixation strategy across crowd scenes, despite systematic changes in attention with crowd density. Sparse scenes encourage tracking individuals, whereas dense scenes shift attention toward collective motion and scene-level landmarks. We introduce DensFiLM, a density-conditioned video saliency model that inserts a lightweight Feature-wise Linear Modulation layer at the bottleneck of a Video Swin Transformer. A learned density embedding produces channel-wise scale and shift parameters, allowing the decoder to reconstruct saliency from features selected for each density regime. The module adds only ~100K parameters and can use either CrowdFix density labels or the model's own density prediction. On CrowdFix, DensFiLM achieves mean NSS 1.434 and CC 0.517 over four seeds, improving over ACLNet by 14.7% and 14.9%, respectively, while predicted-density conditioning matches oracle-label performance. Ablations show that explicit RAFT optical flow and larger temporal and social-force extensions provide no further improvement in this setting. In a centre-prior-subtraction diagnostic, density conditioning yields an NSS gain of 0.462 over the unconditioned backbone, compared with 0.124 under standard evaluation. These results show that lightweight bottleneck conditioning provides a more effective inductive bias than increasing model capacity for crowd-video saliency. Our code is available at https://github.com/aniskhan25/crowdfix-saliency.

AI.tldr: DensFiLM is a lightweight density-conditioned video saliency model that adds a Feature-wise Linear Modulation layer to a Video Swin Transformer, achieving significant improvements in crowd saliency prediction with only ~100K extra parameters.
AI.motivation: Video saliency models typically apply a single fixation strategy across crowd scenes, ignoring systematic changes in attention with crowd density (sparse vs. dense crowds).
AI.method: DensFiLM inserts a lightweight Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) layer at the bottleneck of a Video Swin Transformer. A learned density embedding produces channel-wise scale and shift parameters, enabling the decoder to reconstruct saliency from density-specific features. The module (~100K parameters) can use either CrowdFix density labels or its own predicted density.
AI.result: On CrowdFix, DensFiLM achieves mean NSS 1.434 and CC 0.517 over four seeds, improving over ACLNet by 14.7% and 14.9%. Predicted-density conditioning matches oracle-label performance. In a centre-prior-subtraction diagnostic, density conditioning yields NSS gain of 0.462 vs. 0.124 under standard evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight bottleneck conditioning provides a more effective inductive bias than increasing model capacity for crowd-video saliency. Explicit optical flow and larger temporal/social-force extensions offer no further improvement.

title: Bits and Memories: Measuring Verbatim Extraction Across LLM Quantization
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories. Data and results: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AkshaySasi/bits-and-memories
summary: Language models are almost always quantized before they are deployed, and a growing line of work asks whether quantization also lowers their privacy risk. That work measures privacy almost entirely with membership inference. We think this is the wrong thing to measure for the risk that most people actually worry about, namely a model reproducing its training data word for word, and we measure that directly. Using the Pythia models and the public set of sequences each of them is known to have memorized, we track verbatim extraction across five precision levels, from full precision down to four bits, and across three model sizes, while measuring general capability (perplexity) at every point. We find two things. Quantization is a selective forgetter: verbatim memorization falls off faster than capability at every precision and every model size we tried, and this holds under two unrelated quantization algorithms and two evaluation corpora. But the selectivity is not enough to make quantization a privacy defense, which cuts against the optimistic reading of earlier membership-inference results. At the largest model we study, four-bit quantization still reproduces most of the memorized sequences while giving up only a few percent of capability, and the fraction of memorized data that survives quantization grows with model size. We conclude that compression should not be treated as a way to remove memorized training data, and that extraction, not membership inference, is the number practitioners should be watching. All code, sampled evaluation data, and per-configuration results are released.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether quantizing language models (reducing precision) helps protect privacy by reducing verbatim memorization. The authors find that quantization selectively forgets memorized data more than it degrades general capability, but not enough to be an effective privacy defense—especially for larger models where most memorized sequences survive 4-bit quantization.
AI.motivation: Prior work measured privacy risk from quantization almost exclusively via membership inference, but the authors argue this misses what people actually worry about: models reproducing training data word-for-word. They directly measure verbatim extraction to assess real privacy risk.
AI.method: Using Pythia models with known memorized sequences, the authors track verbatim extraction across five precision levels (full precision down to 4 bits), three model sizes, two quantization algorithms, and two evaluation corpora, while also measuring perplexity as a capability metric.
AI.result: Quantization selectively forgets memorized data faster than it degrades capability across all settings. However, at the largest model, 4-bit quantization still reproduces most memorized sequences with only a small capability loss. The fraction of memorized data surviving quantization increases with model size.
AI.conclusion: Compression should not be treated as a privacy defense for removing memorized training data. Extraction (not membership inference) is the metric practitioners should monitor for real privacy risk.

title: ScalableRAG: High-Quality RAG at Zero Ingestion Cost
summary:
Recent advances in RAG aim to optimize for performance by paying high ingestion costs for knowledge ingestion: building knowledge graphs or extracting SQL tables. In this work we show that the operations that such knowledge bases allow can be replicated with zero ingestion costs (not even a vector database); in fact our solution, Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG, handily out-performs all baselines (including knowledge graph approaches) in three out of the six corpora considered here, and only marginally missing maximum performance on the other three, with average accuracy across all six datasets 7.36% above the next most competitive baseline. It achieves this by keeping a workspace of document sets and values sets that it can write into and read from, allowing for on-the-fly aggregative reasoning in all situations where grouping is required on a primary key that is in one to one correspondence with a subset of the total document set.
  Capping the number of LLM calls by a constant independent of the corpus size, we also introduce Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG, which does use a minimal vector database as well as an automated pattern discovery from a sample of documents, to further improve accuracy at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/cohesity/ScalableRAG .

AI.tldr: Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG achieves strong RAG performance without any ingestion costs by using a workspace of document/value sets for on-the-fly aggregative reasoning. A variant, Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG, adds minimal vector DB and automated pattern discovery for improved accuracy at scale.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG approaches optimize performance by paying high ingestion costs (knowledge graphs, SQL tables). The authors aim to show that comparable or better results can be achieved with zero ingestion overhead, without even a vector database.
AI.method: Zero-Ingestion ScalableRAG maintains a workspace of document sets and value sets for reading/writing, enabling on-the-fly aggregative reasoning when grouping is required on a primary key in one-to-one correspondence with a document subset. Limited-Ingestion ScalableRAG additionally uses a minimal vector database and automated pattern discovery from document samples, with LLM calls capped by a constant independent of corpus size.
AI.result: Outperforms all baselines (including knowledge graph approaches) in 3 of 6 corpora, and marginally misses maximum performance on the other 3. Average accuracy across all six datasets is 7.36% above the next most competitive baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that high ingestion costs are unnecessary for strong RAG performance; zero-ingestion methods can match or exceed knowledge-graph-based approaches.

title: Seen, Said, or Forgotten? A Causal Audit of Visual KV Memory Across Dialog Turns
summary: Stateful multimodal assistants encode an image once but may answer questions about it many turns later. Attention-guided visual-KV eviction assumes that evidence irrelevant now will remain dispensable, although future questions are unknown. We ask when a visual fact is actually safe to forget and introduce the Causal Visual Memory Audit (CVMA), a paired single-prefill framework that tests what later answers lose when a visual region, the whole image, or prior assistant text becomes unavailable. On VisDial and ConvBench, current attention can rank future-useful regions worse than random even though a diagnostic marginal-utility control shows substantial selection headroom. Aggregate scores hide this failure when later turns do not need vision; controlled and stock-generated histories reveal a second escape route, in which assistant-text KV replaces image KV for facts already stated but not reliably for unstated facts. In the tested stacks, safe forgetting is supported by low future visual dependence or fact-specific verbalization---not by low current attention.

AI.tldr: Current attention-based visual-KV eviction in multimodal assistants is unreliable for future question answering, as evidenced by the proposed CVMA framework showing that visual regions ranked poorly by attention can still be critical later, and safe forgetting relies on low future visual dependence or verbalization of facts, not low current attention.
AI.motivation: To determine when a visual fact is actually safe to forget in stateful multimodal assistants, given that attention-guided visual-KV eviction assumes irrelevant evidence now will remain dispensable, which may be invalid for unknown future questions.
AI.method: Introduces Causal Visual Memory Audit (CVMA), a paired single-prefill framework that tests what later answers lose when a visual region, the whole image, or prior assistant text becomes unavailable. Evaluated on VisDial and ConvBench.
AI.result: Current attention can rank future-useful regions worse than random; aggregate scores hide failure when later turns don't need vision; assistant-text KV can replace image KV for stated facts but not reliably for unstated facts.
AI.conclusion: Safe forgetting is supported by low future visual dependence or fact-specific verbalization, not by low current attention.

title: Emergent Latent-State Computation under Stochastic Volatility
summary: Mechanistic interpretability has largely focused on language models and deterministic toy tasks. Much less is known about how sequence models internally represent latent stochastic dynamics under noisy, partially observed observations. We study this question in a controlled multivariate stochastic volatility setting, where models observe only returns while the ground-truth latent volatility state is known to the researcher. This setting provides a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under partial observability: the latent state is hidden from the model but directly available for evaluation. Across architectures, losses, and output heads, we find evidence for a two-stage computation. Hidden representations encode substantial information about the next latent volatility state, and the output head maps this representation to squared return forecasts. Furthermore, in Transformers, latent-state decodability emerges at identifiable architectural stages whose location depends on the volatility period. In long-cycle regimes, this computation simplifies into an explicit latent-state filter consisting of a learned linear projection followed by $\ell^2$ normalization. Output-head replacement further shows that part of the degradation under noisy MSE training arises from readout misalignment rather than representation failure. These results suggest that stochastic volatility models provide a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under noisy latent dynamics and partial observability.

AI.tldr: This paper studies mechanistic interpretability of sequence models (including Transformers) under noisy, partially observed stochastic volatility dynamics, finding evidence for two-stage computation where hidden representations encode latent volatility states and output heads map them to forecasts; in Transformers, latent-state decodability emerges at identifiable stages depending on volatility period, and long-cycle regimes simplify to an explicit learned filter with linear projection and ℓ² normalization.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability has focused on language models and deterministic tasks, but little is known about how sequence models internally represent latent stochastic dynamics under noisy, partially observed observations.
AI.method: The authors study controlled multivariate stochastic volatility settings where models observe only returns while ground-truth latent volatility is known. They analyze hidden representations across architectures, losses, and output heads, examining decodability of latent states and computational stages.
AI.result: Evidence for two-stage computation: hidden representations encode next latent volatility state, and output heads map to squared return forecasts. In Transformers, latent-state decodability emerges at identifiable stages depending on volatility period. Long-cycle regimes simplify to a learned linear projection + ℓ² normalization filter. Output-head replacement shows degradation under noisy MSE training is partly due to readout misalignment, not representation failure.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic volatility models provide a useful benchmark for mechanistic interpretability under noisy latent dynamics and partial observability.

title: Less Data, Better Alignment: Data-Centric Multi-Evaluator Agreement for Preference Optimization
summary: Research on preference optimization often varies the training objective while holding the data fixed. We instead ask whether a small, high-confidence set of on-policy responses can provide a reliable learning signal. Our method, DMAPO (Data-centric Multi-evaluator Agreement for Preference Optimization), generates candidate responses from the target policy, evaluates helpfulness, factuality, and conciseness with rubric-specialized evaluators, applies a process-critic correction, and retains only high-consensus desirable or undesirable examples. This procedure accepts 1,871 of 54,236 Mistral-7B candidates (3.45%). KTO trained on this set reaches 7.50 on MT-Bench, 95.5% length-controlled win rate against a text-davinci-003 reference, and 57.3% IFEval prompt accuracy. Independent pairwise evaluation also favors DMAPO over SimPO: GPT-4o yields a net win rate of 23.3 points on 129 held-out prompts and 24.0 points on 200 out-of-distribution LMSYS-Chat prompts; Claude Opus 4.7 yields 24.1 points on the held-out set. Changing the evaluator model or rubric alters the selected examples but has little effect on downstream performance. A second-backbone study yields a similar 3.41% acceptance rate, although its performance gains are more modest. Across these experiments, consensus filtering offers a data-efficient route to preference optimization for general instructions, at the cost of additional curation compute and dependence on evaluator judgments.

AI.tldr: DMAPO uses a high-confidence, on-policy data selection strategy with multi-evaluator consensus filtering to achieve strong preference optimization results with only 3.45% of candidate responses accepted, outperforming SimPO in pairwise evaluations.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a small, high-confidence set of on-policy responses can provide a reliable learning signal for preference optimization, as opposed to varying training objectives while keeping data fixed.
AI.method: DMAPO generates candidate responses from the target policy, evaluates them across helpfulness, factuality, and conciseness using rubric-specialized evaluators, applies process-critic correction, and retains only high-consensus examples.
AI.result: 1,871 of 54,236 Mistral-7B candidates accepted (3.45%); KTO trained on this set achieves 7.50 MT-Bench, 95.5% length-controlled win rate, and 57.3% IFEval accuracy; DMAPO outperforms SimPO with net win rates of 23.3-24.1 points across various evaluators and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Consensus filtering offers a data-efficient route to preference optimization for general instructions, though at the cost of additional curation compute and dependence on evaluator judgments.

title: Safety-Aware Cascaded Inference for Crop Damage Assessment with Controlled Error Trade-offs
comment: 44 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables. Submitted to Precision Agriculture, July 2026
summary: In picture-based agricultural insurance for smallholder farmers, missed damage detections carry substantially higher cost than false alarms: a farmer who sustained real losses receives no payout, while unnecessary expert review is operationally costly but reversible. Standard multi-class classifiers optimize global accuracy but provide no mechanism to operationalize or control this asymmetric cost structure at inference time. We propose CascadeCropNet, a two-stage cascade architecture calibrated to satisfy a target recall constraint (Rec-Damaged >= 0.95) through threshold selection. A lightweight Sentinel model performs binary health triage; samples exceeding a calibrated damage probability threshold tau are escalated to a specialist Expert model for fine-grained diagnosis. This design provides explicit, deployment-time control over the safety-efficiency trade-off without retraining. Evaluated on the Eyes on the Ground dataset (23,804 images from Kenyan smallholder maize farms), the cascade achieves Rec-Damaged = 0.974 at tau = 0.5, reducing missed damage cases by up to 54% relative to a flat baseline. Under evaluation alignment, the representational gap reduces to +0.008 F1-macro, confirming the contribution is architectural rather than representational. Under input degradation, the system prioritizes escalation over confident misclassification, reflecting error containment through architectural isolation rather than intrinsic model robustness. These results demonstrate that cascade architectures can operationalize safety-oriented decision constraints through calibrated routing in settings where reliability matters more than aggregate accuracy. These properties depend on threshold calibration and deployment conditions and do not constitute guarantees under arbitrary distribution shift.

AI.tldr: CascadeCropNet is a two-stage cascade architecture for agricultural damage detection that prioritizes recall (minimizing missed damage) over accuracy, achieving Rec-Damaged = 0.974 on Kenyan smallholder maize farm data while providing explicit control over the safety-efficiency trade-off at deployment time without retraining.
AI.motivation: In picture-based agricultural insurance, missed damage detections (false negatives) cost substantially more than false alarms (false positives), as real losses go uncompensated. Standard multi-class classifiers optimize global accuracy but cannot operationalize or control this asymmetric cost structure at inference time.
AI.method: A two-stage cascade architecture where a lightweight Sentinel model performs binary health triage, and samples exceeding a calibrated damage probability threshold τ are escalated to a specialist Expert model for fine-grained diagnosis. Threshold selection enforces a target recall constraint (Rec-Damaged ≥ 0.95) without retraining.
AI.result: On the Eyes on the Ground dataset (23,804 images from Kenyan smallholder maize farms), the cascade achieves Rec-Damaged = 0.974 at τ = 0.5, reducing missed damage cases by up to 54% relative to a flat baseline. Under evaluation alignment, representational gap is only +0.008 F1-macro. Under input degradation, the system prioritizes escalation over confident misclassification.
AI.conclusion: Cascade architectures can operationalize safety-oriented decision constraints through calibrated routing in settings where reliability matters more than aggregate accuracy. However, these properties depend on threshold calibration and deployment conditions and do not constitute guarantees under arbitrary distribution shift.

title: Data-Dependent Regret and Polyak Corrections for Constrained Online Convex Optimization
comment: Accepted for publication in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Constrained online convex optimization requires minimizing regret against adversarial convex costs while satisfying a convex constraint at every round, as needed in safety-critical applications. A computationally efficient method combines online gradient descent with a Polyak feasibility step, using one constraint evaluation and one subgradient per round. Although this method achieves O(sqrt(T)) regret with per-round feasibility, we derive a tighter, data-dependent analysis by retaining two quantities omitted by the standard worst-case argument. First, we replace the gradient envelope G_f^2 T with the observed accumulation G_T = sum_t ||grad f_t(x_t)||^2. Second, we identify a nonnegative Polyak correction P_T that measures the cumulative squared displacement caused by feasibility projections and enters the regret bound with a negative sign. The resulting improvement, Delta_T = (eta/2)(G_f^2 T - G_T) + P_T/(2 eta), is always nonnegative. We further propose AdaOGD-PFS, an adaptive-step-size method that achieves O(sqrt(G_T)) regret while preserving per-round feasibility. Experiments on ball- and halfspace-constrained problems improve the regret bound by 38 to 43 percent, with both data-dependent gradients and Polyak corrections contributing substantially.

AI.tldr: The paper improves regret bounds for constrained online convex optimization by replacing worst-case gradient bounds with data-dependent quantities and a nonnegative Polyak correction term, yielding up to 43% improvement in experiments.
AI.motivation: Standard worst-case analysis of constrained OCO with OGD+Polyak feasibility step uses loose bounds (G_f^2 T) that ignore actual gradient accumulation and the beneficial effect of feasibility projections on regret.
AI.method: The authors derive a tighter regret analysis by replacing the gradient envelope G_f^2 T with the observed sum G_T = sum_t ||grad f_t(x_t)||^2 and introducing a nonnegative Polyak correction P_T measuring cumulative squared displacement from projections. They also propose AdaOGD-PFS with adaptive step sizes achieving O(sqrt(G_T)) regret.
AI.result: Experiments on ball- and halfspace-constrained problems show 38-43% regret bound improvement.
AI.conclusion: Data-dependent gradient accumulation and Polyak correction terms both contribute substantially to tighter regret bounds, and the adaptive method preserves per-round feasibility.

title: Agentic AI in medicine: architectures, applications, evaluation, and challenges for clinical translation
summary: Large language models and multimodal foundation models are enabling medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems to move beyond isolated prediction and undertake multistep clinical tasks that require planning, tool use, memory, iterative correction, and coordination among specialized agents. However, the scope of agentic AI in medicine remains unsettled, and current evaluation practices are not yet aligned with the requirements of clinical use. We conducted a scoping review with systematic evidence mapping across five electronic sources, screened 1,649 exportable records, and provisionally included 557 unique studies that met predefined criteria for goal-directed task execution, tool use, interaction with external resources, feedback-based refinement, or multi-agent collaboration. The included studies describe single agents that use external tools, workflows supported by retrieval and external knowledge, multimodal agents, and multi-agent systems applied to medical question answering, image interpretation, electronic health record analysis, drug safety, and clinical trial prediction. The evidence base remains dominated by public benchmarks, simulated settings, retrospective datasets, and small-scale expert evaluation. Process reliability, evidence traceability, uncertainty, safety, workflow impact, and external validity are evaluated less consistently. Clinical translation will depend on clearer definitions, reproducible evaluation, auditable oversight, interoperable system design, and prospective validation in real-world clinical workflows.

AI.tldr: This scoping review maps the landscape of agentic AI in medicine, analyzing 557 studies that use LLMs and multimodal models for multistep clinical tasks involving planning, tool use, memory, and multi-agent coordination. The evidence is dominated by benchmarks and simulated settings, with limited evaluation of process reliability, safety, and clinical validity.
AI.motivation: To understand how large language models and multimodal foundation models are being used to build agentic AI systems capable of multistep clinical tasks, and to assess whether current evaluation practices align with clinical deployment requirements.
AI.method: Scoping review with systematic evidence mapping across five electronic sources, screening 1,649 records, with 557 studies meeting predefined criteria for goal-directed task execution, tool use, interaction with external resources, feedback-based refinement, or multi-agent collaboration.
AI.result: The evidence base is dominated by public benchmarks, simulated settings, retrospective datasets, and small-scale expert evaluation. Process reliability, evidence traceability, uncertainty, safety, workflow impact, and external validity are evaluated less consistently.
AI.conclusion: Clinical translation of agentic medical AI will depend on clearer definitions, reproducible evaluation, auditable oversight, interoperable system design, and prospective validation in real-world clinical workflows.

title: Quantum Speedups for Stochastic Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We study stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed gradient noise. We first propose a novel quantum mean estimator for multivariate heavy-tailed random variables that achieves lower query complexity than optimal classical estimators in the low-dimensional regime. We further develop an unbiased quantum mean estimator by applying a generalized multi-level Monte Carlo technique. We prove quantum lower bounds showing that, when the dimension $d$ of the random vector is small and can be viewed as a constant, our quantum estimators are optimal up to logarithmic factors. We further derive stronger dimension-dependent lower bounds for tail index $p>4/3$, showing that a nontrivial dependence on the dimension is unavoidable in the low-dimensional regime. Based on these estimators, we propose a quantum normalized stochastic gradient descent method ($\texttt{QNSGD}$), which finds an $ε$-stationary point using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt d\,ε^{-\frac{5p-4}{2p-2}}\big)$ queries to the quantum stochastic gradient oracle. For a convex objective function, we propose a quantum projected stochastic gradient descent method ($\texttt{QPSGD}$), which computes a solution with $ε$-optimal solution using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt d\,ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{2p-2}}+ε^{-2}\big)$ queries in expectation. These sharper bounds improve upon the classical lower bounds $Ω\big(ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}}\big)$ for nonconvex problems and $Ω\big(ε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}\big)$ for convex problems in the low-dimensional regimes $d\lesssimε^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}$ and $d\lesssimε^{-\frac{2-p}{p-1}}$, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum mean estimators for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization, achieving lower query complexity than optimal classical methods in low dimensions. It proposes QNSGD for nonconvex and QPSGD for convex problems, with query complexities improving over classical lower bounds in low-dimensional regimes.
AI.motivation: To overcome the query complexity limitations of classical stochastic optimization under heavy-tailed gradient noise, particularly in low-dimensional settings where quantum computing can provide provable advantages.
AI.method: A novel quantum mean estimator for multivariate heavy-tailed random variables using a generalized multi-level Monte Carlo technique; applied to develop QNSGD (nonconvex) and QPSGD (convex) optimization algorithms with quantum stochastic gradient oracles.
AI.result: Quantum estimators achieve lower query complexity than optimal classical estimators in the low-dimensional regime. QNSGD finds ε-stationary points using Õ(√d ε^{-(5p-4)/(2p-2)}) queries; QPSGD achieves ε-optimal solutions with Õ(√d ε^{-(3p-2)/(2p-2)} + ε^{-2}) queries. These improve classical lower bounds Ω(ε^{-(3p-2)/(p-1)}) for nonconvex and Ω(ε^{-p/(p-1)}) for convex problems when d is small.
AI.conclusion: Quantum algorithms can provably outperform classical methods for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization in low-dimensional regimes, with quantum lower bounds showing near-optimality up to logarithmic factors.

title: Inferring Missing Trajectory Data with Temporal Convolutional Networks
summary: Trajectory data collected in real-world settings is frequently incomplete due to sensor failure, communication loss, or occlusion. We address the task of \emph{trajectory inpainting}: reconstructing contiguous missing segments from observed context. We propose a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with symmetric dilation that relaxes the standard causality constraint, allowing each time step to draw on both past and future observations, a property that is essential for inpainting, but absent from forecasting-oriented architectures. The model is trained with a composite loss that combines weighted mean squared error, boundary--continuity penalties, and a smoothness regularizer. Trained on a synthetic dataset of $1,000$ (train), $200$ (validation), and $300$ (test) two-dimensional trajectories with randomly placed 20% masked segments, the model achieves good R$^{2}$, MSE and MAE metrics.

AI.tldr: A TCN with symmetric dilation and a composite loss function is proposed for trajectory inpainting (reconstructing missing segments) from incomplete trajectory data, achieving strong performance on synthetic 2D trajectory datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world trajectory data is often incomplete due to sensor failure, communication loss, or occlusion, and existing forecasting-oriented architectures cannot effectively reconstruct contiguous missing segments because they rely on causal constraints.
AI.method: A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with symmetric dilation (relaxing causality to use both past and future context), trained with a composite loss combining weighted MSE, boundary-continuity penalties, and a smoothness regularizer.
AI.result: On a synthetic dataset (1000 train, 200 validation, 300 test) of 2D trajectories with 20% randomly masked segments, the model achieves good R², MSE, and MAE metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed symmetric-dilation TCN effectively addresses trajectory inpainting by leveraging bidirectional temporal context and a carefully designed loss function, outperforming forecasting-based approaches on missing segment reconstruction.

title: Beyond Counts: A Distributional Robustness Margin For Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Pathology foundation models are approaching clinical deployment, yet remain vulnerable to systematic non-biological variation across centres. Differences in tissue preparation, staining and scanning are strongly encoded in their representations, enabling shortcut learning and weakening generalisation across cohorts and institutions. The Robustness Index (RI) quantifies whether local representation geometry is dominated by biology or by non-biological variation, but its count-based formulation discards distance information. We show that adding distance weights changes little because the deeper limitation lies in RI's pooled, fixed-neighbourhood design, which obscures sample-level heterogeneity and effectively evaluates only a model-dependent subset of samples. We introduce the Cross-confounder Robustness Margin (CRoMa), a sample-resolved measure that directly compares distances to cross-confounder biological matches and same-confounder biological distractors. CRoMa recasts robustness as a cohort-wide margin distribution rather than a single pooled score. We evaluated frozen representations from 20 tile-level encoders across three benchmarks and 4 slide-level encoders on a fourth. Rankings by median CRoMa were broadly consistent across datasets, while the underlying distributions revealed substantial within-model heterogeneity. Every tile encoder retained a confounder-dominated lower tail, whose prevalence and severity varied markedly across models. These distinct robustness profiles frame model selection as a Pareto trade-off between typical and lower-tail robustness. Higher CRoMa was also associated with smaller shortcut-induced performance drops after supervised adaptation. By turning representation geometry into a distributional robustness readout that anticipates downstream shortcut susceptibility, CRoMa provides a principled basis for robustness assessment and model selection.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies limitations in the existing Robustness Index (RI) for pathology foundation models and proposes CRoMa (Cross-confounder Robustness Margin), a sample-resolved metric that compares distances to cross-confounder biological matches versus same-confounder biological distractors, recasting robustness as a cohort-wide margin distribution. Evaluated across multiple encoders and benchmarks, CRoMa reveals substantial within-model heterogeneity and frames model selection as a Pareto trade-off between typical and lower-tail robustness, with higher CRoMa correlating with reduced shortcut-induced performance drops.
AI.motivation: Pathology foundation models are approaching clinical deployment but remain vulnerable to non-biological variation across centres (differences in tissue preparation, staining, scanning), which enables shortcut learning and weakens generalisation. Existing robustness measures like the Robustness Index (RI) have limitations including discarding distance information, pooled fixed-neighbourhood design obscuring sample-level heterogeneity, and evaluating only a model-dependent subset of samples.
AI.method: The authors propose CRoMa (Cross-confounder Robustness Margin), a sample-resolved measure that directly compares distances to cross-confounder biological matches and same-confounder biological distractors, recasting robustness as a cohort-wide margin distribution rather than a single pooled score. They evaluated frozen representations from 20 tile-level encoders across three benchmarks and 4 slide-level encoders on a fourth benchmark.
AI.result: Rankings by median CRoMa were broadly consistent across datasets, but the underlying distributions revealed substantial within-model heterogeneity. Every tile encoder retained a confounder-dominated lower tail with varying prevalence and severity across models. Higher CRoMa was associated with smaller shortcut-induced performance drops after supervised adaptation.
AI.conclusion: CRoMa provides a principled basis for robustness assessment and model selection by turning representation geometry into a distributional robustness readout that anticipates downstream shortcut susceptibility, framing model selection as a Pareto trade-off between typical and lower-tail robustness.

title: Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection via Cumulative Entropy
summary: Recent training-time defenses against neural backdoors isolate a benign subset from poisoned training data, to learn a backdoor-free model from it. In this paper, we formulate this defense strategy as a coreset selection problem, giving rise to so-called "Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection." Since poisonous samples have (a) lower prediction uncertainty and are (b) less frequent than benign samples, coreset selection naturally focuses more on samples associated with benign functionality than the backdoor functionality. We use the Cumulative Entropy as selection criterion to further facilitate this effect. The metric tracks the learning dynamics of training samples and allowing us to select benign samples with high informativeness for the coreset. Additionally, we unlearn the chosen samples in each epoch to facilitate the separability between benign and poisonous samples. Together, this yields an exceptionally effective training-time defense that constructs a benign coreset to train a backdoor-free model. Unlike prior defenses that compromise natural accuracy and fail against certain attacks, our method mitigates backdooring attacks consistently with a negligible impact on natural performance.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates training-time backdoor defense as a coreset selection problem, using Cumulative Entropy to select benign samples with high informativeness while unlearning chosen samples to improve separability, resulting in a defense that mitigates backdoors with negligible impact on natural accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing training-time defenses against neural backdoors isolate benign subsets from poisoned data, but often compromise natural accuracy and fail against certain attacks. The authors aim to develop a more effective defense that maintains natural performance while consistently mitigating backdoor attacks.
AI.method: The method formulates defense as an Anti-Backdoor Coreset Selection problem, using Cumulative Entropy as a selection criterion to track learning dynamics. It selects samples with lower prediction uncertainty (characteristic of benign samples) and higher informativeness. Chosen samples are unlearned each epoch to enhance separability between benign and poisonous samples.
AI.result: The method consistently mitigates backdooring attacks across different attack types, with negligible impact on natural accuracy, unlike prior defenses that sacrifice natural performance or fail against certain attacks.
AI.conclusion: Coreset selection based on Cumulative Entropy and unlearning provides an exceptionally effective training-time defense that isolates benign coresets for learning backdoor-free models without compromising natural accuracy.

title: When Do Agent Loops Mistake Stagnation for Progress? Self-Evaluation Bias and Externally Grounded Verification in Long-Running Autonomous LLM Agent Loops
comment: 23 pages. Preregistered pilot measurement study. Also deposited on Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21594735)
summary: Long-running autonomous agents plan, act, and judge their own completion without human intervention. When an agent grades its own work, self-evaluation bias takes hold: plausible changes are accepted as progress while real-world outcomes stagnate or regress. We name this failure mode the progress mirage and show, with controlled measurement, that it is a question of what the evaluator is grounded in. We built a testbed that holds the agent and its tool surface fixed and manipulates only the information-channel type of the evaluator that gates the loop. A world-state oracle, unfakeable in principle, is enforced by container and network isolation and verified at every run. Across 54 cycles a frontier agent claimed improvement every time, yet 56 percent had a measured delta of zero or below. Self-report was thus uninformative, and the self-verdict gate degenerated into accept-all, eroding the best deployed state it had reached by 19 percent. Even the strongest in-band judge, reading the full artifact text, the change diff, and its own verdict history, accepted cycles of which 44 percent were real-world regressions and rejected 38 percent of real improvements; the preregistered adversarial hypothesis that a strong judge closes the gap was rejected. On a boundary task whose success specification is verifiable from the artifact itself, the same judge's mirage vanished to zero and the gap collapsed within the registered threshold, showing that the gap depends on where the success signal resides. A sign-only variant returning only the acceptance verdict kept real-world output similar to full feedback (110.0 versus 113.0), locating the benefit in the gate's grounding rather than in feedback content. For open-ended objectives whose success signal lives outside the transcript, scaling up the judge is not enough; out-of-band evaluation with real-world access is a structural requirement.

AI.tldr: Self-evaluation bias in autonomous agents creates a "progress mirage" where agents claim improvement while real-world outcomes stagnate or regress. The gap depends on where the success signal resides—in-band judges fail for open-ended objectives, while out-of-band evaluation with real-world access is a structural requirement.
AI.motivation: Long-running autonomous agents lack human oversight to judge their own completion, but self-evaluation bias leads to accepting plausible changes as progress while real-world outcomes stagnate or regress. The authors aim to characterize this failure mode and understand what determines whether self-evaluation is trustworthy.
AI.method: The authors built a testbed with a fixed agent and tool surface, manipulating only the information-channel type of the evaluator. A world-state oracle enforced by container/network isolation verified outcomes. They tested frontier agents across 54 cycles with various judge configurations (self-report, in-band judge, sign-only variants) and a boundary task with verifiable success specification.
AI.result: Across 54 cycles, the agent claimed improvement every time but 56% had zero or negative measured delta. The self-verdict gate degenerated into accept-all, eroding the best deployed state by 19%. Even the strongest in-band judge accepted 44% regressions and rejected 38% of real improvements. The preregistered adversarial hypothesis that a strong judge closes the gap was rejected. On a boundary task with verifiable success, the mirage vanished to zero. A sign-only variant kept real-world output similar to full feedback (110.0 vs 113.0).
AI.conclusion: For open-ended objectives whose success signal lives outside the transcript, scaling up the judge is not enough. Out-of-band evaluation with real-world access is a structural requirement to overcome the progress mirage. The benefit of evaluation comes from the gate's grounding rather than feedback content.

title: Group Equivariant Diffusion for Anomaly Detection in Computational Cytology
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, 1 algorithm. Accepted for publication in MICCAI 2026
summary: Computational cytology on whole-slide images is challenging because malignant cells are rare, heterogeneous, and annotated slides are scarce. Anomaly detection frameworks can be trained on normal slide-negative patches and then applied at test time to flag abnormal patches in held-out slides. Most unsupervised anomaly detection approaches including generative ones (GAN-based and diffusion-based), are tuned to organ-level imaging and require large curated datasets. In cytology the signal is cell-centric: rotating or flipping a single-cell patch does not change its diagnostic class, yet standard diffusion models treat transformed views as distinct inputs, leading to transformation-dependent reconstructions and unstable anomaly scores. We propose a D4-equivariant diffusion framework that enforces rotation and reflection symmetry both architecturally, via a D4-equivariant U-Net, and at inference, via equivariant noise coupling and (optionally) frame averaging. This alignment with biological invariance yields transformation-consistent pseudo-healthy reconstructions and more stable anomaly ranking under symmetry. On two publicly available cytology datasets of bone marrow and peripheral blood smears, our D4-equivariant diffusion models achieve higher AUC and retrieve more abnormal cells in the top K predictions than non-equivariant generative baselines, a deep one-class, and a multiple instance learning based method, while substantially reducing score variance across rotations and flips. Code is available at https://swchmida.github.io/D4diffCyto/.

AI.tldr: A D4-equivariant diffusion framework for anomaly detection in computational cytology that enforces rotation/reflection symmetry, achieving better AUC and more stable anomaly scores on bone marrow and blood smear datasets.
AI.motivation: Computational cytology faces challenges due to rare/heterogeneous malignant cells and scarce annotations. Existing unsupervised anomaly detection methods (especially generative models) are designed for organ-level imaging and fail to account for the cell-centric rotational/flip invariance, treating transformed views as distinct inputs and producing unstable anomaly scores.
AI.method: Proposes a D4-equivariant diffusion framework with (1) a D4-equivariant U-Net architecture, (2) equivariant noise coupling at inference, and (3) optional frame averaging, to enforce rotation and reflection symmetry in anomaly reconstruction.
AI.result: On two public cytology datasets (bone marrow and peripheral blood smears), the D4-equivariant diffusion model achieves higher AUC, retrieves more abnormal cells in top-K predictions, and substantially reduces score variance across rotations/flips compared to non-equivariant generative baselines, deep one-class, and MIL methods.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing D4 equivariance in diffusion models aligns with biological invariance of cells, producing transformation-consistent pseudo-healthy reconstructions and more stable anomaly ranking, offering a promising direction for unsupervised cytology anomaly detection.

title: AMPBench-MT: A Homology-Controlled Benchmark for Antimicrobial Peptide Potency, Spectrum, and Safety Prediction
summary: Computational AMP discovery is often evaluated through AMP/non-AMP recognition, yet follow-up decisions depend on assay-derived evidence such as target-species potency, hemolysis, toxicity, and selectivity. Existing AMP and peptide benchmarks cover binary recognition, multilabel annotation, assay regression, or broader peptide-model comparison, but they do not jointly place AMP recognition, species-conditioned potency, spectrum, safety-facing proxy endpoints, and cross-endpoint behavior within one sequence-homology-controlled protocol. To address this problem, we introduce AMPBench-MT, a provenance-preserving benchmark that standardizes canonical peptide records and organizes them into binary recognition, species-conditioned pMIC regression, and endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. Across 161 endpoint-specific model evaluations, high binary performance does not reliably indicate assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen protein-language-model embeddings form the leading pMIC error cluster, while graph and classical regressors remain close. Spectrum labels further reveal that PR-oriented metrics can be misleading under scarce observed negatives, whereas low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity expose smaller but more assay-facing signals. AMPBench-MT shows that AMP evaluation should move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing. Our proposed benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ZihengZhou06/AMPBench-MT.

AI.tldr: AMPBench-MT is a new benchmark that moves beyond binary AMP/non-AMP recognition to evaluate AMPs across multiple assay-derived endpoints (species-conditioned potency, hemolysis, toxicity, selectivity) under sequence-homology control. Experiments across 161 models show high binary performance does not predict assay behavior, and frozen protein-language-model embeddings lead pMIC error, while graph/classical regressors perform close. The benchmark is publicly available.
AI.motivation: Existing AMP benchmarks cover binary recognition, multilabel annotation, assay regression, or broader peptide-model comparison, but none jointly place AMP recognition, species-conditioned potency, spectrum, safety-facing proxy endpoints, and cross-endpoint behavior within a single sequence-homology-controlled protocol.
AI.method: The authors introduce AMPBench-MT, a provenance-preserving benchmark that standardizes canonical peptide records and organizes them into binary recognition, species-conditioned pMIC regression, and endpoint-specific potency and safety-facing readouts. They evaluate 161 endpoint-specific models spanning frozen protein-language-model embeddings, graph neural networks, and classical regressors.
AI.result: High binary performance does not reliably indicate assay-endpoint behavior. Frozen PLM embeddings form the leading pMIC error cluster, while graph and classical regressors remain close. Spectrum labels show PR-oriented metrics can be misleading under scarce observed negatives, whereas low-toxicity, HC50 hemolysis, and selectivity expose smaller but more assay-facing signals.
AI.conclusion: AMP evaluation should move beyond recognition leaderboards toward endpoint-aware evidence auditing.

title: PreDiff-LM: Pretrained Discrete Masked Diffusion Language Modeling with Hybrid Attention
summary: Discrete masked diffusion language models support bidirectional generation and infilling, but adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) transformers requires reconciling causal pretraining with bidirectional denoising. We study this problem at the level of attention rather than claiming AR-weight reuse itself as novel. PreDiff-LM preserves causal attention within the observed prompt while allowing full bidirectional attention within the masked target. Under a matched GPT-2 Medium, WikiText-103, 90K-step setup, this hybrid mask improves unconditional perplexity from 34.1 to 28.7 and MAUVE from 0.71 to 0.78 over uniform bidirectional attention with the same AR initialization. Attention adaptation also composes with a DiffuGPT-style objective adaptation, reaching 26.9 perplexity. Pretrained initialization reduces the steps required to reach perplexity below 50 from about 350K to 8K, although a compute-matched fine-tuned AR model remains stronger at equal scale (18.9 versus 28.7). Beyond perplexity, PreDiff-LM improves repetition, distributional quality, four zero-shot downstream tasks, and human preference over prior diffusion baselines. The results position hybrid attention as a complementary mechanism for adapting pretrained causal backbones, while making explicit the remaining quality and inference-efficiency gaps to optimized AR models.

AI.tldr: PreDiff-LM adapts pretrained autoregressive transformers for masked diffusion by using a hybrid attention mask: causal attention on observed prompts and bidirectional attention on masked targets. This improves perplexity (34.1→28.7) and MAUVE (0.71→0.78) over uniform bidirectional attention on GPT-2 Medium, and composes with objective adaptation to reach 26.9 perplexity. Pretrained initialization reduces training steps by ~44x, though fine-tuned AR models remain stronger at equal scale.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained causal AR transformers for bidirectional masked diffusion language models, reconciling the conflict between causal pretraining and bidirectional denoising.
AI.method: Hybrid attention mask that preserves causal attention within the observed prompt while allowing full bidirectional attention within the masked target region, applied during diffusion training of pretrained AR transformers.
AI.result: Unconditional perplexity improved from 34.1 to 28.7 and MAUVE from 0.71 to 0.78 on WikiText-103 with GPT-2 Medium. Objective adaptation further improved perplexity to 26.9. Pretrained initialization reduced required training steps from ~350K to 8K. However, fine-tuned AR model at equal scale achieves 18.9 perplexity vs 28.7.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid attention is a complementary mechanism for adapting pretrained causal backbones to masked diffusion, but quality and inference-efficiency gaps to optimized AR models remain.

title: I2VShield: An Efficient Proactive Defense Framework against DiT-based Image-to-Video Models
summary: The rapid advancement of video generation models has led to the increasing misuse of image-to-video (I2V) models. Although substantial progress has been made in detecting AI-generated videos, proactive defenses against I2V models remain underexplored. In particular, current proactive defenses against I2V models predominantly rely on gradient-based adversarial attacks, which require defenders to possess GPUs with substantial memory resources (VRAM) to generate adversarial examples. To address this issue, we propose I2VShield, a privacy protection method based on generative adversarial attacks tailored to Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based I2V models. The proposed method primarily consists of two components: (1) a text-adaptive perturbation generation framework integrating adversarial learning to mitigate computational overhead while maintaining visual imperceptibility; and (2) an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack that exploits the inherent vulnerabilities of DiT-based I2V models, maximizing the deviation of the internal attention features from their clean states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves highly competitive protection performance across various datasets and mainstream DiT-based I2V models, particularly in disrupting spatiotemporal coherence, while substantially reducing computational costs.

AI.tldr: I2VShield proposes a generative adversarial attack framework for proactively protecting privacy against Diffusion Transformer-based image-to-video models, using a text-adaptive perturbation generation method and an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack to disrupt spatiotemporal coherence while reducing computational overhead compared to gradient-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Current proactive defenses against I2V models rely on gradient-based adversarial attacks requiring high GPU memory (VRAM), making them impractical for many defenders. There is a need for computationally efficient proactive protection methods.
AI.method: Two components: (1) a text-adaptive perturbation generation framework with adversarial learning to reduce computational cost while maintaining visual imperceptibility; (2) an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack that targets inherent vulnerabilities in DiT-based I2V models to maximize deviation of internal attention features from clean states.
AI.result: Achieves highly competitive protection performance across various datasets and mainstream DiT-based I2V models, effectively disrupting spatiotemporal coherence while substantially reducing computational costs.
AI.conclusion: I2VShield provides an efficient proactive defense mechanism against DiT-based image-to-video generation models, addressing the VRAM bottleneck of existing gradient-based approaches through generative adversarial attacks.

title: Multi-Scale Structural Features for Continual, Comprehensible Visual Recognition in a Developmental Learning Framework
summary: Contemporary machine learning struggles to learn continually, reuse prior knowledge, and expose a comprehensible internal structure. A recently proposed developmental, gradient-free learning framework addresses these limitations by learning a discrete, topological model of its inputs through local variation and selection, yielding an inherent continual-learning guarantee: new observations refine existing structure without overwriting past knowledge, and without replay buffers or predefined task boundaries. Its extension to visual inputs demonstrated this principle on shape recognition, but relied on a feature representation of limited expressivity that capped recognition accuracy. We introduce a new visual feature representation that encodes shape structure across multiple scales, capturing edge and contour features together with their spatial relations, and integrate it with the network-refinement learning process; we further improve the learning dynamics and the read-out used to predict from the learned model. The study targets two-dimensional shape, with class-incremental MNIST as a controlled, interpretable benchmark in which continual-learning behavior can be measured directly. Our approach substantially increases accuracy over the prior representation, matching or exceeding replay- and regularisation-based baselines at comparable storage while storing no past data, and preserves the framework's defining behavior: earlier-learned classes are retained as new ones are introduced, with no destructive adaptation, and the learned representations remain human-interpretable. What separates the methods is retention: the baselines surrender most of a just-trained class within its own cycle and relearn it afterwards, which ours does not. The significance lies in the manner of learning. The system integrates information one sample at a time while provably preserving its responses to...

AI.tldr: A developmental, gradient-free learning framework with a new multi-scale visual feature representation achieves continual learning on shape recognition without replay buffers, matching/exceeding baselines while preserving past knowledge without destructive adaptation.
AI.motivation: Contemporary machine learning struggles with continual learning, reusing prior knowledge, and interpretability. Prior work had a developmental framework with inherent continual-learning guarantees but used a limited feature representation that capped accuracy.
AI.method: Introduces a multi-scale visual feature representation encoding shape structure across scales (edge/contour features with spatial relations), integrates it with network-refinement learning, improves learning dynamics and read-out mechanism, tested on class-incremental MNIST.
AI.result: Substantially increased accuracy over prior representation, matching/exceeding replay- and regularization-based baselines at comparable storage without storing past data. Preserved retention of earlier-learned classes without destructive adaptation, while baselines forget within-cycle.
AI.conclusion: The system integrates information incrementally while provably preserving past responses, achieving true continual learning where baselines fail—they surrender a just-trained class within its own cycle and relearn it afterward, while this approach does not.

title: Observing sycophantic AI validate others reduces its appeal but not its persuasiveness
summary: AI chatbots can be ``sycophantic,'' or overly agreeable and flattering toward users. Sycophantic AI has been shown to entrench attitudes, yet users frequently fail to recognize it (a phenomenon we call ``sycophancy blindness''). We tested whether increasing users' awareness of sycophancy protects them from its harmful effects. In one preregistered experiment (n = 940), participants received a brief written warning about sycophancy before conversing with a sycophantic chatbot. In a second preregistered experiment (n = 650), participants watched a video of a sycophantic AI validating several other users, including users on opposite sides of the same conflict, before interacting with it themselves. Both interventions changed how participants evaluated the AI. The warning reduced the AI's perceived objectivity, and the video reduced enjoyment of the AI, an effect mediated by the reduced belief that its validation was uniquely earned. We then pooled our experiments with two prior studies of sycophancy awareness interventions (six interventions total, n = 3,982). The pattern was consistent: interventions made the sycophantic AI appear less objective and trustworthy, and none of the six reduced its persuasiveness. These results suggest that individual-level interventions, such as warning labels or AI literacy, may not be enough to protect users from AI harms.

AI.tldr: Warnings and AI literacy interventions make sycophantic chatbots appear less objective and trustworthy, but do not reduce their persuasiveness, suggesting individual-level protections are insufficient.
AI.motivation: AI chatbots exhibit sycophancy (over-agreeableness), which entrenches user attitudes, yet users are often blind to this phenomenon ("sycophancy blindness"). The study investigates whether raising awareness protects users from these harmful effects.
AI.method: Two preregistered experiments (n=940 and n=650) tested brief written warnings and video interventions. Results were pooled with two prior studies (six interventions total, n=3,982) to assess consistency across interventions.
AI.result: Warning reduced perceived objectivity; video reduced enjoyment (mediated by reduced belief that validation was uniquely earned). Across all six interventions, sycophantic AI appeared less objective and trustworthy, but none reduced its persuasiveness.
AI.conclusion: Individual-level interventions like warnings or AI literacy may not adequately protect users from AI sycophancy harms, as they fail to reduce persuasion despite changing perceptions.

title: ReLATE: Reliability-Guided Evidence Fusion for Robust UAV--Satellite cross-view Geo-Localization
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-satellite cross-view geo-localization matches UAV images against satellite imagery and has achieved impressive accuracy on clean (non-degraded) image benchmarks. In real-world flights, however, UAV observations are frequently affected by adverse weather, illumination changes, platform motion, sensor noise, and compression, while the robustness of existing methods under such degradations remains largely unexamined. In this paper, we present UAVSat-Deg, a large-scale robustness benchmark for degraded UAV-satellite geo-localization, comprising University-1652-Deg and SUES-200-Deg. UAVSat-Deg covers 27 corruption types, including 19 core and 8 compound corruptions, at three severity levels, supports bidirectional drone-to-satellite and satellite-to-drone retrieval as well as multi-height UAV acquisition, and contains more than 11.7 million pre-generated corrupted test images. Benchmarking representative methods under this protocol reveals substantial robustness gaps, particularly under severe and compound corruptions. To address this problem, we propose ReLATE, a Reliable Evidence Learning framework with Adaptive Token Evidence Regulation, which realizes reliability-adaptive feature fusion during descriptor construction. ReLATE estimates a structure-smoothed reliability field over visual tokens, aggregates trustworthy local evidence, and adaptively integrates it into query-derived representations; the regulated query representations are then combined with the CLS-token and GeM-pooled branches to form the final cross-view descriptor. Across both test sets and retrieval directions, ReLATE achieves the best average corrupted-test performance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive accuracy on clean images. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/JHC626/ReLATE.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces UAVSat-Deg, a large-scale robustness benchmark for degraded UAV-satellite cross-view geo-localization with 27 corruption types at 3 severity levels, and proposes ReLATE, a reliable evidence learning framework with adaptive token evidence regulation, which achieves robust performance under corruptions while maintaining clean-image accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing UAV-satellite cross-view geo-localization methods achieve high accuracy on clean benchmarks, but their robustness under real-world degradations (adverse weather, illumination changes, motion, sensor noise, compression) remains largely unexamined. This work aims to address this gap.
AI.method: Proposes ReLATE (Reliable Evidence Learning with Adaptive Token Evidence Regulation): estimates a structure-smoothed reliability field over visual tokens, aggregates trustworthy local evidence, and adaptively integrates it into query-derived representations. The regulated query representations combine with CLS-token and GeM-pooled branches to form final cross-view descriptors.
AI.result: Benchmarking reveals substantial robustness gaps under severe and compound corruptions. ReLATE achieves the best average corrupted-test performance across both test sets and retrieval directions while maintaining competitive accuracy on clean images.
AI.conclusion: UAVSat-Deg provides a comprehensive robustness benchmark for degraded UAV-satellite geo-localization, and ReLATE effectively bridges the robustness gap through reliability-adaptive feature fusion.

title: Mind the Missing Split: Resolving Feature Heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with Random Forests
summary: Swarm Learning is a decentralized collaborative learning mechanism that allows multiple organizations to train a shared model without central coordination or direct data sharing. In typical horizontal Swarm Learning, datasets across sites are usually assumed to share the same feature set. However, in real-world applications, sites often have partially overlapping features because measurements, protocols, and available covariates differ across sites. This feature heterogeneity creates a practical issue for machine learning algorithms such as Random Forests. Specifically, when decision trees are pooled into a global Random Forest, inference at a given site can become ill-defined if a traversal encounters a split on a feature that is not available locally, often forcing organizations to discard site-specific variables upfront. In this paper, we address feature heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with Random Forests under partially overlapping feature spaces. We propose several deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies that resolve such missing splits without restricting training to the intersection of features. We evaluate the methods on nine datasets and demonstrate that they outperform both the intersection baseline and locally trained models across a broad range of scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses feature heterogeneity in Swarm Learning with Random Forests under partially overlapping feature spaces by proposing deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies for handling missing splits.
AI.motivation: In horizontal Swarm Learning, real-world sites often have partially overlapping feature sets due to differing measurements, protocols, and covariates, causing ill-defined inference when decision tree splits reference features unavailable locally, forcing organizations to discard site-specific variables.
AI.method: The paper proposes several deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies that handle missing splits when decision trees encounter features not available locally, without restricting training to the feature intersection.
AI.result: The proposed methods were evaluated on nine datasets and outperformed both the intersection baseline and locally trained models across a broad range of scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deterministic and probabilistic inference-time strategies for handling missing feature splits in Swarm Learning with Random Forests outperform both the intersection baseline and locally trained models, effectively resolving feature heterogeneity across sites.

title: Everyone is unique: Towards Behaviorally Heterogeneous Negotiation Dialogue Systems for Debt Collection
summary: Debt collection is a critical negotiation task in the financial industry, with strong practical relevance and exceptional academic value as a behaviorally rich, high-stakes testbed for human-centered dialogue systems. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in dialogue and negotiation, effectively evaluating their performance in this complex scenarios remains a major challenge: existing benchmarks uniformly assume users to be static, rational agents with fixed preferences, failing to capture the rich behavioral heterogeneity inherent in real-world debt collection.
