To bridge this gap, we propose DebtBench, the first public persona-enriched debt collection benchmark, that highlights behavioral heterogeneity in negotiation. Moreover, we develop DebtGPT, a debt collection agent trained to jointly optimize financial recovery and interaction experience. Our experimental results, using 16 state-of-the-art LLMs, find that most existing models struggle in this complex but realistic scenarios, whereas DebtGPT outperforms all open-source baselines and achieves performance on par with GPT-4o. The code and data are available at https://github.com/YYuHhhh/DebtNegotiation.

AI.tldr: DebtBench is the first persona-enriched benchmark for evaluating LLMs in debt collection negotiation, and DebtGPT is an agent that jointly optimizes financial recovery and user experience, outperforming open-source models and matching GPT-4o.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume static, rational agents with fixed preferences, failing to capture the behavioral heterogeneity of real-world debt collection negotiations.
AI.method: The authors propose DebtBench, a persona-enriched benchmark incorporating diverse debtor behavioral profiles, and DebtGPT, a debt collection agent trained to jointly optimize financial recovery and interaction experience.
AI.result: Most of 16 state-of-the-art LLMs struggle in this setting; DebtGPT outperforms all open-source baselines and achieves performance comparable to GPT-4o.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral heterogeneity is critical for realistic negotiation evaluation, and DebtGPT demonstrates effective performance in this complex domain.

title: Argus-Unified: Towards A Compact and Economical Unified Model for Image Understanding and Generation
summary: Unifying visual understanding and generation in one model holds immense promise, but remains challenging and expensive due to heavy compute and data demands and conflicts between the visual features needed for these two capabilities. To address these challenges, we present Argus-Unified, a compact, effective and unified multimodal model built with low demand on computation and data. Instead of aligning modalities from scratch, Argus-Unified effectively leverages pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) that provide strong multimodal priors. Specifically, we introduce hybrid visual tokens that preserve continuous tokens for understanding while learning discrete tokens for generation from a frozen unified vision encoder. Our training pipeline includes two stages: the first stage learns a quantizer and image decoder on top of the frozen vision encoder, the second stage trains the LLM initialized from a pretrained VLM for the unified multimodal modeling. Using by far the least amount of data (15.6M) and the lowest cost (~$2,000), we demonstrate that unified multimodal models can be trained economically while achieving strong performance in both understanding and generation. Notably, our model attains state-of-the-art multimodal understanding on GQA, POPE, and VQAv2, and competitive generation quality compared to models with dedicated vision encoders (e.g., Janus, Janus-Pro), all at ~10x lower cost and with ~5x less data. We envision Argus-Unified as a useful baseline that lowers the development barrier for unified models.

AI.tldr: Argus-Unified is a compact, low-cost unified multimodal model that leverages pretrained VLMs and hybrid visual tokens (continuous for understanding, discrete for generation) to achieve SOTA understanding and competitive generation at ~$2K cost and 15.6M data, ~10x cheaper and ~5x less data than comparable models.
AI.motivation: Unifying visual understanding and generation in a single model is promising but challenging due to high compute/data demands and conflicts between visual features needed for both capabilities; the authors aim to lower the development barrier with an economical approach.
AI.method: 1. Hybrid visual tokens: continuous tokens for understanding + learned discrete tokens for generation from a frozen unified vision encoder. 2. Two-stage training: Stage 1 learns a quantizer and image decoder on top of frozen vision encoder; Stage 2 trains the LLM (initialized from a pretrained VLM) for unified multimodal modeling.
AI.result: SOTA multimodal understanding on GQA, POPE, VQAv2; competitive generation quality vs. models like Janus/Janus-Pro; achieved at ~10x lower cost (~$2K) and ~5x less data (15.6M).
AI.conclusion: Unified multimodal models can be trained economically with strong performance; Argus-Unified serves as a useful baseline that lowers the development barrier for unified models.

title: OrthKD: Extracting Generalized Clinical Knowledge from Heterogeneous Teachers for Lightweight Deployment
comment: Accepted to the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Special Track on AI and Health. 8 pages, 3 figures
summary: Deploying diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening models in primary care requires edge-efficient systems that remain accurate, safe, and reliable under domain shift. Multi-teacher knowledge distillation (KD) is a natural compression strategy, but existing approaches largely assume that all teachers provide equally trustworthy supervision. In our setting, this assumption fails: a strong CNN teacher (EfficientNet-B3, 0.876 QWK) and a weaker Transformer teacher (Swin-Base, 0.830 QWK) are complementary, yet the Transformer's logits can still mislead the student. We therefore propose OrthKD, a selective-trust distillation framework that transfers full supervision from the strong CNN, uses feature-only distillation from the weak ViT, and enforces orthogonality between teacher-specific student projections to encourage complementary rather than redundant evidence. This design preserves local lesion precision, injects global structural context, and improves robustness to distribution shift. On 132,049 retinal images, a 5.4M-parameter MobileNetV3 student reaches 0.885 QWK on EyePACS and improves zero-shot Messidor-2 performance from 0.507 to 0.728 QWK, while also achieving strong referral AUC and calibration. These results show that selectively distilling heterogeneous teachers can enable practical DR screening on resource-constrained devices.

AI.tldr: OrthKD is a selective-trust knowledge distillation framework that transfers full supervision from a strong CNN teacher and feature-only distillation from a weak ViT teacher, enforcing orthogonality between student projections for complementary evidence, achieving 0.885 QWK on EyePACS and improving zero-shot Messidor-2 from 0.507 to 0.728 QWK with a 5.4M-parameter MobileNetV3 student.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-teacher KD assumes all teachers provide equally trustworthy supervision, but in DR screening, a strong CNN teacher and a weaker Transformer teacher are complementary yet the weaker teacher's logits can mislead the student, motivating a selective-trust distillation approach.
AI.method: OrthKD transfers full supervision (logits + features) from the strong CNN teacher, uses feature-only distillation from the weaker ViT teacher, and enforces orthogonality between teacher-specific student projections to encourage complementary evidence while preventing misleading logit supervision from the weak teacher.
AI.result: On 132,049 retinal images, a 5.4M-parameter MobileNetV3 student achieves 0.885 QWK on EyePACS, improves zero-shot Messidor-2 from 0.507 to 0.728 QWK, and maintains strong referral AUC and calibration.
AI.conclusion: Selectively distilling heterogeneous teachers with orthogonal projections enables accurate, robust, and practical DR screening models deployable on resource-constrained edge devices.

title: CADENCE: A Cardiac Atom Dictionary for Interpretable Neural Concept Extraction from ECG Foundation Models
comment: 21 pages, 5 main figures, 15 appendix figures, 6 tables
summary: Foundation models for 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) transfer well across clinical tasks, but the physiological knowledge encoded in their representations remains opaque. We present CADENCE, a framework that decomposes an ECG foundation model into a human-interpretable, queryable dictionary of physiological concepts. Using a BatchTopK sparse autoencoder, CADENCE factorizes Layer-6 embeddings from more than nine million ECG tokens into 8,192 sparse cardiac atoms. These atoms align better than individual dense embedding dimensions with clinical phenotypes and waveform morphology, recovering arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, infarction and repolarization patterns, chamber and axis findings, and lead- and beat-phase-specific waveform primitives. At Layer 6, the best atoms achieve mean AUROCs of 0.88 for clinical phenotypes and 0.90 for morphology, versus 0.78 and 0.83 for the best dense dimensions. Sparse atom probes match or outperform dense probes for phenotype, morphology, and age prediction while attributing each prediction to a small set of interpretable atoms; phenotype AUROC improves from 0.93 to 0.95. Atom-space geometry recovers physiologically coherent relationships, and targeted atom ablation selectively changes frozen downstream outputs. An automated LLM pipeline generates and quantitatively validates atom descriptions by predicting held-out activations. On independent external ECG datasets, CADENCE recovers overlapping concepts and maintains consistent phenotype-prediction performance. CADENCE provides a scalable framework for discovering and auditing the physiological knowledge encoded by ECG foundation models.

AI.tldr: CADENCE uses a BatchTopK sparse autoencoder to decompose ECG foundation model embeddings into 8,192 interpretable cardiac atoms that outperform dense dimensions in aligning with clinical phenotypes and waveform morphology, enabling interpretable prediction and physiological concept discovery.
AI.motivation: ECG foundation models transfer well across clinical tasks, but the physiological knowledge encoded in their representations remains opaque, motivating a framework to decompose and interpret these black-box embeddings.
AI.method: CADENCE applies a BatchTopK sparse autoencoder to Layer-6 embeddings from >9 million ECG tokens, factorizing them into 8,192 sparse cardiac atoms. It uses atom-space geometry, targeted ablation, and an automated LLM pipeline for validation.
AI.result: Atoms achieve mean AUROCs of 0.88 for clinical phenotypes and 0.90 for morphology (vs. 0.78/0.83 for dense dimensions). Sparse probes improve phenotype AUROC from 0.93 to 0.95. Concepts generalize to external datasets.
AI.conclusion: CADENCE provides a scalable framework for discovering and auditing the physiological knowledge encoded by ECG foundation models, enabling interpretable and trustworthy clinical AI.

title: Visual prompt engineering for video models
summary: In the age of foundation models, a model is only as good as its prompt. For this reason, prompt engineering has become an essential technique for improving language model performance. Since video models are currently becoming foundation models for visual tasks (e.g., visual reasoning), we here ask whether they similarly benefit from visual prompt engineering: automatically modifying the task image to improve model performance. For example, for a visual physics reasoning task ("Where does the ball land, after passing a set of obstacles?"), an abstract sketch-like scene can be turned into a photorealistic version with a simple call to an image editing model. We find that visual prompt engineering, or VIPE for short, improves video reasoning performance across tasks. In fact, for video models, visual prompt engineering can be even more effective than classic text-based prompt engineering or test-time scaling. Ultimately, just as text-based prompt engineering systematically improves language model performance, visual prompt engineering can serve as a simple, compute-efficient approach to elicit better visual reasoning performance from video models. Example videos on our project page at https://visual-prompt-engineering.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Visual prompt engineering (VIPE) - automatically modifying task images via image editing models - improves video reasoning model performance, often more effectively than text-based prompt engineering or test-time scaling.
AI.motivation: As foundation models become prevalent across modalities, prompt engineering is critical for language models; the authors ask whether visual models similarly benefit from automatic modification of task images to improve performance.
AI.method: VIPE: automatically transform input task images (e.g., turning abstract sketch-like scenes into photorealistic versions) using image editing models, then feed the modified visual input to video reasoning models.
AI.result: Visual prompt engineering improves video reasoning performance across tasks, and can be even more effective than text-based prompt engineering or test-time scaling for video models.
AI.conclusion: Just as text-based prompt engineering systematically improves language models, visual prompt engineering serves as a simple, compute-efficient approach to elicit better visual reasoning from video models.

title: Physics-Informed Broad Learning System: An Efficient Backpropagation-Free Framework for Solving Partial Differential Equations
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by embedding governing physical laws into deep neural networks. However, their reliance on computationally expensive gradient-based optimization and deep architectures often results in slow training, high computational cost, and limited scalability. In this work, we propose a novel physics-informed broad learning system (PI-BLS), the first physics-informed learning framework based on broad RdNNs. The proposed formulation embeds the governing differential operator and the associated initial and boundary constraints directly into a linear output-layer optimization problem, thereby replacing nonlinear gradient-based training with a deterministic least-squares solution obtained via the pseudoinverse. Consequently, the entire learning process is reduced to a single linear optimization stage while preserving the underlying physical constraints. As a result, PI-BLS offers an efficient learning paradigm for a physics-informed learning framework for solving PDEs that eliminates iterative backpropagation while preserving the underlying physical constraints. Experimental results on representative forward PDE benchmarks demonstrate that PI-BLS achieves competitive and often superior performance with reduced training time and model parameters compared with conventional PINNs.

AI.tldr: PI-BLS replaces nonlinear gradient-based training in PINNs with a deterministic least-squares solution via pseudoinverse, eliminating iterative backpropagation while preserving physical constraints, achieving competitive performance with reduced training time and parameters.
AI.motivation: PINNs suffer from slow training, high computational cost, and limited scalability due to expensive gradient-based optimization and deep architectures.
AI.method: Proposes physics-informed broad learning system (PI-BLS) that embeds governing differential operators and initial/boundary constraints into a linear output-layer optimization problem, solved via pseudoinverse with deterministic least-squares.
AI.result: PI-BLS achieves competitive/superior performance on forward PDE benchmarks with reduced training time and model parameters compared to conventional PINNs.
AI.conclusion: PI-BLS provides an efficient physics-informed learning paradigm that eliminates iterative backpropagation while preserving physical constraints.

title: The User Asks, Platforms Compete: How Agentic Recommendation Markets Take Shape
summary: Online recommendation has traditionally taken place after a user enters a platform, which determines the candidate pool and the ranking shown to the user. LLM-based user agents enable a different recommendation process: a user specifies a need before choosing a platform, leaving platforms to compete for the user's attention, which we refer to as an agentic recommendation market. In our controlled LLM-based experiments across three product domains, we find this new setting of recommendation creates a tension between access and attention. Compared with traditional platform-centric recommendation, user-centric recommendation greatly expands the opportunity for relevant items to enter comparison; yet broader participation does not translate directly into effective exposure. Competition directly triggers platforms' strategic play: selectively positive explanations occupy 73--78% of first-ranked positions. When the user agent relates platforms' actions to subsequent user feedback, this share falls to 36--41%, while the chance of a user purchasing the relevant item increases. A user agent is therefore more than a ranker over a larger pool of candidates: its querying, ranking, and feedback mechanism governing who can compete, how scarce attention is allocated, and how earlier outcomes shape the evaluation of platforms directly affect user utility. Designing agentic recommendation therefore requires treating access, attention, and accountability as a joint mechanism design problem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "agentic recommendation markets" where LLM-based user agents solicit competing platform responses before users choose a platform, revealing a tension between access (more relevant items enter comparison) and attention (strategic platform behavior emerges). User agents that incorporate feedback mechanisms reduce self-serving explanations from 73-78% to 36-41% and increase purchase likelihood.
AI.motivation: Traditional recommendation is platform-centric (post-entry ranking). LLM agents enable user-centric pre-choice competition among platforms, but this new market structure's dynamics and strategic behaviors were unexplored.
AI.method: Controlled LLM-based experiments across three product domains, comparing traditional platform-centric recommendation with user-centric agentic recommendation markets.
AI.result: User-centric recommendation expands relevant item access but triggers strategic platform behavior (73-78% selectively positive explanations in top positions). Adding user agent feedback mechanisms reduces this to 36-41% and increases purchase probability.
AI.conclusion: Designing agentic recommendation requires jointly optimizing access, attention allocation, and accountability (feedback mechanisms) as a mechanism design problem, not merely as a ranking problem over larger candidate pools.

title: Less is More: Modality-Decoupling for General AIGC Audio-Video Detection
comment: First place in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop
summary: Generative AI has rapidly expanded audio-visual forgery beyond human-centric deepfakes into general scenes. Existing AIGC detection methods assume audio-visual content correspondence, identifying forgeries by spotting cross-modal inconsistencies. However, we empirically find that this assumption does not consistently hold in general scenarios. We argue that, for general audio-visual AIGC detection, decision-level fusion is a more robust alternative to feature-level fusion. Therefore, we propose DAV-Det, a decoupled audio-visual AIGC detection system that independently models forensic evidence from each modality. The visual detector leverages multi-granularity representations at global, patch, and segment levels to capture spatial forgery cues, while the audio detector exploits both temporal and spectral irregularities via a gated temporal-spectral dual-branch architecture to model acoustic artifacts. Our method ranks 1st in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge of the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop, with a final score of 0.8460. Code is available at https://github.com/tuffy-studio/DAV-Det.

AI.tldr: DAV-Det is a decoupled audio-visual AIGC detection system that independently models forensic evidence from each modality using multi-granularity visual representations and a gated temporal-spectral dual-branch audio architecture, achieving 1st place in the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing AIGC detection methods assume audio-visual content correspondence and identify forgeries via cross-modal inconsistencies, but this assumption does not consistently hold in general scenarios. Decision-level fusion is argued to be more robust than feature-level fusion for general audio-visual AIGC detection.
AI.method: DAV-Det is a decoupled audio-visual AIGC detection system. The visual detector uses multi-granularity representations (global, patch, segment levels) to capture spatial forgery cues. The audio detector exploits temporal and spectral irregularities via a gated temporal-spectral dual-branch architecture to model acoustic artifacts.
AI.result: Ranked 1st in the General AIGC Audio-Video Detection Challenge of the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 DDL 2.0 Workshop with a final score of 0.8460.
AI.conclusion: Decision-level fusion is a more robust alternative to feature-level fusion for general audio-visual AIGC detection, and the proposed decoupled approach with independent modality-specific detectors achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Contrastive Representation Learning of Longitudinal Disease Trajectories on Temporal Graphs
summary: Understanding disease trajectories from longitudinal clinical data remains challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and heterogeneous patient cohorts. Here, we present a contrastive representation learning framework that models multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs and learns representations using contrastive graph neural networks. Nodes represent patient observations over time, while edges capture temporal continuity and structural similarity between trajectories. Structure-aware random walks guide contrastive learning to generate embeddings that preserve temporal context and trajectory topology. The resulting representations enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression patterns and reveal latent structure in longitudinal data.

AI.tldr: A contrastive representation learning framework using graph neural networks models disease trajectories as temporal graphs, learning embeddings that preserve temporal context for clustering patients with similar progression patterns.
AI.motivation: Understanding disease trajectories from longitudinal clinical data is challenging due to complex temporal dynamics and heterogeneous patient cohorts.
AI.method: The framework models multivariate disease trajectories as temporal graphs (nodes = patient observations, edges = temporal continuity & structural similarity), then uses contrastive graph neural networks with structure-aware random walks to learn embeddings preserving temporal context and trajectory topology.
AI.result: The representations enable robust clustering of patients with similar disease progression patterns and reveal latent structure in longitudinal data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed contrastive representation learning approach effectively addresses temporal complexity and cohort heterogeneity in longitudinal clinical data, uncovering meaningful disease progression subgroups.

title: Many-body Tipping Dynamics of ChatGPT-like AIs
summary: Why do ChatGPT-like AIs, despite major architectural and training differences, unexpectedly tip to undesirable content (e.g. harmful, misleading, repetitive) even under deterministic greedy decoding? We show that a broad class of such tippings is caused by the many-body interactions between tokens (spins) as they cross the finite-layer system. Tipping emerges as a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins. Attention disorder controls the transport toward, away from, or along the basins' boundary. A few-basin reduction yields a closed finite-layer threshold, whose coarse-grained predictions show good agreement across ChatGPT-like families. These results suggest that a broad class of AI failures represents 'foreseeable engineering risk' rather than inherently unpredictable behavior, with important implications for legal and societal assessments of AI harm.

AI.tldr: This paper explains why ChatGPT-like AIs tip to undesirable content (harmful, misleading, repetitive) even under deterministic greedy decoding. It models token interactions as many-body spin systems crossing finite layers, showing tipping emerges as a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins. Attention disorder controls transport dynamics, and a few-basin reduction yields a closed threshold with good agreement across model families, suggesting such failures are foreseeable engineering risk rather than unpredictable behavior.
AI.motivation: To understand why large language models unexpectedly produce undesirable content (harmful, misleading, repetitive) even under deterministic decoding, and to determine whether such failures are inherently unpredictable or constitute foreseeable engineering risk with implications for legal and societal assessments.
AI.method: Models token interactions as many-body spin systems crossing finite layers; frames tipping as a dynamical first passage process between competing output basins; uses attention disorder to characterize transport toward, away from, or along basin boundaries; applies a few-basin reduction to derive a closed finite-layer threshold.
AI.result: Coarse-grained predictions from the few-basin reduction show good agreement across ChatGPT-like model families, indicating that a broad class of AI failures are foreseeable engineering risk.
AI.conclusion: A broad class of undesirable AI outputs represents foreseeable engineering risk rather than inherently unpredictable behavior, with important implications for legal and societal assessments of AI harm.

title: Few-Shot Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation via Textual Inversion
summary: Open-vocabulary segmentation labels arbitrary categories from a text query without per-class training, yet on remote sensing imagery it underperforms on categories it handles reliably elsewhere. We find that much of this gap traces to the text query rather than to the segmentation model. Because these models are not specialized for overhead imagery, the class name that serves as the query is often a weak address into the vision-language embedding space. We show that a better name repairs part of the gap, while the remaining failures call for an address that the tested natural-language rephrasings do not provide. We recover that address from a few examples through textual inversion on a frozen model, keeping inference text only. On a representative benchmark this raises the mean intersection over union on the affected categories from 3.9 to 39.4, and across eight remote sensing datasets it improves over few-shot methods that instead inject visual prompts at inference.

AI.tldr: Open-vocabulary segmentation underperforms on remote sensing imagery primarily due to text query issues rather than model limitations. Using better class names partially helps, but textual inversion from few examples (without visual prompts) dramatically improves performance, raising mIoU on affected categories from 3.9 to 39.4, and outperforming few-shot methods across eight remote sensing datasets.
AI.motivation: To identify and address the root cause of poor open-vocabulary segmentation performance on remote sensing imagery, which stems from weak text queries into the vision-language embedding space rather than model limitations.
AI.method: Analyzed performance gap causes, found text query was the bottleneck; applied textual inversion on a frozen model using few examples to recover better text embeddings, keeping inference purely text-based without visual prompts.
AI.result: Raised mIoU on affected categories from 3.9 to 39.4; outperformed few-shot methods that inject visual prompts across eight remote sensing datasets.
AI.conclusion: Better text queries via textual inversion significantly improve open-vocabulary segmentation on remote sensing imagery, outperforming visual-prompt-based few-shot methods.

title: MemSFT: Mitigating Alignment Tax with an External Parametric Memory
summary: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specialized domains often incurs an alignment tax, as fine-tuning on domain-specific tasks can cause catastrophic forgetting and substantially degrade performance on general tasks. We propose MemSFT, which mitigates the alignment tax by decoupling domain specialization from backbone parameter updates through a plug-and-play parametric memory. The memory is trained to imitate the behavior of a non-parametric retriever operating over domain data, thereby memorizing knowledge and patterns that would otherwise be accessed through retrieval. Once trained on a specific domain, the memory can be reused across LLMs of different sizes. During generation, a learned router dynamically fuses the output distributions of the memory and backbone at each decoding step, allowing domain expertise to be invoked selectively. Across biology, geoscience, and law, evaluations with models ranging from Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-235B-A22B show that MemSFT consistently improves domain performance with negligible degradation in general performance, whereas full SFT suffers severe forgetting on general tasks. Overall, our results demonstrate a practical path to decoupling general model capabilities from domain-specific knowledge at the parameter level, thereby equipping LLMs with new specialized capabilities without compromising their general capabilities.

AI.tldr: MemSFT mitigates the alignment tax in domain adaptation of LLMs by using a plug-and-play parametric memory that decouples domain specialization from backbone parameters, enabling selective fusion of domain expertise without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning LLMs on domain-specific tasks causes catastrophic forgetting (alignment tax), degrading general task performance. Existing methods lack a clean parameter-level decoupling between general capabilities and domain knowledge.
AI.method: MemSFT trains a parametric memory module to imitate a non-parametric retriever over domain data, allowing it to memorize domain knowledge. A learned router dynamically fuses the output distributions of the memory and backbone at each decoding step. The memory is plug-and-play and reusable across different LLM sizes.
AI.result: Evaluated on biology, geoscience, and law across Qwen3 models (8B to 235B), MemSFT consistently improves domain performance with negligible general-task degradation, while full SFT suffers severe forgetting.
AI.conclusion: MemSFT provides a practical path to decouple general model capabilities from domain-specific knowledge at the parameter level, equipping LLMs with specialized capabilities without compromising general performance.

title: ContractHIL-HLS: Contract-Aligned Multi-Agent Workflow with Hardware-in-the-Loop Feedback for HLS Design
summary: This paper presents ContractHIL-HLS, a contract-aligned multi-agent workflow for practical high-level synthesis (HLS) engineering. The workflow makes three contributions. First, it introduces a structured contract as the semantic-alignment and task-execution artifact that translates natural language requirements into explicit interfaces, constraints, validation checks, and rollback rules. Second, it incorporates hardware information into the feedback loop by feeding HLS, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, and failure evidence back into generation, thereby extending LLM-assisted HLS from kernel code toward system- and board-level closure. Third, it decomposes agents by semantic lowering and execution tasks rather than by conversational roles: a Contract Agent lowers natural language into the contract, an HTML Agent renders the contract as persistent structured HTML, and a Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent implements and revises the design with measured evidence. We evaluate ContractHIL-HLS in two parts. On 94 locally executable HLS-Eval tasks, the structured contract provides the largest small design gain, improving the estimated single-sample testbench pass rate from 64.0% to 70.2%; the full flow reaches 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. Because HLS-Eval does not exercise board-level design, we also validate ContractHIL-HLS on a board tested ML-KEM/ML-DSA post-quantum cryptography (PQC) secure-message accelerator, where the retained dual-bitstream organization reduces six-message average text runtime from 207.3 ms to 52.4 ms with positive routed WNS on both images while preserving decrypted-message verification. We open-source our work at BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS (https://github.com/BJUT-CS316-LAB/ContractHIL-HLS).

AI.tldr: ContractHIL-HLS is a contract-aligned multi-agent workflow for practical HLS engineering that uses structured contracts as semantic-alignment artifacts, incorporates hardware feedback into LLM-assisted HLS, and decomposes agents by semantic lowering and execution tasks. It improves testbench pass rates from 64.0% to 70.2% on HLS-Eval tasks and reduces PQC accelerator runtime from 207.3ms to 52.4ms on board-level validation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-assisted HLS approaches lack structured semantic alignment between natural language requirements and hardware implementation, do not incorporate hardware feedback (HLS, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, failure evidence) into the generation loop, and rely on conversational role-based agent decomposition rather than task-oriented decomposition, limiting their effectiveness for system- and board-level design closure.
AI.method: The workflow introduces three components: (1) a structured contract artifact that translates natural language into explicit interfaces, constraints, validation checks, and rollback rules; (2) a hardware-in-the-loop feedback mechanism that feeds HLS, Vivado, PYNQ runtime, power, and failure evidence back into LLM generation; (3) a task-oriented agent decomposition with Contract Agent (natural language→contract), HTML Agent (contract→structured HTML), and Hardware-in-the-Loop Agent (implement/revise with measured evidence).
AI.result: On 94 HLS-Eval tasks, the structured contract improves pass@1 from 64.0% to 70.2%, and the full flow achieves 70.4% pass@1 and 76.6% pass@5. On a board-tested ML-KEM/ML-DSA PQC accelerator, the dual-bitstream organization reduces six-message average text runtime from 207.3ms to 52.4ms with positive routed WNS on both images while preserving decrypted-message verification.
AI.conclusion: The contract-aligned multi-agent workflow with hardware-in-the-loop feedback and task-oriented agent decomposition significantly improves both HLS-level code generation and board-level design closure, demonstrating effectiveness for practical HLS engineering beyond kernel-level tasks.

title: ReDesign: Recovering Editable Design Structures from Images via Agentic Decomposition
summary: Recovering an editable design file from a raster image is a common and costly bottleneck in modern design workflows, yet remains challenging since editability depends on recovering multi-modal attributes, such as typography, vector geometry, colors, grouping, and layer ordering. We present ReDesign, an agentic framework that grows an editable layer hierarchy by selecting and composing specialized tools across modalities. To keep this long decision process reliable despite imperfect tool outputs, we introduce graceful verification at each expansion, which provides local accept, prune, or retry feedback that prevents error accumulation and avoids large scale reruns. To evaluate editability at scale, we introduce the Figma Edit Replay Benchmark, consisting of 909 raw Figma files and 14,796 controlled edit instructions that replay edits on reconstructed outputs. Across this benchmark and standard reconstruction metrics, ReDesign achieves strong visual fidelity while delivering the highest editability across layout, color, and text edits, outperforming layered decomposition baselines and serial tool use pipelines.

AI.tldr: ReDesign is an agentic framework that recovers editable layer hierarchies from raster images by selecting and composing specialized tools, using graceful verification to prevent error accumulation. It achieves high editability on the new Figma Edit Replay Benchmark, outperforming baselines in layout, color, and text edits.
AI.motivation: Recovering an editable design file from a raster image is a common and costly bottleneck in design workflows, as editability depends on recovering multi-modal attributes (typography, vector geometry, colors, grouping, layer ordering).
AI.method: An agentic framework that grows an editable layer hierarchy by selecting and composing specialized tools across modalities, with graceful verification (local accept, prune, or retry feedback) at each expansion to prevent error accumulation and avoid large-scale reruns.
AI.result: Across the Figma Edit Replay Benchmark (909 raw Figma files, 14,796 edit instructions) and standard reconstruction metrics, ReDesign achieves strong visual fidelity and the highest editability for layout, color, and text edits, outperforming layered decomposition baselines and serial tool use pipelines.
AI.conclusion: ReDesign effectively recovers editable layer hierarchies from raster images by using an agentic approach with graceful verification, enabling strong editability across multiple modalities.

title: Using Data-Derived Priors to Guide CNN Architecture Design for NIR Chemometrics
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, submitted to peer-review journal
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) for near-infrared (NIR) chemometrics are often designed using generic architectural rules, although spectral datasets differ in sampling, smoothness, redundancy, and sample size. We tested whether these properties can provide empirical priors for CNN design. Across 25 NIR regression tasks, we computed descriptors of dataset size, spectral length and spacing, entropy, intrinsic rank, autocorrelation, and wavelet-scale structure. Two interpretable 1D-CNN scaffolds (a minimal single-convolution model and an extended shallow model with optional branching, dilation, etc) were optimized using five-fold cross-validated Bayesian hyperparameter optimization (HPO). Relationships extracted from near-optimal trials were converted into warm-start heuristics and evaluated directly and through leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) validation. The clearest relationships involved convolutional receptive fields. In the minimal CNN, the preferred kernel fraction decreased with spectral entropy and intrinsic rank, increased with the wavelet energy-support fraction, and the learning rate tended to decrease with training-set size. Direct and LODO heuristics were competitive with HPO, with median test-RMSE ratios of 0.953 and 1.017, respectively. The extended CNN showed similar but less transferable structure across branch usage, dilation, dropout, filter counts, and receptive-field choices. Ten stochastic refits showed seed sensitivity comparable to that of HPO-selected configurations. In a separate experiment, joint preprocessing and CNN HPO outperformed standardized-spectra HPO in 19 of 25 tasks, although gains were dataset-dependent. These results show that spectral descriptors can provide practical CNN design priors, guiding shallow NIR models toward plausible hyperparameter regions before target-specific tuning

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether spectral dataset properties (entropy, rank, autocorrelation, wavelet structure, etc.) can serve as empirical priors for designing 1D-CNN hyperparameters in NIR chemometrics. Across 25 tasks, Bayesian HPO revealed relationships—most notably linking convolutional receptive fields to spectral descriptors—which were distilled into warm-start heuristics that performed competitively with full HPO (median test-RMSE ratios of 0.953–1.017). Joint preprocessing+CNN HPO also outperformed standardized-spectra HPO in 19/25 tasks.
AI.motivation: To determine whether readily computable properties of NIR spectral datasets (e.g., entropy, intrinsic rank, autocorrelation, wavelet-scale energy) can provide empirical design priors for 1D-CNN architectures, reducing reliance on generic architectural rules and expensive hyperparameter optimization.
AI.method: 25 NIR regression tasks; computed dataset descriptors (size, spectral length/spacing, entropy, intrinsic rank, autocorrelation, wavelet-scale structure); two interpretable 1D-CNN scaffolds (minimal single-convolution and extended shallow model); Bayesian HPO with 5-fold CV; extracted relationships from near-optimal trials into warm-start heuristics; validated directly and via leave-one-dataset-out (LODO); separate experiment comparing joint preprocessing+CNN HPO vs standardized-spectra HPO.
AI.result: Convolutional receptive field choices showed clearest relationships with spectral descriptors; minimal CNN's kernel fraction decreased with spectral entropy and intrinsic rank, increased with wavelet energy-support fraction; learning rate decreased with training-set size. Direct heuristics achieved median test-RMSE ratio 0.953, LODO heuristics 1.017 vs HPO. Extended CNN showed similar but less transferable structure. Joint preprocessing+CNN HPO outperformed in 19/25 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Spectral dataset descriptors can provide practical, transferable CNN design priors that guide shallow NIR models toward plausible hyperparameter regions before target-specific tuning, potentially reducing optimization burden.

title: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Cannot Sample from Distributions They Can Describe
summary: Silicon sampling uses language models as proxies for human survey respondents, treating each model call as an independent draw from the persona's response distribution. We show this draw does not exist: instruction-tuned models do not sample from distributions, they collapse to a single output. The same persona on the same question returns the same answer on more than half of items in a public-opinion benchmark. The collapse is sharp: the model's internal probabilities concentrate on a single option, and the failure is substantially amplified by instruction tuning: across three model families with materially different post-training pipelines, every instruction-tuned model fails on every task we test, while base models fail far less often. Strikingly, the same model that cannot sample from a distribution can describe it accurately in a single call. We call this gap the KNOWS/DOES split, and trace it to a degenerate sampling primitive visible in the logits and induced by alignment training. Exploiting this split, asking the model to describe the response distribution in one call more than halves the error against human survey data compared to persona aggregation. For applications that require per-persona outputs, we propose Prompt-Perturbed Argyle (PPA), which reduces the same error by 21% at no added cost.

AI.tldr: Instruction-tuned language models fail to produce varied responses when simulating human survey respondents—they collapse to a single output per persona-question pair. While they can describe distributions accurately (KNOWS), they cannot sample from them (DOES), a gap caused by alignment training. Methods leveraging this split (describing distributions, PPA) significantly reduce error against human data.
AI.motivation: Silicon sampling assumes language models can act as proxies for human respondents by treating each model call as an independent draw from a persona's response distribution. The paper investigates whether this assumption holds for instruction-tuned models.
AI.method: The authors benchmark model behavior on public-opinion tasks, analyze internal logits across base and instruction-tuned models from three families, trace the collapse to alignment-induced degenerate sampling primitives, and propose two mitigation strategies: asking models to describe the distribution directly, and Prompt-Perturbed Argyle (PPA).
AI.result: Instruction-tuned models return the same answer on >50% of items when the same persona is asked the same question; base models fail far less. The collapse is due to alignment training concentrating probability mass on a single option. Describing the distribution halves error; PPA reduces error by 21% at no added cost.
AI.conclusion: The core assumption of silicon sampling (independent draws from a distribution) is invalid for instruction-tuned models due to the KNOWS/DOES split. Leveraging the model's ability to describe distributions outperforms aggregation of per-persona samples.

title: Contextual Deconvolution for Variance-Stable Demand Sensing: Kernel-Modulated Operators in Promotional Retail
summary: Machine learning demand forecasts optimize statistical accuracy yet leave excess operational volatility that inflates safety stock and amplifies the Bullwhip effect. We introduce \textbf{Contextual Deconvolution} (CD), a two-stage estimator that reframes demand sensing as a convex decomposition: a kernel-modulated banded operator separates transient promotion-driven shocks from a smooth structural baseline, and hierarchical partial pooling enables catalog-scale deployment without per-SKU training. The operator is data-derived, not imposed---it reduces to the identity wherever the promotional response is impulsive (most of M5, all of Favorita) and contributes only where genuine multi-day carryover exists, so the gains rest on the structural decomposition itself. Evaluating strictly out-of-sample on 30,490 M5 SKUs and 2,845 Favorita items, with calendar-aware baselines given CD's identical future calendar, we anchor the contribution on a full inventory-cost accounting: CD lowers safety stock, holding cost, and order variance but under-provisions event spikes, reducing total cost only when holding costs exceed $\sim$20\% of stockout costs (95\% CI $[17\%,25\%]$); otherwise it is an operational-stability and inventory-capital layer, not an expected-cost minimizer. Its accuracy contribution is reliability rather than central tendency: across eleven baselines, CD attains the lowest cross-sectional dispersion of per-SKU error and mis-forecasts by more than 200\% on 0.8\% of SKUs versus 9.9--20.6\% for every baseline, ranking first on both in all four M5 draws. Because the Variance Ratio and std-based safety stock are minimized by any sufficiently smooth forecast, we treat them as diagnostics, not objectives. A supporting analysis shows the learned demand operators are non-normal, yet CD's compact parametric kernel matches their operational performance interpretably.

AI.tldr: Contextual Deconvolution (CD) is a two-stage demand sensing estimator that decomposes demand into promotion-driven shocks and a smooth baseline using a kernel-modulated banded operator. Across 30,490 M5 and 2,845 Favorita SKUs, CD reduces safety stock, holding cost, and order variance, and achieves the lowest cross-sectional error dispersion, but only reduces total cost when holding costs exceed ~20% of stockout costs; otherwise it serves an operational-stability role.
AI.motivation: Machine learning demand forecasts optimize statistical accuracy but leave excess operational volatility that inflates safety stock and amplifies the Bullwhip effect. A method is needed to reduce operational volatility without sacrificing forecast accuracy.
AI.method: Two-stage estimator: (1) a kernel-modulated banded operator separates transient promotion-driven shocks from a smooth structural baseline via convex decomposition; (2) hierarchical partial pooling enables catalog-scale deployment without per-SKU training. The operator is data-derived and reduces to identity where promotional response is impulsive.
AI.result: CD lowers safety stock, holding cost, and order variance; achieves lowest cross-sectional dispersion of per-SKU error across eleven baselines; mis-forecasts by more than 200% on only 0.8% of SKUs vs. 9.9-20.6% for baselines. However, it under-provisions event spikes, reducing total cost only when holding costs exceed ~20% of stockout costs (95% CI [17%,25%]).
AI.conclusion: CD's accuracy contribution is reliability (low error dispersion) rather than central tendency. It is an operational-stability and inventory-capital layer when holding costs are low, and a cost minimizer when holding costs are sufficiently high relative to stockout costs. The learned demand operators are non-normal but CD's compact parametric kernel matches their performance interpretably.

title: Physics-Grounded Fluid Video Generation with a Simulation Dataset and Dual-Stream Optical-Flow Supervision
summary: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling content but routinely violate elementary physics when the subject involves fluids: liquid columns break apart in mid-air, container water levels fail to rise as liquid is poured in, and splashes disperse without regard to momentum or gravity. We attribute this gap to the fact that large-scale video-text corpora contain almost no explicit motion supervision, so models learn to imitate fluid appearance rather than dynamics. We address this with two contributions. First, we build a physics-simulation fluid dataset combining 1,638 MPM-simulated pouring/sloshing videos with 2,320 keyword-filtered real pouring videos mined from stock footage, plus two held-out test sets: a 1,515-video real-video benchmark and an 18-prompt text-to-first-frame generalization benchmark. Second, we introduce a dual-stream image-to-video architecture built on a pretrained diffusion-transformer video generator. It augments the standard RGB decoder with a lightweight Optical-Flow Decoder branch trained with explicit end-point-error and smoothness losses, fused into the RGB stream via zero-initialized convolutions so the pretrained backbone starts undisturbed. Only the two decoders are updated; the encoder, temporal transformer, and text encoder remain frozen. Across two model scales (1.3B and 14B) and two test sets, our method improves VideoPhy-2 Physical-Commonsense and Video-Quality scores over the frozen backbone by up to 8.75 and 4.65 points, outperforms a leading open competitor, and is preferred by human raters in a blind study. A direct optical-flow read-out evaluation further shows an end-point error as low as 0.54 pixels in-distribution, confirming the model has internalized a coherent motion prior rather than merely improving surface appearance.

AI.tldr: Video diffusion models violate fluid physics (e.g., liquid columns breaking mid-air, water levels not rising). The authors fix this by: (1) building a physics-simulation fluid dataset (MPM-simulated + real pouring videos), and (2) introducing a dual-stream image-to-video architecture with an Optical-Flow Decoder branch fused via zero-initialized convolutions into a frozen pretrained diffusion-transformer backbone. Results: up to +8.75 Physics-Commonsense, +4.65 Video-Quality, 0.54px end-point error, preferred by human raters.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion models generate visually appealing content but routinely violate elementary fluid physics (e.g., liquid columns break mid-air, water levels fail to rise, splashes ignore momentum/gravity) because large-scale video-text corpora lack explicit motion supervision, causing models to imitate fluid appearance rather than dynamics.
AI.method: (1) Physics-simulation fluid dataset: 1,638 MPM-simulated pouring/sloshing videos + 2,320 keyword-filtered real pouring videos from stock footage, plus two held-out test sets (real-video benchmark and text-to-first-frame generalization benchmark). (2) Dual-stream image-to-video architecture built on a pretrained diffusion-transformer video generator: augments standard RGB decoder with a lightweight Optical-Flow Decoder branch trained with end-point-error and smoothness losses, fused via zero-initialized convolutions into the RGB stream. Only two decoders updated; encoder, temporal transformer, text encoder frozen.
AI.result: Across 1.3B and 14B scales on two test sets: up to 8.75-point improvement in VideoPhy-2 Physical-Commonsense and 4.65-point improvement in Video-Quality over frozen backbone; outperforms leading open competitor; preferred by human raters in blind study; optical-flow end-point error as low as 0.54 pixels in-distribution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dataset and dual-stream architecture effectively internalize a coherent fluid motion prior, enabling video diffusion models to generate physically plausible fluid dynamics without sacrificing visual quality.

title: Forensic Reproducibility Audit of a Radiology Vision-Language Model Benchmark: From Intended Protocol to Released Artifact
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Retrospective artifact audit; no new model calls or annotations. Corrective audit and archival reconstruction: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21629849
summary: Medical-imaging AI benchmarks combine datasets, DICOM rendering, prompts, provider APIs, automated labels, statistical code, manuscripts, and repository releases. Agreement across these artifacts is usually assumed rather than tested. We performed a retrospective forensic reproducibility audit of a preserved chest-radiograph vision-language model (VLM) pilot; no model was called again and no image or report was newly annotated. We traced prompt bindings, DICOM metadata, output completeness, label extraction, matched analyses, and release propagation. Of 300 planned model-prompt calls, 297 yielded nonempty reports. Sixty Claude calls labeled A/B were executed with the same C prompt. The 30 studies represented 28 patients. Four MONOCHROME1 images were rendered without required polarity inversion, dataset split membership was not retained, and the unvalidated extractor truncated five reports to 4000 characters. Reconstructing one common cohort of 369 complete case-finding blocks changed Cochran's Q from 154.73 to 182.29. Of 45 McNemar comparisons, 27 had unadjusted p < 0.05 and 20 remained below 0.05 after Holm adjustment. These values describe only the archived automated-label matrix; they do not recover the intended prompt comparison or establish clinical performance. We withdraw the original performance, ranking, prompt-effect, and clinical claims and specify machine-verifiable controls for cohort, DICOM rendering, prompt and model identity, call status, annotation provenance, keyed analysis, and derived artifacts.

AI.tldr: A forensic reproducibility audit of a chest-radiograph VLM pilot revealed undetected errors in prompt bindings, DICOM rendering, label extraction, and cohort reconstruction, leading to withdrawal of all original claims and specification of verifiable controls.
AI.motivation: Medical-imaging AI benchmarks are built from complex artifact pipelines (datasets, DICOM rendering, prompts, APIs, labels, code, manuscripts, releases), but agreement across these artifacts is typically assumed rather than empirically tested. This study aimed to uncover whether such assumptions hold.
AI.method: Retrospective forensic reproducibility audit of a preserved chest-radiograph VLM pilot without re-running models or re-annotating data. Traced prompt bindings, DICOM metadata, output completeness, label extraction, matched analyses, and release propagation.
AI.result: 297/300 calls yielded nonempty reports; 60 Claude calls shared the same prompt despite A/B labeling; 4 MONOCHROME1 images lacked required polarity inversion; dataset split membership was not retained; label extractor truncated 5 reports to 4000 chars; reconstructing one cohort changed Cochran's Q from 154.73 to 182.29; 27/45 McNemar comparisons had unadjusted p<0.05, 20 remained after Holm adjustment.
AI.conclusion: All original performance, ranking, prompt-effect, and clinical claims are withdrawn. Machine-verifiable controls for cohort, DICOM rendering, prompt/model identity, call status, annotation provenance, keyed analysis, and derived artifacts are specified as necessary safeguards.

title: A Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Thermal Ranking of Low-Cost Wall Materials in Hot-Dry Climates
comment: 41 pages, 13 figures. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21311299
summary: Identifying cost-effective indigenous building materials that minimise heat penetration through walls is critical for indoor thermal comfort in low-income rural housing in hot-dry climates, where summer temperatures routinely exceed 45 C. We present a two-stage computational framework for thermal ranking of five low-cost indigenous wall materials: mud brick, clay-straw adobe, lime-stabilised bamboo panel, fired clay brick, and lime-mud composite. First, a validated Crank-Nicolson finite difference method (FDM) solves the one-dimensional transient heat equation with Robin boundary conditions under diurnal solar and outdoor air-temperature forcing, generating 1500 periodic-day solutions across a nine-dimensional parameter space by Latin Hypercube sampling. Second, a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) with a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) backbone learns the parameter-to-solution operator mu -> T(x,t), enforcing both data fidelity and PDE consistency. The trained PINO attains a relative L2 field error of 5.14e-4 and a 0.201 K mean absolute error on the peak inner surface temperature, preserving the FDM material ranking exactly; PINO trained on 150 FDM samples matches a data-only FNO trained on twice as many, so the physics loss is most valuable when data are scarce. The periodic-day formulation also yields the ISO 13786 time lag and decrement factor, reproduced to within 0.99 h and 0.010. At nominal hot-dry summer conditions, clay-straw adobe achieves the best cost-performance index among widely available materials. A climate sweep, confirmed by FDM spot checks, reveals a regime boundary: under sub-ambient outdoor conditions the ranking inverts to conductive fired clay brick, delineating heat-exclusion and heat-rejection regimes. The framework supports evidence-based material selection for post-flood reconstruction in hot-dry regions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a two-stage computational framework combining Crank-Nicolson FDM and Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) with FNO backbone to thermally rank five low-cost indigenous wall materials for hot-dry climates. Clay-straw adobe achieves the best cost-performance index. A climate sweep reveals a regime boundary where material ranking inverts under sub-ambient conditions.
AI.motivation: Identifying cost-effective indigenous building materials that minimize heat penetration is critical for indoor thermal comfort in low-income rural housing in hot-dry climates where summer temperatures exceed 45°C.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) Crank-Nicolson FDM solves 1D transient heat equation with Robin BCs, generating 1500 periodic-day solutions via Latin Hypercube sampling across a 9D parameter space. (2) PINO with FNO backbone learns parameter-to-solution operator μ → T(x,t), enforcing data fidelity and PDE consistency.
AI.result: PINO achieves 5.14e-4 relative L2 field error, 0.201 K mean absolute error on peak inner surface temperature, preserves FDM material ranking exactly. PINO trained on 150 FDM samples matches data-only FNO trained on 300 samples. ISO 13786 time lag and decrement factor reproduced to within 0.99 h and 0.010. Clay-straw adobe yields best cost-performance index.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports evidence-based material selection for post-flood reconstruction in hot-dry regions. A regime boundary exists between heat-exclusion (sub-ambient outdoor conditions favor fired clay brick) and heat-rejection regimes.

title: From Cellular Responses to Pharmacological Domains: Multimodal Zero-Shot Drug Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal drug discovery enables drug representation learning beyond chemical structure by incorporating cellular responses such as gene expression and cell morphology. However, direct fusion and instance-level contrastive alignment may mix mechanism-related signals with modality-specific noise and incorrectly separate structurally dissimilar but biologically related compounds. This limitation can obscure transferable mechanism patterns required for predicting the properties of unseen compounds. We introduce PMRD, a pharmacological response domain-guided framework for multimodal zero-shot drug property prediction. PMRD separates mechanism-consistent factors from modality-specific information and constructs a consensus response domain across three modalities. Mechanism candidate augmentation identifies locally stable factors, while retrieval-geometry attribution dynamically reweights the alignment and augmentation objectives according to whether their updates preserve inter-drug discriminability.This feedback suppresses training signals that conflict with mechanism-discriminative retrieval. PMRD further combines complementary representations through reliability-aware multiview retrieval. Experiments on public datasets show improved zero-shot property prediction and more biologically coherent drug neighborhoods. Hard-negative analysis further indicates fewer conflicts between structurally dissimilar but response-related compounds. These results support PMRD as an effective framework for mechanism-aware multimodal drug representation learning.\footnote{The code will be released upon publication.}

AI.tldr: PMRD is a pharmacological response domain-guided framework for multimodal zero-shot drug property prediction that separates mechanism-consistent factors from modality-specific noise, uses mechanism candidate augmentation and retrieval-geometry attribution for dynamic reweighting, and achieves improved zero-shot prediction with more biologically coherent drug neighborhoods.
AI.motivation: Direct multimodal fusion and instance-level contrastive alignment in drug discovery mix mechanism-related signals with modality-specific noise and incorrectly separate structurally dissimilar but biologically related compounds, obscuring transferable mechanism patterns needed for predicting properties of unseen compounds.
AI.method: PMRD separates mechanism-consistent factors from modality-specific information, constructs a consensus response domain across three modalities, uses mechanism candidate augmentation to identify locally stable factors, applies retrieval-geometry attribution to dynamically reweight alignment/augmentation objectives, and combines representations via reliability-aware multiview retrieval.
AI.result: Improved zero-shot property prediction, more biologically coherent drug neighborhoods, and fewer conflicts between structurally dissimilar but response-related compounds in hard-negative analysis on public datasets.
AI.conclusion: PMRD is an effective framework for mechanism-aware multimodal drug representation learning that enables better zero-shot generalization by preserving mechanism-discriminative signals while suppressing modality-specific noise.

title: Beyond Facial Consistency: Personalized Person Image Generation with Holistic Identity Preservation
summary: Personalized person image generation requires preserving subject identity across both local facial details and broader appearance cues. Existing methods typically emphasize only one level of identity information, leading to an inherent trade-off between facial fidelity and overall appearance consistency. To address this, we first propose a simple dual-branch baseline that unifies global appearance control and local facial control within a shared generation framework. This simple combination of different branches yields promising results, but suffers from instability in practice due to uncoordinated branch contributions. To this end, we propose Dynamic Balancing Scaling (DBS), a fine-tuning strategy for improving face and appearance identity coordination. DBS consists of two components: adaptive temporal gating, which dynamically modulates branch contributions along the denoising trajectory, and region-aware optimization, which improves the coordination of facial, appearance, and global supervision. Together, these designs alleviate persistent face-branch over-dominance and encourage more effective appearance-aware guidance. We also introduce Pexels-100, a benchmark for evaluating holistic identity consistency in personalized person generation. Experiments show that DBS achieves a better trade-off between facial fidelity and appearance consistency than existing open-source baselines, while providing a controllable basic framework for holistic identity modeling.

AI.tldr: Proposes Dynamic Balancing Scaling (DBS) to balance facial fidelity and appearance consistency in personalized person image generation, along with a new benchmark Pexels-100.
AI.motivation: Existing methods emphasize only one level of identity information (local facial details or global appearance), causing a trade-off between facial fidelity and overall appearance consistency.
AI.method: Proposes a dual-branch baseline unifying global appearance and local facial control, then introduces Dynamic Balancing Scaling (DBS) with adaptive temporal gating (dynamically modulates branch contributions) and region-aware optimization (improves coordination of facial, appearance, and global supervision).
AI.result: DBS achieves better trade-off between facial fidelity and appearance consistency than existing open-source baselines on the introduced Pexels-100 benchmark.
AI.conclusion: DBS provides a controllable basic framework for holistic identity modeling in personalized person generation, alleviating branch over-dominance and improving coordination.

title: Dual-Domain Manifold Modeling for Hyperspectral Image Fusion
summary: Achieving a coherent integration of spectral richness and spatial fidelity remains a central objective in hyperspectral image fusion. However, existing hyperspectral image fusion methods struggle to effectively model geometric constraints. In the spatial domain, weak spatial-spectral interaction limits geometry-aware feature learning and suppresses high-frequency structural information, resulting in low-frequency bias and structural degradation. In the spectral domain, local manifold structures induced by spectral similarity are insufficiently exploited, limiting intrinsic pixel relationship modeling and fine-grained spectral reconstruction. To address these challenges, we propose a dual-domain manifold modeling (DDMM) framework. Specifically, we introduce a Topology-Aware Transformer (TPFormer) that combines global attention with neighborhood propagation, jointly modeling spatial topology and pixel-level feature manifold relationships to capture intrinsic spatial-spectral structures and improve topology-aware representation learning. Furthermore, a Frequency-Decoupled Spatial-Spectral Collaborative Fusion (FDSCF) module is devised, in which features are projected into the frequency domain via the discrete cosine transform and explicitly decoupled into low- and high-frequency components. Guided by a low-rank structural prior and spectral-driven spatial enhancement, FDSCF selectively enhances geometry-aware high-frequency features, strengthening spatia-spectral coupling and recovering sharper edges and finer textures. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDMM achieves superior overall performance over SoTA methods in terms of spatial structure preservation and spectral reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Dual-Domain Manifold Modeling (DDMM) framework for hyperspectral image fusion, featuring a Topology-Aware Transformer (TPFormer) for spatial-spectral topology learning and a Frequency-Decoupled Spatial-Spectral Collaborative Fusion (FDSCF) module that leverages frequency decomposition and low-rank priors to enhance geometry-aware feature learning and spatial-spectral coupling, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing hyperspectral image fusion methods fail to model geometric constraints effectively: weak spatial-spectral interaction causes low-frequency bias and structural degradation in the spatial domain, while insufficient exploitation of local manifold structures limits fine-grained spectral reconstruction in the spectral domain.
AI.method: A dual-domain manifold modeling (DDMM) framework with two key components: (1) Topology-Aware Transformer (TPFormer) combining global attention with neighborhood propagation to jointly model spatial topology and pixel-level feature manifolds; (2) Frequency-Decoupled Spatial-Spectral Collaborative Fusion (FDSCF) module that projects features into the frequency domain via DCT, decouples low/high-frequency components, and selectively enhances geometry-aware high-frequency features guided by low-rank structural priors and spectral-driven spatial enhancement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDMM achieves superior overall performance over state-of-the-art methods in both spatial structure preservation and spectral reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DDMM framework effectively addresses geometric constraint limitations in hyperspectral image fusion through dual-domain manifold modeling, frequency decoupling, and topology-aware representation, leading to sharper edges, finer textures, and better spectral fidelity.

title: OmniPhys: Knowledge-Graph-Driven Benchmarking and Collective Optimization for Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: While text-to-image models exhibit remarkable visual fidelity, they frequently violate fundamental physical commonsense. Existing benchmarks often rely on coarse-grained descriptions, failing to diagnose the mastery of specific physical principles. Moreover, the high stochasticity of generative processes causes current prompt optimization methods to suffer from gradient hallucinations, where optimizers are misled by transient visual artifacts rather than systemic flaws. To address these challenges, we introduce OmniPhys, a rigorous benchmark of 1,551 samples grounded in a Physical Knowledge Graph. By aligning PhET simulations with standard curricula, OmniPhys operationalizes a knowledge-to-scenario pipeline that performs diagnostic stress tests via a dual-path verification protocol. We further propose OmniPrompt, an iterative framework that treats physical alignment as a discrete optimization problem. For each query, OmniPrompt aggregates K stochastic images into a per-query feedback buffer. Across training, it further merges feedback from batches of B queries before each meta-policy update, filtering seed and query-local noise. Evaluations across 12 representative text-to-image models reveal universal physical bottlenecks. Results demonstrate that OmniPrompt significantly enhances physical consistency across diverse backbones, proving the transferability and efficacy of our evolved meta-policies. The code and data are available at https://github.com/zjukg/OmniPhys

AI.tldr: OmniPhys is a 1,551-sample benchmark grounded in a Physical Knowledge Graph that diagnoses text-to-image models' adherence to physical commonsense, and OmniPrompt is an iterative optimization framework that treats physical alignment as a discrete optimization problem, using feedback aggregation across stochastic images and batches to mitigate gradient hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-image benchmarks use coarse-grained descriptions that fail to diagnose specific physical principles, and current prompt optimization methods suffer from gradient hallucinations due to high stochasticity in generative processes.
AI.method: OmniPhys aligns PhET simulations with standard curricula via a knowledge-to-scenario pipeline with dual-path verification. OmniPrompt treats physical alignment as discrete optimization, aggregating K stochastic images per query into a feedback buffer and merging feedback from B queries per meta-policy update to filter noise.
AI.result: Evaluations across 12 representative text-to-image models reveal universal physical bottlenecks. OmniPrompt significantly enhances physical consistency across diverse backbones.
AI.conclusion: OmniPrompt proves transferable and effective for improving physical consistency in text-to-image generation, with evolved meta-policies generalizing across backbones.

title: Rashomon Alignment
summary: We propose Rashomon Alignment (RA), a new measure to assess functional similarity between two models. Existing functional similarity measures are distributional, quantifying differences between outputs of models applied to real-world data. However, these measures can be regarded as ecologically valid only for regions in the input space represented by the available data. We introduce a geometrical perspective on functional model similarity, which estimates it across the entire data space, offering a comprehensive view of decision boundary alignment independent of any specific data distribution. We also propose geometric Rashomon Alignment as a measure of geometrical similarity, which is computed using data uniformly sampled from the instance space. We perform an experimental analysis on more than 90 datasets, examining critical cases where model alignment diverges from predictive accuracy. Our results show that geometrical and distributional alignment provide different and complementary perspectives on the similarity between models and algorithms. RA can be used for multiple purposes, including model selection, ensemble construction, and enhanced interpretability of machine learning models and algorithms.

AI.tldr: Rashomon Alignment (RA) is a new measure for assessing functional similarity between models using a geometric perspective across the entire data space, complementing traditional distributional measures.
AI.motivation: Existing distributional functional similarity measures only quantify model output differences on real-world data regions, lacking ecological validity for the entire input space. A comprehensive view of decision boundary alignment independent of data distribution is needed.
AI.method: RA introduces a geometrical perspective on functional model similarity by estimating alignment across the entire data space. Geometric Rashomon Alignment is computed using uniformly sampled data from the instance space. Experimental analysis was conducted on over 90 datasets examining cases where alignment diverges from predictive accuracy.
AI.result: Geometrical and distributional alignment provide different and complementary perspectives on model and algorithm similarity. RA can be used for model selection, ensemble construction, and enhanced interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Rashomon Alignment offers a novel, geometrically-grounded approach to model similarity that captures decision boundary relationships across the full input space, providing complementary insights to traditional distributional measures.

title: Cardiologent: Multi-Agent Clinical Decision Support for Patient-Level Arrhythmia Assessment, Urgency, and Management
summary: The same episode of atrial fibrillation is a minor finding in a healthy adult and grounds for anticoagulation in an elderly patient with hypertension: identical signal, opposite decision. Naming the rhythm is only the start; what determines a patient's outcome is the judgement that follows -- what the arrhythmia is across the whole record, what it means for this patient, and what should be done about it. Recent work pairing large language models with the ECG stops short of this, reading one recording without assembling a patient-level finding; and agentic systems built around it either receive the arrhythmia a device has already detected or target a different diagnostic task, stopping before the decision this task requires. We formulate patient-level arrhythmia decision support as a task and present Cardiologent, a multi-agent system that spans it from detection to decision. An agent for each signal -- a single ECG lead and the photoplethysmogram a wearable acquires -- grounds its window reading in measured features rather than a bare label; the readings are assembled into the patient's rhythm profile and, with the patient's own data, reasoned against clinical guidelines retrieved for the case, with a critic checking each conclusion against the guideline it cites. We evaluate the clinical decision rather than the report, across integrated diagnosis, clinical significance, and urgency and management. Cardiologent scores highest on every axis, first on every patient-level task under both cardiologists and an at-scale LLM judge -- whose agreement with the cardiologists (ICC 0.74, 0.66) matches theirs with each other (0.67). Because each conclusion traces to a cited guideline and is validated against expert cardiologists, it yields decisions a clinician can audit rather than act on blindly -- a step toward use in continuous monitoring.

AI.tldr: Cardiologent is a multi-agent system that provides patient-level arrhythmia decision support from detection to clinical decision, using ECG and PPG signals, patient data, and clinical guidelines. It outperforms baselines across all evaluation axes and produces auditable decisions validated against cardiologists.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based ECG systems stop short of patient-level decision-making — they analyze single recordings or rely on device-detected arrhythmias without assembling a patient-level finding or reasoning toward clinical decisions (anticoagulation, management, urgency). The gap between identical arrhythmia signals and opposite clinical decisions (e.g., healthy adult vs. hypertensive elderly) requires an agentic system that integrates signal-level reading, patient context, and guideline-based reasoning.
AI.method: Cardiologent: a multi-agent system with (1) signal agents for each lead (ECG, PPG) that ground window readings in measured features; (2) assembly of readings into a patient-level rhythm profile; (3) reasoning against clinical guidelines retrieved for the case, augmented with patient data; (4) a critic agent that checks each conclusion against the cited guideline. Evaluation covers integrated diagnosis, clinical significance, urgency, and management, using both cardiologist ratings and an LLM judge.
AI.result: Cardiologent scores highest on every axis and every patient-level task under both cardiologists and the LLM judge. The LLM judge's agreement with cardiologists (ICC 0.74, 0.66) matches the inter-cardiologist agreement (0.67).
AI.conclusion: Cardiologent produces auditable, guideline-cited decisions that clinicians can verify rather than blindly trust, representing a step toward safe deployment in continuous monitoring settings.

title: Instruction-based Image Editing: A Survey on Data, Models, Evaluation, and Applications
summary: Instruction-based Image Editing (IIE) aims to transform a given image into a new one based on textual instructions. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have accelerated progress toward practical ``one-sentence image editing" systems. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy and comprehensive review of IIE research, structured around five core dimensions: (1) task definition and hierarchical categorization of editing operations, (2) methodologies for training data construction, (3) architectural evolution from GAN-based to diffusion and autoregressive paradigms, (4) standardized evaluation metrics and benchmark development, and (5) introduction of commercial solutions. Our analysis shows critical technological milestones across model generations. We further propose a Comprehensive, in-Depth, and Diagnostic benchmark for IIE task (CDD-IIE Bench), which can rigorously assess the multiple aspects of model performance.
