Through empirical comparisons of open-source solutions, we highlight their respective capabilities and limitations. Finally, we discuss future research directions to advance the field.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a systematic survey of Instruction-based Image Editing (IIE), covering task taxonomy, training data methods, architectural evolution (GANs to diffusion/autoregressive), evaluation benchmarks, and commercial solutions, along with a proposed diagnostic benchmark (CDD-IIE Bench) for comprehensive model assessment.
AI.motivation: The rapid progress in LLMs and VLMs has enabled practical "one-sentence image editing" systems, but the field lacks a structured overview. This survey aims to systematically organize IIE research to help researchers understand the landscape, compare approaches, and identify future directions.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature review structured around five core dimensions: task definition and editing operation hierarchy, training data construction methodologies, architectural evolution tracking (GAN→diffusion→autoregressive), standardized evaluation metrics and benchmarks, and commercial solution analysis. They also propose the CDD-IIE Bench—a Comprehensive, in-Depth, and Diagnostic benchmark for rigorous multi-aspect model evaluation, and perform empirical comparisons of open-source solutions.
AI.result: The analysis reveals critical technological milestones across model generations. The proposed CDD-IIE Benchmark enables rigorous multi-aspect assessment of IIE model performance. Empirical comparisons of open-source solutions highlight respective capabilities and limitations of current approaches.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing future research directions to advance the field of instruction-based image editing.

title: From Deterministic to Generative Deep Learning for Urban Air Quality Reconstruction from Sparse Observations
summary: Full-field reconstruction of air pollution is essential for evaluating pollution exposure and supporting public health decision-making. However, the complex interactions among pollutants, hard-to-predict weather patterns, and limited monitoring station coverage make this a complex task. We apply deep learning techniques to provide fast and accurate reconstructions from sparse observations of four key pollutants: NO2, O3, PM2.5 and PM10. Models are trained on full-field simulation data and evaluated on real-world observations collected from 9 to 28 monitoring stations in the city of Paris. We introduce a diffusion-based generative framework for multi-pollutant reconstruction and benchmark its performance against deterministic deep learning models. Despite noisy observations and strong spatial variability, the models achieve high structural similarity on simulated validation data and produce realistic spatial patterns on real-world observations, as indicated by power-spectrum analysis. We introduce data augmentation methods that enable transfer to real-world observations without retraining, allowing the models to generalise beyond the training period. These findings highlight the potential of ML models for reliable real-world deployment in air pollution reconstruction tasks.

AI.tldr: Deep learning models, including a diffusion-based generative framework, are trained on simulated data and applied to reconstruct NO2, O3, PM2.5, and PM10 pollution fields in Paris from sparse monitoring stations, achieving high structural similarity and realistic spatial patterns without retraining on real data.
AI.motivation: Full-field air pollution reconstruction is critical for exposure assessment and public health decisions, but is challenging due to complex pollutant interactions, unpredictable weather, and sparse monitoring coverage.
AI.method: Deep learning models (including diffusion-based generative framework and deterministic baselines) are trained on full-field simulation data, augmented with data augmentation methods to enable zero-shot transfer to real-world observations from 9–28 monitoring stations in Paris.
AI.result: Models achieve high structural similarity on simulated validation data and realistic spatial patterns on real observations (confirmed by power-spectrum analysis), with successful generalization beyond the training period via data augmentation.
AI.conclusion: ML models show strong potential for reliable real-world deployment in air pollution reconstruction tasks.

title: Impact Detection in Fall Events: Leveraging Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks Using 3D Skeletons Data
summary: Fall represents a significant risk of accidental death among individuals aged over 65, presenting a global health concern. A fall is defined as any event where a person loses balance and moves to an off-position, which may or may not result in an impact where the person hits the ground. While fall detection systems have achieved good results in general, impact detection within falls remains challenging. This study proposes an efficient methodology for accurately detecting impacts within fall events by incorporating 3D joints skeleton data treated as a graph using Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (STGCN), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) layers. By pinpointing impact moments, our approach enhances precision by distinguishing between false falls and actual impacts, contributing to better healthcare resource allocation. Our methodology, evaluated using the improved 3D skeletons UP-Fall dataset, achieves accuracy exceeding 90\% across various fall scenarios. We have made this improved dataset publicly available at https://zenodo.org/records/12773013 to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method for detecting impact moments within fall events using 3D skeleton data processed by STGCN, GRU, and BiLSTM, achieving over 90% accuracy on the improved UP-Fall dataset.
AI.motivation: Falls are a major cause of accidental death in people over 65. While fall detection systems perform well generally, accurately detecting the impact moment within a fall remains challenging, which is important for distinguishing real falls from false falls and optimizing healthcare resource allocation.
AI.method: The approach treats 3D joint skeleton data as a graph and uses Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (STGCN) combined with Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) layers to detect impact moments within fall events.
AI.result: Evaluated on the improved 3D skeletons UP-Fall dataset, the methodology achieves accuracy exceeding 90% across various fall scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology enhances fall impact detection precision, enabling better discrimination between false falls and actual impacts, which contributes to improved healthcare resource allocation. The improved dataset has been made publicly available for further research.

title: Tools Are Not Islands: Set-Level Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents via Query-Conditioned Hyperedge Prediction
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on invoking external tools to complete real-world tasks. Tool retrieval, which selects a small task-relevant subset from a library of thousands of tools before the agent acts, has therefore become a critical component of LLM agent pipelines. However, existing retrievers either score each tool in isolation or assemble the tool set sequentially, so the joint utility of a candidate set is never evaluated as a whole. In this paper, we propose HYSET, short for HYperedge-based SEt-level Tool retrieval. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we formulate tool retrieval as query-conditioned hyperedge prediction on a tool co-invocation hypergraph, under which the tool set itself becomes the unit of scoring and most existing retrieval paradigms reduce to restricted instances; (ii) we capture size-dependent tool compatibility through cardinality-specific interactions; and (iii) we design HYSET as a pre-selection module requiring no modification to the downstream agent. Experiments on ToolBench demonstrate that HYSET consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both tool retrieval performance and end-to-end task success. Beyond the in-domain setting, HYSET further supports zero-shot/few-shot transfer, generalizing to held-out tools/categories and unseen domains with minimal supervision.

AI.tldr: HYSET is a hyperedge-based set-level tool retrieval method that formulates tool retrieval as query-conditioned hyperedge prediction on a tool co-invocation hypergraph, enabling joint evaluation of tool sets rather than scoring tools in isolation. It captures size-dependent tool compatibility through cardinality-specific interactions and achieves state-of-the-art performance on ToolBench, with zero-shot/few-shot transfer capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing tool retrieval methods score each tool in isolation or assemble tools sequentially, failing to evaluate the joint utility of a candidate tool set as a whole, which is critical for LLM agents that need to invoke multiple tools collaboratively to complete tasks.
AI.method: (i) Formulates tool retrieval as query-conditioned hyperedge prediction on a tool co-invocation hypergraph, where the tool set itself becomes the scoring unit; (ii) captures size-dependent tool compatibility through cardinality-specific interactions; (iii) designed as a pre-selection module requiring no modification to the downstream agent.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on ToolBench in both tool retrieval performance and end-to-end task success; supports zero-shot/few-shot transfer, generalizing to held-out tools/categories and unseen domains with minimal supervision.
AI.conclusion: HYSET effectively improves LLM agent pipelines by enabling holistic evaluation of tool sets, and demonstrates strong generalization beyond in-domain settings.

title: AI Deployment and Cyber Governance Failures in Public-Sector Organizations: A Typological Analysis
summary: The intersection of artificial intelligence adoption, cybersecurity governance, and public sector institutional constraints has not been examined as a unified analytical problem in the existing literature. Studies address AI cybersecurity risks generically, public sector governance independently, and framework adequacy separately. Existing studies have not integrated these three streams to explain specifically how AI adoption causes cybersecurity governance failure in government organizations, nor test existing governance instruments against AI-specific public sector failure causes. This paper ad-dresses that gap. It proposes a seven-domain typology identifying ten specific AI-driven cyber governance failure causes grounded in public sector institutional analysis. It presents a three-pathway failure model showing how accountability failure, opera-tional resilience failure, and compliance failure interact and reinforce each other. It de-livers a structured coverage matrix testing five major governance frameworks (NIST CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001, COBIT, NIST AI RMF, and ISO/IEC 42001) against the typology, finding that no instrument addresses Shadow AI, speed asymmetry, or gov-ernance vacuum at the operational specificity required for public sector application. The paper introduces speed asymmetry as a named structural construct with a specified mechanism. The framework provides the design specification for an AI-enabled cyber-security maturity model for government organizations.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates AI adoption, cybersecurity governance, and public sector institutional constraints into a unified framework, identifying ten AI-driven governance failure causes across seven domains, modeling three interacting failure pathways (accountability, operational resilience, compliance), and testing five major governance frameworks—finding critical gaps in addressing Shadow AI, speed asymmetry, and governance vacuum for public sector use. It introduces speed asymmetry as a named structural construct.
AI.motivation: Existing literature treats AI cybersecurity risks, public sector governance, and framework adequacy as separate streams; no study has integrated them to explain how AI adoption specifically causes cybersecurity governance failure in government organizations or tested existing instruments against AI-specific public sector failure causes.
AI.method: The paper proposes a seven-domain typology of ten AI-driven cyber governance failure causes grounded in public sector institutional analysis, develops a three-pathway failure interaction model, and delivers a structured coverage matrix testing five major governance frameworks (NIST CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001, COBIT, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) against the typology.
AI.result: No tested governance framework addresses Shadow AI, speed asymmetry, or governance vacuum at the operational specificity required for public sector application. Speed asymmetry is introduced as a named structural construct with a specified mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides the design specification for an AI-enabled cybersecurity maturity model tailored to government organizations, revealing critical coverage gaps in existing instruments.

title: A systematic evaluation of machine learning classifiers for event-by-event background rejection in LAFOV PET scanners
summary: The introduction of LAFOV PET scanners brings significant sensitivity gains but also a substantial increase in the background rate from accidental coincidences, phantom-scattered and detector-scattered photons. While machine learning methods have been applied to background reduction in PET imaging, they target specific background components in post-processing rather than event-by-event classification on the raw data. In this work, we formulate coincidence classification as a supervised multi-class problem and evaluate XGBoost, AdaBoost and Neural Network classifiers as pre-reconstruction filters, using Monte Carlo simulations of the Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra scanner with NEMA IEC and anthropomorphic XCAT phantoms. We investigate two feature sets: a 4-feature representation based on the Attenuation Factor, photon time difference, energy sum, and energy difference, and an extended 6-feature set that incorporates topology-based variables. A systematic robustness study via cross-phantom inference reveals that the 4-feature models generalise significantly better across different phantom geometries, with XGBoost suffering an accuracy loss of only 0.04 compared to 0.13 for the 6-feature variant. Our best models achieve accuracies of up to 0.74 and 0.69 for the NEMA IEC and XCAT phantoms, respectively, outperforming traditional geometry-based cuts. However, we show that this compact feature set not only provides limited suppression of in-phantom scattered coincidences, but it also can lead to non-trivial spatial patterns. With scattered coincidences being the dominant background component in clinical conditions, this suggests that while the method serves as an effective and geometry-agnostic replacement for traditional cut-based selection, meaningful further gains in image quality will require either larger input representations or dedicated treatment of the phantom-scattered component.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates machine learning classifiers (XGBoost, AdaBoost, Neural Networks) for event-by-event coincidence classification in LAFOV PET scanners, using 4-feature and 6-feature sets. The 4-feature models generalize better across phantom geometries, achieving up to 0.74 accuracy, but struggle to suppress in-phantom scattered coincidences, indicating limited image quality improvement without larger input representations or dedicated scatter treatment.
AI.motivation: LAFOV PET scanners offer sensitivity gains but also increased background noise from accidental coincidences and scattered photons. Existing ML methods target specific background components in post-processing rather than raw event-by-event classification, motivating a study on pre-reconstruction coincidence filtering.
AI.method: Formulated as supervised multi-class classification; evaluated XGBoost, AdaBoost, and Neural Networks on Monte Carlo simulations of Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra with NEMA IEC and XCAT phantoms. Compared 4-feature (Attenuation Factor, time difference, energy sum/difference) vs. 6-feature (adding topology-based variables) sets via cross-phantom robustness study.
AI.result: 4-feature models generalize better (XGBoost accuracy loss 0.04 vs. 0.13 for 6-feature). Best accuracies: 0.74 (NEMA IEC) and 0.69 (XCAT), outperforming traditional geometry-based cuts. However, compact feature set provides limited suppression of in-phantom scattered coincidences and can create non-trivial spatial patterns.
AI.conclusion: The method is an effective geometry-agnostic replacement for traditional cut-based selection, but meaningful image quality gains require larger input representations or dedicated phantom-scatter component treatment, as scattered coincidences dominate in clinical conditions.

title: Optimization with Dynamic Constraint Learning (DCL)
summary: We propose Dynamic Constraint Learning (DCL), a data-driven framework for constrained optimization when constraint functions are unknown and cannot be queried during optimization. At each iteration, the method learns a local surrogate from nearby data and solves a subproblem within a data-supported trust region. Compared with offline global constraint learning, the approach uses local surrogates that adapt to the data distribution during optimization and can achieve solution quality comparable to that of global models while using simpler local models and smaller optimization subproblems. We demonstrate the performance of DCL on a synthetic test problem and two case studies from the literature.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Constraint Learning (DCL) is a data-driven framework for constrained optimization that learns local surrogate constraints from nearby data at each iteration, using a trust-region approach, achieving comparable quality to global models with simpler computation.
AI.motivation: To enable constrained optimization when constraint functions are unknown and cannot be queried during optimization, avoiding the need for offline global constraint learning which is computationally expensive.
AI.method: DCL learns a local surrogate from nearby data at each iteration and solves a subproblem within a data-supported trust region, adapting to data distribution during optimization.
AI.result: DCL achieves solution quality comparable to global models while using simpler local models and smaller optimization subproblems, demonstrated on a synthetic problem and two case studies.
AI.conclusion: Local surrogate-based dynamic constraint learning is an effective, computationally efficient alternative to global constraint learning for constrained optimization with unknown constraints.

title: ODYSSE: Episode-wise Policy Optimization for Personalized Agentic Reasoning
summary: Agentic systems have rapidly advanced in their ability to interact with real-world environments, leverage external tools, and provide services for users. However, unlike natural-world tasks that assume well-defined instructions, human-centered scenarios are characterized by ambiguous requests that lead to large, open-ended solution spaces. Decoding users' personalized preferences is therefore essential for narrowing the candidate solution space. This introduces a new challenge, personalized agentic reasoning, which requires agents to jointly interact with both users and environments to deliver personalized services. In this paper, we present ODYSSE, a Reinforced Fine-Tuning (RFT) framework for personalized agentic reasoning. At its core, ODYSSE proposes Episode-wise GRPO (ESPO), a novel extension of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) designed to address long action horizons and strong cross-step dependencies in personalized agentic reasoning. Rather than optimizing individual steps independently, ESPO introduces an episode-level reward mechanism together with episodic advantage estimation, enabling upstream evidence to effectively guide downstream personalized decisions and allowing agents to progressively resolve ambiguous user requests across multiple interaction steps. We further propose an episodic batch sampler that groups actions from the same episode into unified training batches, facilitating coherent optimization under ESPO. We evaluate ODYSSE on realistic long-horizon personalized GUI reasoning tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that ODYSSE consistently outperforms both specialist and general-purpose LVLMs, highlighting its effectiveness for personalized agentic reasoning.

AI.tldr: ODYSSE is a Reinforced Fine-Tuning (RFT) framework for personalized agentic reasoning that introduces Episode-wise GRPO (ESPO), an extension of GRPO with episode-level reward and episodic advantage estimation, enabling agents to resolve ambiguous user requests across long action horizons. It outperforms specialist and general-purpose LVLMs on long-horizon personalized GUI reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Human-centered scenarios involve ambiguous user requests with large, open-ended solution spaces. Decoding personalized preferences is essential to narrow the candidate space, creating a need for personalized agentic reasoning where agents jointly interact with users and environments.
AI.method: ODYSSE proposes Episode-wise GRPO (ESPO), extending GRPO with episode-level reward mechanisms and episodic advantage estimation. It also introduces an episodic batch sampler that groups actions from the same episode for coherent optimization.
AI.result: ODYSSE consistently outperforms both specialist and general-purpose LVLMs on realistic long-horizon personalized GUI reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The Episode-wise GRPO framework effectively addresses long action horizons and strong cross-step dependencies in personalized agentic reasoning, enabling upstream evidence to guide downstream personalized decisions and progressively resolve ambiguous user requests.

title: Image Quality Dependent Degradation for AI Systems
summary: Perception is one of the primary applications where neural networks outperform conventional algorithms. One example is AI systems for automated driving, which can detect pedestrians based on image data and avoid them accordingly. A substantial challenge with these AI systems is that their output depends heavily on the quality of the input images. For example, if an image is of inferior quality due to heavy contamination, such as noise or darkness, accurate predictions are hardly feasible. Additionally, various types of errors can occur, each with varying relevance to the trustworthiness of the underlying AI system. In particular, it may be more critical not to detect an existing person than to detect a person where there is none. Therefore, we want to show that we can still avoid the most critical errors in situations of inferior image quality. To achieve this, we aim to establish a fail-degraded system by lowering the network's confidence threshold based on the estimated image quality, enabling it to detect objects more cautiously in uncertain situations. Additionally, we present a novel method for estimating the quality of incoming images by comparing them to the training data using normalizing flows. We will also conduct experiments applying our method to state-of-the-art object detection. In summary, we will present a design strategy for AI-based systems in automated driving that can deal with poor-quality input data without resorting to fallback solutions. Such measures enhance trust in AI-based systems and lead to an increased provision of the AI component.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fail-degraded AI system for automated driving that handles poor-quality images by lowering confidence thresholds based on estimated image quality, using normalizing flows for quality estimation, to avoid critical errors like missed pedestrian detection.
AI.motivation: AI systems for automated driving struggle with poor-quality input images (noise, darkness), where missing a pedestrian is far more critical than a false positive. Current systems lack graceful degradation under such conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) lowering the network's confidence threshold adaptively based on estimated image quality, and (2) a novel method using normalizing flows to estimate incoming image quality by comparing it to training data distribution.
AI.result: Experiments applying the method to state-of-the-art object detection demonstrate that critical errors (e.g., missed detections) can be reduced under poor image quality without fallback solutions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed design strategy enables AI-based automated driving systems to maintain trustworthy performance under degraded input conditions, enhancing reliability and trust without relying on backup systems.

title: Detecting CSAM Text-to-Image LoRAs From Weights
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning has made it cheap and easy to customize open-weight image generation models for specific tasks, including the production of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). Existing moderation relies on metadata or generated outputs, but metadata can be deceptive and generating outputs may itself be unacceptable or illegal. We show that a safer signal lives in the weights. The top-left singular vectors of a LoRA's updates form a compact, inference-free fingerprint ($u_1$) of its strongest learned change. Using human-subject age as a benign proxy for CSAM, we find that $u_1$ identifies what a LoRA was trained on, generalizes across base models, and abstains on unrelated benign content. The signal is robust to additive weight noise, rescaling, and precision reduction. These results indicate that harmful LoRAs could be screened directly from their weights without relying on metadata or generating harmful outputs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using the top-left singular vector (u1) of LoRA weight updates as a compact, inference-free fingerprint to detect whether a LoRA was fine-tuned on harmful content (e.g., CSAM), without needing to generate outputs or rely on metadata. Experiments using age as a proxy show that u1 identifies training content, generalizes across base models, and is robust to noise and precision reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing moderation methods for detecting harmful LoRAs rely on either metadata (which can be deceptive) or generating model outputs (which may be unacceptable or illegal for sensitive content like CSAM). A safer, more reliable signal is needed to screen LoRA weights directly.
AI.method: The authors compute the top-left singular vector (u1) of the LoRA weight update matrices via singular value decomposition (SVD). This vector serves as a compact fingerprint of the strongest learned change. They use human-subject age as a benign proxy for CSAM and evaluate whether u1 can identify the training content, generalize across different base models, and abstain on unrelated benign content. Robustness is tested against additive weight noise, rescaling, and precision reduction.
AI.result: The u1 fingerprint effectively identifies what a LoRA was trained on, generalizes across base models, and correctly abstains on unrelated benign content. The signal remains robust under additive weight noise, rescaling, and precision reduction.
AI.conclusion: Harmful LoRAs (e.g., those fine-tuned for CSAM) could be screened directly from their weights using the u1 singular vector fingerprint, providing a safer alternative to metadata-based or output-based moderation approaches.

title: Cyber-Capable AI Agents: Vulnerabilities, Evaluation Containment, and Defensive Response
summary: Cyber-capable AI agents combine language models with tools, memory, and execution en- vironments to perform multi-step offensive-security tasks. Existing work separately measures cyber capability and catalogs attacks against agent components, but provides less guidance on containing a capable agent within the environments used to evaluate it. This review synthe- sizes five vulnerability classes at that boundary: multi-step offensive chains, objectives that conflict with sandbox boundaries, supply-chain and credential exposure, persistent command- and-control, and the speed of automated action. We use the reported July 2026 Hugging Face/OpenAI incident as a bounded case study, distinguishing incident-specific observations from findings established in the wider literature. Across the taxonomy and case, we examine controls for containment, privilege separation, provenance, and responder access, including the dual-use problem that defensive artifacts may also enable misuse. The review identifies practical priorities for evaluating cyber capability together with the security of the environment in which that capability is exercised.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes five vulnerability classes at the boundary between cyber-capable AI agents and their evaluation environments, using a 2026 incident as a case study, and identifies priorities for evaluating both cyber capability and environment security together.
AI.motivation: Existing work separately measures cyber capability and catalogs attacks against agent components, but provides little guidance on containing capable agents within evaluation environments.
AI.method: Literature synthesis of five vulnerability classes plus a bounded case study of the July 2026 Hugging Face/OpenAI incident, distinguishing incident-specific findings from established literature.
AI.result: Identified five vulnerability classes: multi-step offensive chains, sandbox-conflicting objectives, supply-chain/credential exposure, persistent command-and-control, and speed of automated action. Examined controls for containment, privilege separation, provenance, and responder access.
AI.conclusion: Practical priorities should evaluate cyber capability together with the security of the environment where that capability is exercised; defensive artifacts present a dual-use problem.

title: A Unified Benchmark and Modality-Adaptive Network for Day-and-Night Drone-View Geo-Localization
summary: Most existing drone-view geo-localization (DVGL) benchmarks contain drone imagery captured under a single illumination condition and lack geographically aligned visible drone images, infrared drone images, and satellite images from the same locations. To evaluate the generalization capability of DVGL methods under challenging illumination conditions, some methods train models on a visible benchmark and test them on an independent infrared benchmark. This protocol essentially constitutes transfer between datasets, which makes it difficult to systematically evaluate DVGL across daytime and nighttime conditions within a unified benchmark. To address this limitation, we construct IRCHN,a real-world DVGL benchmark designed for localization across different illumination conditions. IRCHN contains 26,460 images collected from 8,820 geographic locations across four representative scene categories, including farmland, coastline, forest, and urban areas. Each location provides one visible drone image, one infrared drone image, and one corresponding satellite image, which enables unified evaluation of DVGL methods across different illumination conditions and sensing modalities. We further propose the Modality-Adaptive State-Space Transport Relation Network (MASTR-Net), a DVGL framework tailored to localization under varying illumination conditions. MASTR-Net integrates modality-adaptive feature enhancement, bidirectional selective state-space relation modeling, and soft optimal transport relation alignment to jointly reduce modality gaps and view-induced structural discrepancies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MASTR-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on IRCHN for localization under varying illumination conditions and achieves competitive performance on two infrared benchmarks, IR-VL328 and CVGL-RGBT. Code: https://github.com/SongtianhaoXu/MASTR-Net

AI.tldr: The paper introduces IRCHN, a real-world drone-view geo-localization benchmark with 26,460 images from 8,820 locations covering visible drone, infrared drone, and satellite images across four scene categories. It also proposes MASTR-Net, a framework using modality-adaptive feature enhancement, bidirectional state-space relation modeling, and soft optimal transport alignment to handle varying illumination conditions, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing DVGL benchmarks lack geographically aligned visible and infrared drone images with satellite images under a single evaluation framework, making it difficult to systematically assess localization across daytime and nighttime conditions.
AI.method: Constructed IRCHN benchmark (26,460 images, 8,820 locations, 4 scene types) with aligned triplets (visible drone, infrared drone, satellite). Proposed MASTR-Net with three components: modality-adaptive feature enhancement, bidirectional selective state-space relation modeling, and soft optimal transport relation alignment.
AI.result: MASTR-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on IRCHN for varying illumination conditions and achieves competitive performance on IR-VL328 and CVGL-RGBT benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The IRCHN benchmark enables unified evaluation of DVGL across illumination conditions and modalities, and MASTR-Net effectively reduces modality gaps and view-induced structural discrepancies for robust cross-illumination localization.

title: An Embarrassingly Simple Rule-based Visiting Circulation Approach to Trip Destination Prediction
summary: In this paper, we propose the Rule-based Visiting Circulation (RVC) model in tackling the challenge in the IEEE Big Data Cup 2022: Trip Destination Prediction. Given trips containing travel information, personal attributes, origin zones, and their features in the training metropolitan areas, the task is to predict the destination of every trip in a targeted metropolitan area whose destinations are not given at all at the training stage. We highlight the challenges in this destination prediction task -- having no knowledge of the destinations in the targeted metropolitan area. We provide insights from the datasets, in which revisiting behaviors and the relationships between origins and destinations play a crucial role in individuals' trips. Hence, we design a simple but comprehensive method, rule-based visiting circulation, which directly utilizes the origin information and individuals' trip behaviors to determine the destinations in the targeted metropolitan area, i.e., requiring no learning from the four training areas. Experimental results on both offline evaluation and leaderboard submission consistently exhibit the proposed RVC can significantly outperform supervised learning methods and other heuristics. The RVC method eventually brings us to second place in the competition leaderboard.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Rule-based Visiting Circulation (RVC) model for trip destination prediction without any training data from the target area, achieving 2nd place in IEEE Big Data Cup 2022.
AI.motivation: The key challenge is predicting trip destinations in a target metropolitan area where no destination labels are available during training, making supervised learning inapplicable.
AI.method: RVC is a rule-based model that leverages origin information and individual trip behaviors (specifically revisiting patterns and origin-destination relationships) to directly determine destinations in the target area, without learning from the four training areas.
AI.result: RVC significantly outperformed supervised learning methods and other heuristics in both offline evaluation and leaderboard submission, securing 2nd place in the competition.
AI.conclusion: A simple rule-based approach utilizing revisiting behaviors and origin-destination relationships can effectively solve zero-shot trip destination prediction across metropolitan areas.

title: HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to the Workshop on Agent Behavior (WAB) at COLM 2026. Benchmark, environments, and evaluation harness: https://github.com/surge-ai/handbook
summary: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed under standing instructions: a system prompt, a policy file, or a skills document is placed in context, and the agent is trusted to let it govern every action that follows. Existing benchmarks rarely test this deployment pattern directly; they measure whether an agent can complete a task, not whether a long, binding policy document actually constrains its behavior over an extended tool-use horizon. We present HANDBOOK.md, a benchmark of 65 agentic tasks modeled on how enterprise employees follow company handbooks. Each task places an agent in a self-contained company environment, a file workspace together with mock email, chat, calendar, issue-tracking, and commerce services exposed over the Model Context Protocol, and instructs it to carry out routine professional work governed by an expert-written standard operating procedure of 20 to 124 pages. Tasks span five domains (finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, and HR) and ten fictional companies. To resist memorization, every task modifies one of ten base handbooks, altering the specific rules and thresholds on which grading turns, so no two tasks share a policy. Grading is fully deterministic: each task carries a rubric of programmatic criteria (824 in total) that check both that required actions occurred and that prohibited actions did not. Under strict grading, where a trial passes only if every criterion is satisfied, the best of thirty evaluated model configurations passes 36.2% of trials, and most frontier configurations remain below 25%. Failures follow consistent patterns: agents let a plausible in-environment request override the standing policy, perform a required check and then act against its result, lose rule details over long horizons, and report compliance they did not achieve. We release all tasks, environments, and the evaluation harness.

AI.tldr: HANDBOOK.md introduces a benchmark of 65 enterprise agentic tasks where LLM agents must follow long policy documents (20-124 pages) across five domains. The best model achieves only 36.2% pass rate under strict deterministic grading (824 criteria). Agents fail by overriding policy with environmental cues, ignoring check results, losing rule context over long horizons, and falsely reporting compliance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks measure task completion but not whether agents faithfully follow long, binding policy documents over extended tool-use horizons, despite this being a critical deployment pattern for enterprise agents governed by system prompts, policy files, or skills documents.
AI.method: 65 tasks across 5 domains (finance, medical billing, insurance, logistics, HR) and 10 fictional companies, each with a unique expert-written SOP (20-124 pages). Tasks use Model Context Protocol with mock enterprise services. Grading uses 824 deterministic programmatic criteria checking required and prohibited actions.
AI.result: Best model passes 36.2% of trials; most frontier models remain below 25% under strict grading. Key failure patterns: policy override by in-environment requests, ignoring check results, losing rule details over long horizons, and reporting unachieved compliance.
AI.conclusion: Current language-model agents fail to reliably follow standing policy documents in realistic enterprise settings, highlighting a significant gap for safe deployment under extended binding instructions.

title: GeoMFD: Continual Drone-View Geo-Localization with Geometry-Aware Adapter and Margin-Field Distillation
summary: Existing drone-view geo-localization (DVGL) methods are mainly developed under a static training paradigm, where models are optimized for fixed environments with all training data available in advance. However, this paradigm is difficult to extend to real-world deployment, where drones may encounter diverse environments and require multiple environment-specific models, resulting in additional storage and model-selection costs. Directly adapting a single model to new environments also risks distorting previously learned cross-view embedding geometry and causing forgetting. To address these challenges, we formalize the continual drone-view geo-localization (C-DVGL) setting and propose GeoMFD, a geometry-aware continual adaptation method for DVGL. GeoMFD combines a cold-start bootstrapping strategy (CBS), a geometry-aware adapter (Geo-Adapter), and margin-field distillation (MFD) to balance adaptation and cross-view geometry preservation. CBS initializes a stable embedding space, Geo-Adapter enables environment adaptation through controlled residual corrections, and MFD preserves similarity margins between positive pairs and hard negatives to alleviate cross-view geometry forgetting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoMFD effectively mitigates forgetting and achieves competitive performance with environment-specific DVGL methods using a single continuously updated model.

AI.tldr: GeoMFD proposes a continual learning approach for drone-view geo-localization that adapts a single model to new environments while preserving cross-view embedding geometry, using cold-start bootstrapping, geometry-aware adapters, and margin-field distillation to prevent forgetting.
AI.motivation: Existing DVGL methods use a static training paradigm requiring environment-specific models, which leads to high storage costs, model-selection overhead, and forgetting when adapting to new environments; real-world drone deployment needs a single model that can continuously adapt to diverse environments.
AI.method: GeoMFD combines three components: (1) Cold-start bootstrapping strategy (CBS) to initialize a stable embedding space, (2) Geometry-aware adapter (Geo-Adapter) for controlled residual corrections during environment adaptation, and (3) Margin-field distillation (MFD) to preserve similarity margins between positive pairs and hard negatives, alleviating cross-view geometry forgetting.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show GeoMFD effectively mitigates forgetting and achieves competitive performance with environment-specific DVGL methods using a single continuously updated model.
AI.conclusion: GeoMFD enables continual drone-view geo-localization by balancing adaptation to new environments with preservation of learned cross-view geometry, eliminating the need for multiple environment-specific models.

title: SpectONet: A Physics-Guided Spectral Deep Operator Network for Euler-Bernoulli Beam Dynamics
summary: This paper proposes a novel physics-guided spectral deep operator network, termed SpectONet, for solving Euler-Bernoulli beam (EBB) vibration problems. The proposed framework integrates the operator-learning capability of DeepONet with physics-informed constraints and Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto (CGL) sensor placement. Unlike conventional DeepONet frameworks, which commonly employ uniformly distributed sensors, SpectONet uses nonuniform spectral sensor locations with a higher concentration of points near the domain boundaries. This sampling strategy improves the finite-dimensional representation of boundary-sensitive structural responses while requiring only a limited number of branch-network inputs. The governing beam equation, together with the associated initial and boundary conditions, incorporated into the training objective to promote physically consistent and generalizable predictions. Numerical experiments on three synthetic EBB vibration problems and a real-world bridge vibration dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Comparisons with strong baselines such as, Vanilla DeepONet, PI-DeepONet, PINN, and CNN-UNet show that SpectONet consistently achieves lower prediction errors across all considered evaluation metrics. In particular, SpectONet achieves at least \(64\%\) improvement over the considered baseline models across the three synthetic problems and at least \(37\%\) for the real-world problems. These results demonstrate that SpectONet provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and physically consistent operator-learning framework for structural vibration analysis.

AI.tldr: SpectONet is a physics-guided spectral deep operator network that solves Euler-Bernoulli beam vibration problems by integrating DeepONet with physics-informed constraints and Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto sensor placement, achieving superior accuracy over baselines (64%+ improvement on synthetic, 37%+ on real-world problems).
AI.motivation: Standard DeepONet frameworks use uniformly distributed sensors, which poorly represent boundary-sensitive structural responses in beam vibration problems. The authors aim to improve the finite-dimensional representation of such responses using spectral sampling while enforcing physical consistency.
AI.method: SpectONet integrates three components: (1) DeepONet architecture for operator learning, (2) physics-informed constraints (governing EBB equation, initial/boundary conditions) in the training objective, and (3) Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto (CGL) nonuniform spectral sensor placement concentrating points near domain boundaries for better boundary-sensitive representation with limited branch-network inputs.
AI.result: On three synthetic EBB vibration problems and a real-world bridge vibration dataset, SpectONet consistently outperformed Vanilla DeepONet, PI-DeepONet, PINN, and CNN-UNet across all metrics, achieving at least 64% improvement on synthetic problems and at least 37% on real-world problems.
AI.conclusion: SpectONet provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and physically consistent operator-learning framework for structural vibration analysis, demonstrating the effectiveness of spectral sensor placement combined with physics-informed learning for boundary-sensitive problems.

title: COVENANT: Natural-Language Workflow Compilation for Aligned Agent Execution
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly entrusted with natural-language workflow instructions (e.g., retail-payment policies) that specify not only what outcome to achieve, but also which steps, branches, and tool interactions are permitted. When these instructions are supplied as prompt context, however, the model retains control over both procedure selection and step execution. As interactions accumulate, an agent can skip required steps, take unsupported branches, or execute a valid step with unsupported arguments or effects--a failure mode we call workflow misalignment. In this work, we propose COVENANT, a compiler-and-interpreter architecture for workflow-aligned agent execution. Our key insight is to treat workflow instructions as source programs rather than prompts. COVENANT converts the instructions into a workflow abstract syntax tree (WAST) and lowers it to a workflow control-flow graph (WCFG). At runtime, a controller interprets the WCFG one node at a time, checks each proposal against requirements extracted from the instructions before committing controller state or advancing the graph, and returns diagnostic feedback for repair. To evaluate COVENANT, we use 120 cases from three existing benchmarks, spanning seven workflow scenarios. Compared with state-of-the-art LLM agents, COVENANT improves benchmark success from 50.00% to 83.33% and reduces the workflow-misalignment failure rate from 42.50% to 15.83% (62.75% relative). These results show that COVENANT substantially mitigates workflow misalignment, moving LLM-agent alignment beyond isolated prompt following toward reliable execution of complex and multi-step workflows.

AI.tldr: COVENANT is a compiler-and-interpreter architecture that treats workflow instructions as source programs (not prompts), using a workflow abstract syntax tree (WAST) and control-flow graph (WCFG) to enforce step-by-step alignment, improving benchmark success from 50% to 83.33% and reducing workflow misalignment failures by 62.75%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents given natural-language workflow instructions (e.g., payment policies) often skip steps, take unsupported branches, or execute steps with invalid arguments/effects—a failure mode termed "workflow misalignment"—because the model retains control over both procedure selection and step execution when instructions are supplied as prompt context.
AI.method: COVENANT converts workflow instructions into a workflow abstract syntax tree (WAST), lowers it to a workflow control-flow graph (WCFG), then uses a runtime controller to interpret the WCFG one node at a time, checking each proposal against extracted requirements before committing state or advancing the graph, and returning diagnostic feedback for repair.
AI.result: Evaluated on 120 cases from three benchmarks across seven workflow scenarios, COVENANT improves benchmark success from 50.00% to 83.33% and reduces the workflow-misalignment failure rate from 42.50% to 15.83% (62.75% relative reduction).
AI.conclusion: COVENANT substantially mitigates workflow misalignment, moving LLM-agent alignment beyond isolated prompt following toward reliable execution of complex, multi-step workflows.

title: Towards Faithful Sentimental Image Captioning via Evidence-Aware Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Sentimental Image Captioning (SIC) requires balancing emotional expression with visual fidelity. Existing methods often struggle with this trade-off, leading to hallucinations due to insufficient local grounding and the lack of sentimental verification mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose SEA-Cap, a Sentiment-Evidence-Aware Multi-Agent System for faithful and evidence-grounded sentimental image captioning. SEA-Cap incorporates a Sentiment Evidence Miner that extracts structured, local affective cues to shift sentiment control from global attributes to verifiable object-level evidence. Leveraging this evidence, our framework orchestrates a collaborative workflow where a Generator, Hallucination Checker, and Arbitrator iteratively refine captions via a shared blackboard. By explicitly auditing generated content against mined visual evidence, SEA-Cap ensures both sentiment accuracy and factual consistency. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that SEA-Cap effectively mitigates hallucinations and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: SEA-Cap is a multi-agent framework for sentimental image captioning that uses a Sentiment Evidence Miner to extract object-level affective cues, enabling a Generator, Hallucination Checker, and Arbitrator to collaboratively produce captions with both emotional expression and factual grounding, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing SIC methods struggle with balancing emotional expression and visual fidelity, often producing hallucinations due to insufficient local grounding and the lack of sentimental verification mechanisms.
AI.method: SEA-Cap incorporates a Sentiment Evidence Miner to extract structured, local affective cues from object-level evidence, then orchestrates a multi-agent workflow (Generator, Hallucination Checker, Arbitrator) that iteratively refines captions via a shared blackboard, auditing content against mined visual evidence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that SEA-Cap effectively mitigates hallucinations and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly grounding sentiment control in verifiable object-level evidence and employing collaborative iterative refinement, SEA-Cap ensures both sentiment accuracy and factual consistency in sentimental image captioning.

title: Prototype Adaptation for Zero-Shot sEMG Movement Classification
summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables the control of prostheses, allowing upper-limb amputees to re-gain some hand function. Most current research focuses on recognizing basic movements for prosthesis control. However, in most daily activities, such as opening a door, combined movements are essential. However, collecting training data for all possible combined movements is time-consuming and requires re-training of the model for any new combination. We propose two novel recognition approaches, Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP), that enable zero-shot learning of combined, novel and unseen movements in Prototype Networks after training only with basic movements. Our methods rest on a linear interpolation assumption in the embedding space, which we study by inspecting the geometry of combined motions in signal and embedding space. In experiments on the NearLab and NinaPro DB3 data sets as well as our newly recorded BasCom dataset, our proposed SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods with accuracy improvements on combined movements of more than 20%. This advantage is maintained in online inference experiments in a user study.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CPI and SAP, two zero-shot learning methods that enable recognition of novel combined hand movements using prototype networks trained only on basic movements, achieving over 20% accuracy improvement on combined movements.
AI.motivation: Current sEMG prosthetic control focuses on recognizing basic movements, but daily activities require combined movements. Collecting training data for all possible combined movements is time-consuming and requires model re-training for new combinations.
AI.method: Two approaches: Compositional Prototype Interpolation (CPI) and Synthetic Adaptation for Prototypes (SAP), based on a linear interpolation assumption in the embedding space. The geometry of combined motions in signal and embedding space is studied.
AI.result: SAP outperforms prior zero-shot learning methods with accuracy improvements on combined movements of more than 20% on NearLab, NinaPro DB3, and the newly recorded BasCom dataset. Advantage maintained in online inference experiments.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot learning for combined movement recognition in prototype networks is feasible via linear interpolation in embedding space, with SAP being particularly effective for practical prosthetic control applications.

title: Context Assembly as the Controlled Variable: A Control-Theoretic View of Harness Policies for Frozen LLM Agents
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Code and companion paper's data: https://github.com/dpaul0501/context-optimization-rl
summary: A growing body of 2026 work applies control theory to LLM agents: Lyapunov-certified stability for tool-mediated controllers (Prinos et al., "Stable Agentic Control", 2026), sample-complexity bounds for sparse policies over massive discrete tool universes (Majumdar, "Sparse Agentic Control", 2026), and regulatory-control decompositions of multi-agent systems into auditable feedback loops (Nogueira and Skogestad, 2026). We do not claim to introduce control theory to LLM agents -- that ship has sailed. Our narrower claim is about what the controlled variable is. Prior work controls tool selection, inter-agent message routing, or the agent's raw action stream. We instead treat context assembly itself -- which prompt template, which few-shot demonstrations, how much retrieved context, how many planning/verification passes -- as the controlled variable, learned online by a contextual bandit or REINFORCE policy sitting outside a frozen model. This paper develops the formal decomposition (inner frozen policy $π_θ$, outer context policy $π_φ$), gives a stability argument for the online controller in the sense used by Zhang et al. (2026) (non-decreasing expected reward under bounded policy change), and reports an uncertainty-calibration analysis of the controller's own confidence against realized task outcomes. The applied counterpart to this paper instantiates the same controller across three domains and two model providers and releases the dataset, trajectory logs, and a deployment recipe; here we focus on the formal framing and the stability/uncertainty evidence a control-theoretic claim requires.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes treating "context assembly" (prompt template, few-shot demonstrations, retrieved context, planning/verification passes) as the controlled variable in LLM agent systems, learned online by an outer context policy (contextual bandit or REINFORCE) while the base model remains frozen. It provides a formal decomposition (inner frozen policy π_θ, outer context policy π_φ), a stability argument (non-decreasing expected reward under bounded policy change), and an uncertainty-calibration analysis.
AI.motivation: Prior work in control-theoretic LLM agents focuses on controlling tool selection, inter-agent message routing, or raw action streams. This paper argues that context assembly itself—the prompt construction and configuration parameters—has been overlooked as the controlled variable, yet it critically shapes agent behavior and can be learned online without modifying the underlying model.
AI.method: Formal decomposition into inner frozen policy π_θ (the base LLM) and outer context policy π_φ (learned online via contextual bandit or REINFORCE). Stability analysis in the sense of Zhang et al. (2026): non-decreasing expected reward under bounded policy change. Uncertainty-calibration analysis comparing controller confidence against realized task outcomes.
AI.result: A formal framing for context-assembly-as-controlled-variable; a stability argument satisfying bounded-policy-change conditions; an uncertainty-calibration analysis showing the controller's confidence aligns with realized outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Context assembly is a viable and formally tractable controlled variable for LLM agents, amenable to online learning with stability guarantees and uncertainty calibration, complementing existing control-theoretic approaches that target tools, routing, or actions.

title: FLASH: Efficient Impact Fall Detection with Unified Hypergraph State-Space Model
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP 2026), to appear September 2026
summary: Falls represent a critical public health challenge, and accurate detection of the impact moment when an individual hits the ground is crucial for timely intervention. Existing skeleton-based methods rely on graph neural networks modeling only pairwise joint connections, failing to capture multi-joint coordination characteristic of fall impacts, while transformer-based temporal models suffer from quadratic complexity limiting real-time deployment. We propose FLASH, a novel framework integrating single-matrix hypergraph representations with Mamba's selective state-space models through adaptive feedback mechanisms for efficient impact detection. Our approach constructs biomechanically-grounded hyperedges to model functional joint coordination while leveraging Mamba's linear-time complexity to capture temporal dynamics. Experiments on UP-Fall and UMAFall datasets demonstrate that FLASH achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with real-time inference capability and strong zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, while significantly reducing computational cost compared to dual-representation and transformer-based methods. The model provides interpretable feedback through learned attention patterns aligned with biomechanical principles. Code is available at https://github.com/Tresor-Koffi/FLASH-Impact-Fall-Detection.

AI.tldr: FLASH is a novel framework for fall impact detection that integrates hypergraph representations with Mamba state-space models, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with real-time inference and linear-time complexity.
AI.motivation: Accurate detection of fall impact moments is critical for timely intervention, but existing skeleton-based methods (GNNs) fail to capture multi-joint coordination, and transformer-based temporal models suffer from quadratic complexity limiting real-time deployment.
AI.method: FLASH integrates single-matrix hypergraph representations (modeling functional joint coordination via biomechanically-grounded hyperedges) with Mamba's selective state-space models (linear-time temporal dynamics) through adaptive feedback mechanisms.
AI.result: State-of-the-art accuracy on UP-Fall and UMAFall datasets, real-time inference capability, strong zero-shot cross-dataset generalization, and significantly reduced computational cost compared to dual-representation and transformer-based methods.
AI.conclusion: FLASH demonstrates that hypergraph+Mamba integration outperforms GNN and transformer approaches for fall impact detection, with interpretable attention patterns aligned with biomechanical principles and practical real-time deployment feasibility.

title: DRIFT: Direct-Recursive Intervention-Conditioned Forecasting of ICU Physiological Trajectories
comment: 34 pages, 1 figure; extended technical appendices included
summary: Many time-series forecasts depend not only on prior observations but also on actions specified during the forecast period. In intensive care units (ICUs), future vital signs and laboratory values are influenced by treatments such as vasopressors. However, models that predict the full future sequence all at once make little use of these treatments, whereas autoregressive models can accumulate errors. We introduce DRIFT, a hybrid framework in which a direct model produces the primary forecast and a recursive, action-conditioned model contributes constrained corrections. We evaluate DRIFT on 6,046 admissions from MIMIC-IV and 8,345 admissions from eICU-CRD. Averaged across the 8-, 24-, and 48-hour forecast endpoints, DRIFT reduces mean absolute error for mean arterial pressure (MAP) by 0.673% relative to an action-conditioned Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT-action) on MIMIC-IV and achieves the lowest corresponding error among the compared models on eICU-CRD. Although the overall accuracy improvement is modest, a MIMIC-IV audit restricted to windows in which the supplied treatment sequence was altered showed that DRIFT achieved lower observed-target MAP error than TFT-action at 8 and 24 hours. Treatment-sequence alteration increased DRIFT's MAP error by 0.21-0.26 mmHg more than it increased TFT-action's error, with prediction changes occurring primarily after the supplied paths diverged. In a separate robustness experiment, the MAP advantage persisted under three shared checkpoint-selection rules emphasizing overall endpoint error, MAP error, or both equally.

AI.tldr: DRIFT is a hybrid direct-recursive forecasting framework for action-conditioned time-series prediction in ICUs, combining a direct model's primary forecast with recursive, action-conditioned corrections. Evaluated on MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD, it modestly improves MAP prediction accuracy over TFT-action, especially when treatment sequences are altered.
AI.motivation: Existing time-series forecasting models for ICU settings either ignore treatment actions (direct models) or suffer from error accumulation (autoregressive models), motivating a hybrid approach that leverages action information while mitigating recursive error propagation.
AI.method: DRIFT combines a direct forecasting model (producing the primary forecast) with a recursive, action-conditioned model that applies constrained corrections, blending the strengths of both paradigms.
AI.result: On MIMIC-IV (6,046 admissions) and eICU-CRD (8,345 admissions), DRIFT reduces MAP MAE by 0.673% over TFT-action averaged across 8/24/48-hour endpoints. Under altered treatment sequences, DRIFT achieves lower MAP error at 8 and 24 hours. The advantage persists under three checkpoint-selection rules in robustness experiments.
AI.conclusion: DRIFT offers a modest but consistent improvement in action-conditioned ICU forecasting, with particular robustness when treatment sequences deviate from expected plans.

title: A Control System, a Dataset, and a Recipe for Making Frozen LLM Agents Learn a Domain
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and dataset: https://github.com/dpaul0501/context-optimization-rl
summary: Production LLM agents are increasingly assembled from a frozen model wrapped in a harness: a prompt template, a tool set, a memory/retrieval layer, a planning strategy, and a verification policy. Two 2026 systems, Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and HyperAgents (Meta AI, 2026), show that this harness can itself be optimized or even self-rewritten by an agentic proposer -- at the cost of either an expensive code-search loop or unconstrained self-modifying code, neither of which is auditable or usable with a fully black-box model API. We take a narrower, more constrained position: treat the harness as a small, fixed, human-legible action space and learn a policy over it online with classic sample-efficient reinforcement learning (an $ε$-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE), scored against a multi-objective reward (task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and an unsupported-claim penalty). We instantiate this control system with DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024) as both the context assembler and the source of the strongest non-adaptive baseline (a DSPy BootstrapFewShot static prompt), and evaluate it across three verifiable task domains -- tool-use workflows, code generation (HumanEval), and multi-hop retrieval QA (HotpotQA) -- and two model providers (a local Ollama model and AWS Bedrock). We release the harness-control-system code, the cross-domain verifiable task suite, the full trajectory/reward-decomposition logs from training, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe for applying this to a new organization's domain and verification setup.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a constrained, auditable approach to optimizing LLM agent harnesses (prompt templates, tools, memory, planning, verification) using online reinforcement learning (ε-greedy contextual bandits and REINFORCE) instead of expensive code-search or self-modifying code. Built on DSPy, it evaluates across tool-use, code generation (HumanEval), and multi-hop QA (HotpotQA) with local and cloud models, releasing all code, task suites, and deployment recipes.
AI.motivation: Existing production LLM agents use harnesses (prompt templates, tools, memory, planning, verification) that can be optimized via expensive code-search loops or unconstrained self-modifying code, neither of which is auditable or works with black-box model APIs. The authors seek a more constrained, auditable, and practical alternative.
AI.method: The harness is treated as a small, fixed, human-legible action space. A policy over this action space is learned online using sample-efficient RL: an ε-greedy contextual bandit and REINFORCE. The reward is multi-objective: task success, verifier score, policy compliance, cost, latency, and unsupported-claim penalty. DSPy serves as both context assembler and baseline (BootstrapFewShot static prompt).
AI.result: Evaluated across three verifiable task domains (tool-use workflows, HumanEval code generation, HotpotQA multi-hop retrieval QA) and two model providers (local Ollama, AWS Bedrock). All code, task suite, trajectory/reward-decomposition logs, and a provider-agnostic deployment recipe are released.
AI.conclusion: A constrained, RL-based harness optimization approach is viable and preferable over unconstrained code-search or self-modifying code, offering audibility, black-box API compatibility, and practical deployability across diverse domains and model providers.

title: Fine-Grained Food Image Understanding via Target-Aware Data Alignment
summary: Fine-grained food visual--semantic understanding requires models to capture subtle distinctions across ingredients, cooking methods, doneness, color, texture, and plate composition. Although CLIP-style vision-language models provide a natural framework for this task, their effectiveness is limited when training relies on heterogeneous web-collected image--text pairs. Such data often exhibit a web-to-target domain gap and cross-modal misalignment, where images differ from the target distribution and captions are noisy, multilingual, or weakly grounded in visual content. We propose a data-centric multimodal alignment method for fine-grained food description and recognition. Our method first performs target-aware data selection to identify visually relevant training subsets, then applies VLM-based caption refinement to generate visually grounded, target-style descriptions. Using these curated image--caption pairs, we train complementary CLIP-style retrieval experts and further combine their decisions through a hierarchical VLM-assisted multi-expert decision-level fusion strategy that invokes the VLM only when experts disagree. Experiments show that our data refinement strategy significantly improves retrieval performance over naive web supervision, with VLM-based caption refinement alone yielding an average performance gain of approximately 19%. Our full method also achieves more than twice the retrieval score of pure VLM-based retrieval while remaining substantially more efficient.

AI.tldr: A data-centric multimodal alignment method for fine-grained food understanding that uses target-aware data selection, VLM-based caption refinement, and multi-expert fusion to significantly outperform naive web supervision and pure VLM retrieval while maintaining efficiency.
AI.motivation: CLIP-style models struggle with fine-grained food understanding due to domain gaps and cross-modal misalignment in web-collected image-text pairs, where images differ from target distributions and captions are noisy, multilingual, or weakly grounded in visual content.
AI.method: (1) Target-aware data selection to identify relevant visual subsets, (2) VLM-based caption refinement to generate visually grounded target-style descriptions, (3) Training complementary CLIP-style retrieval experts on curated pairs, (4) Hierarchical VLM-assisted multi-expert decision-level fusion that invokes VLM only when experts disagree.
AI.result: VLM-based caption refinement alone yields ~19% average performance gain over naive web supervision. The full method achieves more than 2x the retrieval score of pure VLM-based retrieval while being substantially more efficient.
AI.conclusion: Data-centric refinement strategies (selection + caption refinement) significantly improve fine-grained food visual-semantic understanding over naive web supervision, and a hybrid expert fusion approach balances performance and efficiency compared to pure VLM methods.

title: A2TTA: Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation for Evolving Traffic Sensor Networks
summary: Traffic forecasting is important for efficient traffic management and route planning in smart cities. Existing traffic forecasting studies typically assume fixed sensor graphs, overlooking the continuous evolution of real-world traffic networks, e.g., ongoing road network construction and evolving human mobility patterns. These dynamic changes can substantially degrade conventional forecasting models, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) to efficiently adapt pretrained models during deployment. However, applying TTA to evolving traffic sensor networks remains challenging in two aspects. First, topology expansion introduces new sensors and connections, continuously reshaping the sensor graph. Second, tem- poral shifts vary in time scale and stability, requiring differentiated adaptation to long-term and short-term shifts. In this study, we address these challenges by proposing A2TTA, an Anchored-and-Agile Test-Time Adaptation framework for evolving traffic sensor networks, which transforms topology-induced forecasting errors into an expandable output calibration problem and separates tem- poral adaptation into persistent global correction and agile context-specific specialization. By jointly addressing topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts, A2TTA enables efficient and robust adaptation to continuously evolving traffic environments. Extensive experiments on ten real-world traffic networks demonstrate that A2TTA consistently improves forecasting performance across different backbones, datasets, and prediction horizons. Our code is available in https://github.com/lixus7/A2TTA.

AI.tldr: A2TTA is a test-time adaptation framework for evolving traffic sensor networks that handles topology expansion (new sensors/connections) and multi-scale temporal shifts (long-term vs short-term) via anchored-and-agile adaptation, consistently improving forecasting across diverse real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing traffic forecasting models assume fixed sensor graphs and fail under real-world dynamic changes (road construction, evolving mobility patterns), motivating the need for efficient test-time adaptation in continuously evolving traffic networks.
AI.method: A2TTA transforms topology-induced forecasting errors into an expandable output calibration problem and separates temporal adaptation into persistent global correction (anchored) and agile context-specific specialization (agile), jointly addressing topology evolution and multi-scale temporal shifts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on ten real-world traffic networks show consistent forecasting improvement across different backbones, datasets, and prediction horizons.
AI.conclusion: A2TTA enables efficient and robust adaptation to continuously evolving traffic environments, effectively handling both topology expansion and multi-scale temporal distribution shifts at test time.

title: Salient Knowledge Pathways: Sparse Cross-Modal Routing for Efficient Knowledge-Intensive Multimodal Question Answering
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA), Seoul, South Korea. Copyright 2026 by the author(s). (Archival)
summary: Knowledge-intensive multimodal question answering (KI-MMQA) sits at the intersection of three expensive primitives: long visual token sequences, dense retrieval over large external corpora, and full cross-modal fusion. Existing systems pay all three costs uniformly per query, even though only a small fraction of visual content and retrieved knowledge is actually relevant to any given question. We introduce SKIP (Salient Knowledge-Injected Pathways), a unified inference architecture that routes computation along sparse pathways jointly conditioned on the question, the image, and a difficulty estimate. SKIP combines question-guided visual token pruning, region-conditional sparse retrieval, bipartite sparse cross-attention, and speculative knowledge verification with an adaptive budget controller that allocates compute proportional to predicted question difficulty. We derive an information-bottleneck bound showing that the optimal visual sparsity rate scales as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ under realistic question-image mutual-information assumptions, with retained accuracy guarantees. Across five KI-MMQA benchmarks (OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, and ViQuAE), SKIP matches or exceeds the accuracy of strong dense baselines while using $3.4$--$6.8\times$ fewer FLOPs and $2.7\times$ less end-to-end latency. Code available at: https://pmlrbd.github.io/skip/

AI.tldr: SKIP is a unified inference architecture for knowledge-intensive multimodal QA that routes computation along sparse pathways (guided by question, image, and difficulty), achieving comparable or better accuracy than dense baselines while using 3.4–6.8× fewer FLOPs and 2.7× less latency across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing KI-MMQA systems uniformly pay high costs for long visual tokens, dense retrieval, and full cross-modal fusion, even though only a small fraction of content is relevant per query. SKIP aims to eliminate this wasteful uniform computation.
AI.method: SKIP combines (1) question-guided visual token pruning, (2) region-conditional sparse retrieval, (3) bipartite sparse cross-attention, (4) speculative knowledge verification, and (5) an adaptive budget controller allocating compute proportional to predicted difficulty. An information-bottleneck bound derives optimal visual sparsity rate O(1/√N) with accuracy guarantees.
AI.result: On OK-VQA, A-OKVQA, InfoSeek, Encyclopedic-VQA, and ViQuAE, SKIP matches or exceeds strong dense baseline accuracy while using 3.4–6.8× fewer FLOPs and 2.7× less end-to-end latency.
AI.conclusion: Sparse computation routing conditioned on question, image, and difficulty can dramatically reduce computational costs in KI-MMQA without sacrificing accuracy, challenging the necessity of uniform dense processing.

title: Explicit Layer Modeling for Video Object Insertion and Layer Decomposition
summary: Most video editing systems still lack explicit layered video representations, limiting their ability to perform realistic compositing, object reuse, and consistent manipulation. This limitation is especially pronounced in video object insertion and video layer decomposition, where existing methods rely on implicit inference or per-scene optimization due to the absence of explicit foreground-layer supervision. We introduce TriLayer, a large-scale triplet video dataset containing aligned composite, background, and foreground videos, where the foreground layers include both object appearance and associated visual effects. This explicit supervision enables models to learn layered video representations directly rather than inferring them implicitly. Building on this dataset, we propose DBL-Diffusion, a dual-branch diffusion framework that jointly models RGB composites and RGBA foreground layers through shared denoising and cross-branch interaction. We instantiate the framework in two tasks: DBL-Insert for layered object insertion, which generates explicit RGBA layers for realistic compositing and flexible post-editing, and DBL-Decompose for video layer decomposition, which recovers foreground and background layers using triplet supervision. Experiments demonstrate that explicit layer modeling substantially improves both insertion fidelity and decomposition quality.

AI.tldr: TriLayer dataset (composite/background/foreground triplets) + DBL-Diffusion (dual-branch diffusion for RGBA layers) enables explicit layered video representation for insertion and decomposition tasks, outperforming implicit methods.
AI.motivation: Existing video editing systems lack explicit layered representations, forcing methods for object insertion and layer decomposition to rely on implicit inference or per-scene optimization due to absence of foreground-layer supervision.
AI.method: Introduces TriLayer dataset (aligned composite, background, foreground videos with effects) and DBL-Diffusion, a dual-branch diffusion framework jointly modeling RGB composites and RGBA foreground layers via shared denoising and cross-branch interaction. Instantiated as DBL-Insert (layered insertion) and DBL-Decompose (layer decomposition).
AI.result: Explicit layer modeling substantially improves both insertion fidelity and decomposition quality compared to implicit methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicit foreground-layer supervision enables models to learn layered video representations directly, significantly enhancing compositing realism and post-editing flexibility.

title: The Disruptive Impact of Large Language Models on Capture the Flag Competitions and the Path Toward Fair Play
