AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates how the depth position of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) affects what models learn, generalize, and keep unchanged across five distinct learning objectives, finding that different tasks have distinct "adaptation geometries" that persist across model families and parameter budgets.
AI.motivation: Transformer adaptation is typically applied uniformly across all layers, even when the intended change is narrow. The authors aim to understand how the choice of adaptation site (which layers are fine-tuned) shapes learning outcomes, generalization, and selectivity—a question that has not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors introduce a controlled benchmark covering five objectives: lexical binding, factual association, behavioral policy learning, causal mapping, and procedural reasoning. They define each objective's "adaptation geometry" by evaluating acquisition, transfer, and boundedness under full-stack LoRA and early-, middle-, or late-layer LoRA, with parameter-matched controls and replication across five model families.
AI.result: Each objective has a distinct adaptation geometry: lexical binding favors early layers for acquisition/boundedness but needs broader updates for transfer; factual association prefers later layers; behavioral learning separates late-layer action acquisition from middle-layer policy gating; causal and procedural transfer benefit most from middle or full-stack adaptation. Patterns persist under parameter-matched controls and replicate across five model families.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation site is a key design variable for controlling what models learn, how they generalize, and what remains unchanged, providing practical guidance for more targeted fine-tuning strategies.

title: OmniDelta: Skill-Driven Budget Allocation for Token Compression in OmniLLMs
summary: Emerging Omni-modal Large Language Models (OmniLLMs) enable unified understanding of text, audio, and video, but their long audio-video token sequences introduce substantial memory and inference costs. Existing compression methods mainly focus on selecting important tokens under fixed budgets, leaving the preceding budget-allocation problem underexplored. We show that direct query-to-audio/video similarity is unreliable for inter-modal budget allocation, and that uniform intra-modal budgets can miss key evidence while retaining redundant content. To address these limitations, we propose OmniDelta, a training-free, skill-driven framework that couples intent-aware inter-modal allocation with content-aware intra-modal allocation. OmniDelta first constructs audio and video skill pools to shift the fixed retained-token budget according to query demand, then reallocates modality budgets over audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy. The resulting local budgets can be combined with existing pruning strategies, preserving the total retained-token ratio while changing where the budget is spent. Experiments on four audio-video benchmarks with two Qwen2.5-Omni models show that OmniDelta establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier across pruning ratios. At 25% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, OmniDelta reduces GPU memory by 22.0% and achieves a 1.64x end-to-end speedup over full-token inference.

AI.tldr: OmniDelta is a training-free framework that improves OmniLLM efficiency by intelligently allocating token retention budgets across audio and video modalities using skill-driven inter-modal and content-aware intra-modal strategies, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and significant memory/speed improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing OmniLLMs suffer from high memory and inference costs due to long audio-video token sequences, and current compression methods only select important tokens under fixed budgets without addressing the preceding budget-allocation problem. Direct query-to-audio/video similarity is unreliable for inter-modal allocation, and uniform intra-modal budgets miss key evidence while retaining redundancy.
AI.method: OmniDelta is a training-free, skill-driven framework with two components: (1) intent-aware inter-modal allocation constructs audio and video skill pools to shift fixed retained-token budgets according to query demand; (2) content-aware intra-modal allocation reallocates modality budgets over audio segments and video frames using local complexity and temporal redundancy. These local budgets can combine with existing pruning strategies while preserving the total retained-token ratio.
AI.result: Experiments on four audio-video benchmarks with two Qwen2.5-Omni models show OmniDelta establishes a new accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier across pruning ratios. At 25% token retention on Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, it reduces GPU memory by 22.0% and achieves 1.64x end-to-end speedup over full-token inference.
AI.conclusion: OmniDelta effectively addresses budget allocation limitations in OmniLLMs by coupling intent-aware and content-aware strategies, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs without training, and can be integrated with existing pruning methods.

title: DecoEvo: Score-Decoupled Co-Evolution of Solver and Rubric-Generator Skills in Text Space
summary: Text-space optimization adapts large language models (LLMs) by editing external natural-language artifacts rather than model weights, so the optimized artifacts remain inspectable and the model can be treated as a black box. However, most existing text-space methods keep evaluation fixed. On open-ended tasks, this can become a bottleneck: once the solver improves on the criteria a rubric measures, omitted dimensions remain invisible to the optimization signal. Simply evolving the rubric is also unreliable when updates are selected by the current solver's score, because apparent progress can come from making the rubric easier to satisfy. We introduce DecoEvo (Decoupled Co-Evolution), which co-evolves a solver skill and a rubric-generator skill under decoupled objectives without using gold rubrics during optimization. The solver skill is updated using criterion-level feedback, while the rubric-generator skill is revised through complementary audits of requirement coverage and response discrimination that are independent of aggregate solver score. This separation focuses generator updates on newly exposed solver weaknesses, reducing repeated emphasis on criteria the solver already satisfies. Under each benchmark's official evaluation, DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, yielding 2.8--5.0\% relative gains over SkillOpt in the five-benchmark average.

AI.tldr: DecoEvo co-evolves a solver skill and a rubric-generator skill with decoupled objectives, improving LLM performance by 2.8-5.0% over SkillOpt across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing text-space optimization for LLMs keeps evaluation fixed, which creates a bottleneck on open-ended tasks: once the solver improves on measured criteria, omitted dimensions are invisible to the optimization signal. Simply evolving the rubric using the solver's score is unreliable because apparent progress can come from making the rubric easier to satisfy.
AI.method: DecoEvo co-evolves two skills—a solver skill and a rubric-generator skill—under decoupled objectives. The solver is updated using criterion-level feedback, while the rubric-generator is revised through complementary audits of requirement coverage and response discrimination, independent of aggregate solver score. This separation prevents the generator from repeatedly emphasizing criteria the solver already satisfies.
AI.result: DecoEvo outperforms all compared methods across five benchmarks and three LLM backbones, achieving 2.8–5.0% relative gains over SkillOpt in the five-benchmark average.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled co-evolution of solver and rubric-generator skills is an effective text-space optimization strategy for open-ended tasks, avoiding the pitfalls of fixed evaluation or score-coupled rubric evolution.

title: Desktop-Delta Bench: Do Computer-Use Models Understand Desktop GUI Transitions?
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act through desktop GUIs to complete long-horizon tasks. Current benchmarks primarily measure end-task success or single-frame grounding. Neither isolates whether a model can reconstruct the causal, task-relevant transition produced by an action- crucial for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure. This is difficult because inference, remote input, app rendering, and screenshot capture are asynchronous: the next observation may be delayed, occluded, transient, or unrelated, then misread as progress and carried into subsequent planning. We introduce Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB), an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances from novel, multi-app Linux trajectories across ~15 applications and 50 task domains. DDB trajectories targets 3 failure dimensions- state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control- through 2 complementary tasks: 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances, including 105 with a cross-trajectory decoy, and 1,550 before-after pairs labeled from 5 actions + its payload. We evaluate 8 closed and open-source model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings, observing consistent gaps. Ordering remains unsaturated: best non-decoy and decoy exact-match rates are 65.1% and 65.7%. Task context improves decoy identification by 6.9 percentage points but reduces non-decoy exact match by 2.2 points; error analysis reveals systematic copying of the presented A-B-C order. Single-action results show that inferring the action family is harder than locating it: click F1 is 0.96 vs, 0.76 for drag, while recognized drags are generally localized well. DDB, thus, complements end-to-end benchmarks by filling the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery.

AI.tldr: Desktop-Delta Bench (DDB) is an offline step-level benchmark with 2,013 human-verified instances across ~15 apps and 50 task domains, evaluating CUAs on state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control through temporal-ordering (463 instances) and before-after pair (1,550) tasks. Best models achieve 65.1% exact-match on ordering; click F1 is 0.96 but drag F1 is 0.76, revealing systematic gaps in action understanding beyond end-task success.
AI.motivation: Current CUA benchmarks only measure end-task success or single-frame grounding, failing to isolate whether models can reconstruct causal, task-relevant transitions from actions—critical for rejecting stale observations, verifying progress, and recovering from failure—especially given asynchronous delays, occlusions, and transient states in real desktop environments.
AI.method: DDB collects 2,013 human-verified instances from novel multi-app Linux trajectories (~15 apps, 50 domains) targeting 3 failure dimensions: state verification, source tracking, and context-aware control. It includes 463 3-frame temporal-ordering instances (105 with cross-trajectory decoys) and 1,550 before-after pairs labeled from 5 action types plus payload. Evaluates 8 model families across 32 ordering and 16 single-action settings.
AI.result: Best non-decoy exact-match: 65.1%; best decoy exact-match: 65.7%. Task context improves decoy ID by 6.9pp but reduces non-decoy EM by 2.2pp. Error analysis shows systematic copying of presented A-B-C order. Click F1=0.96, drag F1=0.76; recognized drags are well-localized, but action family inference is harder than localization.
AI.conclusion: DDB fills the missing diagnostic layer between GUI grounding and final task success, enabling targeted improvements to desktop CUA verification, reliability, and recovery by isolating causal transition understanding as a distinct capability gap.

title: Cognivia: A Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Copilot for Evidence-Based Mental Healthcare
summary: Cognitive distortion amplifies negative emotions and contributes to mental health disorders. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is an effective way to address cognitive distortions, but its large-scale application is limited by the shortage of professional therapists. Although large language models (LLMs) have recently been explored for mental health applications, existing methods still suffer from limited domain specificity, overly flattering responses, and the absence of well-defined annotations for cognitive distortions. This paper proposes Cognivia, an evidence-based artificial intelligence therapist that integrates automatic cognitive distortion identification and rational response generation. Our framework is built on authoritative CBT texts widely regarded as core paradigms and standard references. It is further augmented with mental health question-answer (Q and A) data, and employs multi-stage prompting and structured generation strategies under the supervision of behavioral science experts. Then we fine-tune a lightweight LLM on this augmented CBT dataset to obtain Cognivia. In addition, we propose the first hierarchical quality evaluation framework for assessing LLM-generated rational responses, developed through collaboration between AI researchers and behavioral science experts. Cognivia is evaluated using lexical metrics, LLM-based Judges with two complementary criteria, and human evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts. It consistently outperforms the baseline methods in cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/SNOWTEAM2023/Cognivia.

AI.tldr: Cognivia is an evidence-based AI therapist that integrates automatic cognitive distortion identification and rational response generation, built on authoritative CBT texts and augmented with mental health Q&A data. It uses multi-stage prompting, structured generation, and fine-tunes a lightweight LLM. A novel hierarchical quality evaluation framework is also proposed. Cognivia outperforms baselines in both cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation.
AI.motivation: Cognitive distortions amplify negative emotions and contribute to mental health disorders. While CBT is effective, its large-scale application is limited by therapist shortages. Existing LLM-based mental health approaches suffer from limited domain specificity, overly flattering responses, and lack of well-defined annotations for cognitive distortions.
AI.method: The framework is built on authoritative CBT texts, augmented with mental health Q&A data, employs multi-stage prompting and structured generation strategies under behavioral science expert supervision, and fine-tunes a lightweight LLM on the augmented CBT dataset to obtain Cognivia.
AI.result: Cognivia consistently outperforms baseline methods in cognitive distortion recognition and rational response generation, evaluated using lexical metrics, LLM-based Judges with two complementary criteria, and human evaluation by 10 behavioral science experts.
AI.conclusion: Cognivia demonstrates effectiveness as an evidence-based AI therapist for addressing cognitive distortions, with superior performance validated through multiple evaluation approaches including expert human evaluation.

title: Nudging Sustainable Choices through LLM-Generated Recommendation Explanations
summary: Recommender systems mediate everyday consumption, offering a promising channel for encouraging sustainable choices. Prior research shows that explanations influence users' perceptions of recommendations and can support more informed decisions. We argue that explanations can also serve as behavioral nudges by foregrounding sustainability information at the moment of choice. This study investigates how different behavioral framings of sustainability information in recommendation explanations affect user choices and perceptions. Using generative AI, we generate sustainability-aware explanations by drawing on nudge theory and validate them through human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits. Building on this foundation, we conduct two randomized studies ($N = 529$) in a low involvement domain (instant coffee) and a high involvement domain (hotel bookings), in which participants choose among preference matched recommendations accompanied by these explanations. Our results show that, across both domains, merely disclosing sustainability information in explanations does not change choices, whereas framing that information or invoking a descriptive social norm significantly increases sustainable selections and eases decision-making. Notably, perception and behavior diverge, as plain disclosure improves explanation evaluations without translating into more sustainable selection behavior. Our work demonstrates how LLMs can generate theory-grounded explanations at scale, pointing toward practical explanation-based interventions for social good. We conclude by discussing implications for adaptive explanation design with generative AI.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how sustainability information framed as behavioral nudges (e.g., descriptive social norms) in recommendation explanations can significantly increase sustainable selections, while plain disclosure improves perceptions without changing behavior. The study uses generative AI to create theory-grounded explanations and validates them across low- and high-involvement domains (instant coffee and hotel bookings).
AI.motivation: Recommender systems influence everyday consumption and could encourage sustainable choices, but prior work has not systematically examined how sustainability explanations framed as behavioral nudges affect actual user choices and perceptions.
AI.method: The authors used generative AI (LLMs) to produce sustainability-aware explanations grounded in nudge theory, validated through human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge audits. They then conducted two randomized experiments (N=529) in low-involvement (instant coffee) and high-involvement (hotel bookings) domains, where participants selected among preference-matched recommendations accompanied by different explanation types.
AI.result: Plain disclosure of sustainability information did not change choices. Framing sustainability information or invoking descriptive social norms significantly increased sustainable selections and eased decision-making in both domains. However, perceptions and behavior diverged: plain disclosure improved explanation evaluations but did not lead to more sustainable choices.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can generate theory-grounded explanations at scale for social good. Explanation design matters: behavioral framing (especially social norms) is more effective than mere disclosure for driving sustainable behavior, though disclosure improves user perceptions. This points toward practical, adaptive explanation-based interventions using generative AI.

title: Loss Invariance Determines What Concept Layers Encode: Volume Grounding in Echocardiography
summary:
Objective: Concept bottleneck models route prediction through interpretable intermediate variables, and their validity is normally judged by how accurately those variables are predicted. We ask whether that judgement is sufficient, using left ventricular volumes as the concepts underlying ejection fraction estimation from echocardiographic video.
  Methods: A video transformer encoder was trained on a publicly available echocardiography dataset. End-systolic and end-diastolic volumes formed a concept layer from which ejection fraction was computed analytically, with no residual path to the output. We compared training under an ejection fraction objective alone against training with additional supervision of the volumes in millilitres, and evaluated both on 1276 held-out studies.
  Results: The concept bottleneck did not increase ejection fraction error relative to direct regression, at 6.89 against 7.13 mean absolute error. Without volume supervision, however, the spread of predicted volumes collapsed to 0.1 millilitres against reference spreads of 35.7 and 45.7 millilitres, while correlation was partly preserved. We show that this follows from an invariance property of the objective: ejection fraction is a ratio and is unchanged when both volumes are rescaled, so the loss determines the concept layer only up to scale. Supervision in absolute units reduced volume error from 89.8 to 25.8 millilitres at a cost of 0.4 in ejection fraction error.
  Conclusion: Concept accuracy alone can conceal a concept layer that carries no physical scale.
  Significance: Interpretable intermediate variables in clinical models should be validated against the invariance structure of the training objective, not only against prediction accuracy.

AI.tldr: Concept bottleneck models for ejection fraction estimation from echocardiography can appear to predict concepts (ventricular volumes) accurately when only supervised on the final ratio (EF), but actually collapse the scale of volumes due to an invariance property of the ratio objective. Adding direct volume supervision restores physical scale at minimal cost to EF accuracy.
AI.motivation: To test whether concept prediction accuracy alone is sufficient to validate concept bottleneck models, given that the training objective (EF ratio) is invariant to rescaling of both volumes, potentially allowing the model to learn concepts without meaningful physical scale.
AI.method: A video transformer encoder was trained on echocardiography data with end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes as intermediate concepts, and EF computed analytically. Two conditions were compared: training with EF objective only vs. training with additional supervision on volumes in millilitres, evaluated on 1276 held-out studies.
AI.result: Without volume supervision, predicted volume spread collapsed to 0.1 mL (vs. reference 35.7 and 45.7 mL), though correlation was partly preserved and EF error was 6.89 MAE (comparable to direct regression at 7.13). With volume supervision, volume error reduced from 89.8 to 25.8 mL at a cost of only 0.4 in EF error.
AI.conclusion: Concept accuracy alone can conceal a concept layer that carries no physical scale; interpretable intermediate variables should be validated against the invariance structure of the training objective, not only prediction accuracy.

title: Speculate While You Reason: Teaching Agents to Predict Their Next Tool Call via Joint Agent-Speculator RL
summary: Large language model agents often spend substantial wall-clock time waiting for tool call results. Tool-call speculation can hide this latency by predicting and pre-executing an agent's next tool call if the prediction matches the agent's eventual tool call, but existing speculators are typically separate draft models or cached traces that are poorly aligned with the deployed agent's own behavior. We identify this speculator-agent gap and show that the target agent itself is a strong next-call speculator. This points to a simpler design: unifying the agent and speculator within the same model. In this paper, we introduce the self-speculating agent, a single model that both solves tasks in agent mode and predicts its next tool call from partial trajectories in speculator mode, fully reusing prefix KV cache. To enable this dual-mode agent without degrading performance, we propose a joint agent-speculator reinforcement learning method, which derives speculation targets from the agent's own rollouts and alternates agent and speculator updates. Across agentic search QA and conversational tool-use agentic tasks, our method improves average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B, while preserving agent task success.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes self-speculating agents, which unify the agent and tool-call speculator within a single model to reduce latency. Using a joint reinforcement learning method, it significantly improves next tool-call prediction accuracy (Hit@1 from ~44-49 to ~61-66 on Qwen3-4B models) without degrading task performance.
AI.motivation: LLM agents waste wall-clock time waiting for tool call results. Existing speculation approaches use separate draft models or cached traces, creating a misalignment (speculator-agent gap) between the speculator and the deployed agent's behavior.
AI.method: The paper introduces self-speculating agents: a single model operating in dual modes—agent mode (solving tasks) and speculator mode (predicting next tool call from partial trajectories). A joint agent-speculator reinforcement learning method is proposed, deriving speculation targets from the agent's own rollouts and alternating between agent and speculator updates, while fully reusing the prefix KV cache.
AI.result: On agentic search QA and conversational tool-use tasks, the method improved average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B, while preserving agent task success.
AI.conclusion: The target agent itself serves as a strong next-call speculator, and unifying agent and speculator within the same model through joint RL training effectively bridges the speculator-agent gap, yielding substantial latency-hiding benefits without task performance degradation.

title: Distributed Constraint Optimization via Online Learning and Iterative Pricing with Application to Large-Scale Satellite Scheduling
summary: Distributed constraint optimization problems (DCOPs) provide a popular framework for distributed decision making under limited communication, but many real-world instances are too large to solve monolithically. We address this challenge from two complementary directions. We revisit the connection between DCOPs and potential games, and adapt modern online learning algorithms for equilibrium finding to DCOPs. We show that these algorithms are competitive with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms. We then turn to decomposition frameworks for large-scale DCOPs, motivated by large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling. We propose a new framework that separates a DCOP into two interacting subproblems: a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation, and independent local optimization problems for scheduling. To couple the two levels, we develop a novel iterative pricing method that updates the meta-level utilities using feedback from the local optimizers. Combining our online learning methods with our iterative pricing framework, we obtain near-optimal performance on real-world decentralized satellite scheduling problem instances, fulfilling over 99% of observation requests compared with 87% for state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses large-scale DCOPs by (1) adapting online learning algorithms for equilibrium finding to DCOPs, showing competitiveness with incomplete DCOP algorithms, and (2) proposing a decomposition framework with iterative pricing for large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling, achieving 99% fulfillment of observation requests vs. 87% for baselines.
AI.motivation: Many real-world DCOP instances are too large to solve monolithically, motivating the need for scalable approaches for distributed decision making under limited communication.
AI.method: (1) Revisits the connection between DCOPs and potential games, adapting modern online learning algorithms for equilibrium finding to DCOPs. (2) Proposes a decomposition framework separating a DCOP into a high-level meta-DCOP for task allocation and independent local optimization problems for scheduling, coupled via a novel iterative pricing method that updates meta-level utilities using local feedback.
AI.result: Online learning algorithms are competitive with representative incomplete DCOP algorithms. The combined approach achieves near-optimal performance on real-world decentralized satellite scheduling, fulfilling over 99% of observation requests compared with 87% for state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed decomposition framework with iterative pricing, combined with online learning methods, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on large-scale decentralized satellite scheduling problems.

title: HiSkill: Empowering LLM Agents with Hierarchical Skill Graphs
summary: Skills have become an important abstraction for enabling large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experience in long-horizon interactive tasks. However, existing trajectory-to-skill methods often produce flat collections of high-level textual skills that are stored and retrieved independently, leaving skill relations underutilized and maintaining a gap between high-level skills and executable actions. In this paper, we propose HiSkill, a hierarchical skill graph framework that organizes interaction trajectories into a directed graph with skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges. Specifically, the graph connects reusable high-level skills with executable action templates, while also capturing decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, and recovery relations among them. At inference time, HiSkill retrieves a compact task-relevant subgraph and performs subgraph-guided task execution, where a symbolic task state, an active skill, and the retrieved subgraph guide the LLM agent to switch skills, select AtomicOps, and ground executable actions iteratively. Experiments on three interactive environments show that HiSkill outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing inference token consumption, demonstrating the effectiveness of bridging high-level skills and executable action grounding through a hierarchical skill graph. Our data and code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/HiSkill.

AI.tldr: HiSkill introduces a hierarchical skill graph framework that organizes LLM agent trajectories into a directed graph with skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges, enabling efficient subgraph-guided task execution that bridges high-level skills with executable actions while reducing inference tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory-to-skill methods produce flat collections of high-level textual skills stored and retrieved independently, leaving skill relations underutilized and maintaining a gap between high-level skills and executable actions.
AI.method: HiSkill organizes interaction trajectories into a directed graph with skill nodes, AtomicOp nodes, and typed edges capturing decomposition, temporal transition, compatibility, support, and recovery relations. At inference, a compact task-relevant subgraph is retrieved to guide the LLM agent in switching skills, selecting AtomicOps, and grounding executable actions iteratively.
AI.result: HiSkill outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three interactive environments while reducing inference token consumption.
AI.conclusion: Bridging high-level skills and executable action grounding through a hierarchical skill graph is effective for long-horizon interactive tasks.

title: Runtime Uncertainty Monitoring for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems Using Bayesian Networks
comment: This paper got accepted for Ninth International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety Engineering (WAISE 2026): https://www.waise.org/
summary: This paper investigates how multi-agent systems (MAS)-based on large language models (LLMs) can support actuarial risk modelling, with a particular focus on uncertainty quantification. Actuarial workflows represent a high-stakes decision-support setting where unreliable outputs may lead to incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance. To address uncertainty introduced by the probabilistic nature of LLMs and dependencies between agents, a multi-agent framework is proposed in which specialised agents perform data preparation, modelling, review, and explanation tasks under a central hub. The main contribution is a novel approach to uncertainty propagation using token-level log-probabilities and a Bayesian Network. Importantly, log probabilities are not treated as direct probabilities of correctness or task success. Instead, length-normalised log-probability summaries are transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates before incorporation into the Bayesian Network. Results show that the framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-agent LLM framework for actuarial risk modelling that propagates uncertainty using token-level log-probabilities transformed into calibrated confidence estimates and integrated into a Bayesian Network, achieving baseline performance with added insights into workflow stability and uncertainty propagation.
AI.motivation: Actuarial workflows are high-stakes decision-support settings where unreliable LLM outputs can cause incorrect risk assessment, unfair pricing, and regulatory non-compliance; thus, addressing uncertainty from LLM stochasticity and inter-agent dependencies is critical.
AI.method: A multi-agent framework with specialized agents (data preparation, modelling, review, explanation) coordinated by a central hub; uncertainty is propagated via length-normalized token-level log-probabilities transformed into calibrated task-level confidence estimates, then integrated into a Bayesian Network.
AI.result: The framework reproduces baseline actuarial performance while providing additional insight into workflow stability and runtime uncertainty propagation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses uncertainty in LLM-based MAS for actuarial modelling, offering a principled uncertainty quantification method without sacrificing performance.

title: Distributing Security Controls Through Harness Engineering
summary: AI coding agents are being adopted at historic speed, yet security and risk concerns remain the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI across organizations. Existing security controls for coding agents are not systematically distributed to engineering teams, and vendor-native solutions introduce ecosystem dependencies that may not suit every deployment context. This paper investigates whether off-the-shelf security controls can be implemented on commercial AI coding agents and scaled to a distributed user base via a custom agent harness. A phased testing methodology was applied across four agent configurations --- two commercial agents with and without controls, a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness --- using a 23-test suite derived from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. SHarD (Secure Harness Distribution), a distributable harness built on the Pi agent harness, demonstrated that three categories of security controls --- OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction --- can be embedded and distributed via a single install command while retaining equivalent efficacy to direct installation on commercial agents. SHarD achieved an adjusted score of 100\%, matching the best securely configured commercial agent, with no regression across any test category. Notable observations include evidence that model non-determinism produces inconsistent security outcomes and that autonomous agent behavior can cross system boundaries in ways that OS sandboxing directly mitigates. Initial characteristics toward a control harness fitness framework are proposed, and a third research question is identified for future investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SHarD, a distributable security harness for AI coding agents that embeds OS sandboxing, skill scanning, and tool restriction controls. It achieves a 100% adjusted security score across a 23-test OWASP-based suite, matching top commercial configurations, while being deployable via a single install command.
AI.motivation: Security concerns are the primary barrier to scaling agentic AI, and existing security controls are not systematically distributed to engineering teams; vendor-native solutions introduce ecosystem dependencies that may not suit every deployment context.
AI.method: A phased testing methodology using a 23-test suite derived from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, applied across four agent configurations: two commercial agents with and without controls, a baseline harness, and a security-hardened harness (SHarD).
AI.result: SHarD achieved a 100% adjusted security score, matching the best securely configured commercial agent with no regression. Evidence showed model non-determinism causes inconsistent security outcomes, and OS sandboxing mitigates cross-boundary autonomous behavior.
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf security controls can be embedded and distributed via a custom agent harness (SHarD) with equivalent efficacy to direct installation on commercial agents. Initial characteristics toward a control harness fitness framework are proposed.

title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation
summary: Evaluating AI agents in interactive environments is hindered by fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Existing efforts focus on narrow settings, remain limited in scale, or require costly reruns, leaving much of the empirical record incomparable. We introduce Messier, a unified corpus of 957,253 records that span 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,205 verifiers. Messier consolidates public benchmark scores and supplements them with five-agent runs across six underrepresented professional and scientific domains, including a recent legal benchmark. Each record is standardized by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, and aggregation rule, with SOC/NAICS classifications for occupational and industry analysis. Using this corpus, we show frontier progress is uneven across benchmark types, with "function calling" saturated, "programming" improving the fastest, and "enterprise workflows" remaining the most challenging. Furthermore, counterfactual rescoring shows that strict all-pass aggregation in multi-verifier tasks can obscure progress and artificially alter agent rankings. From these standardized records, we derive capability scales that align with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman \r{ho} = 0.81 and can be specialized by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. Messier provides a foundational, reusable infrastructure for agent capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and fine-grained analysis of evaluation failures.

AI.tldr: Messier is a unified corpus of 957,253 records spanning 30 benchmarks, 714 agents, and 11,891 tasks, standardizing AI agent evaluation data to enable cross-benchmark comparison, capability scaling, and analysis of evaluation failures.
AI.motivation: AI agent evaluation is fragmented across diverse benchmarks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules, making empirical results incomparable and hindering progress tracking.
AI.method: Consolidated public benchmark records and supplemented them with new five-agent runs across six professional/scientific domains. Standardized each record by model, scaffold, environment, task, verifier, and aggregation rule, with SOC/NAICS classifications.
AI.result: Frontier progress is uneven: "function calling" is saturated, "programming" improving fastest, and "enterprise workflows" remain most challenging. Strict all-pass aggregation in multi-verifier tasks obscures progress and alters rankings. Derived capability scales align with Epoch's ECI at Spearman ρ=0.81.
AI.conclusion: Messier provides foundational, reusable infrastructure for agent capability scaling, benchmark auditing, and fine-grained evaluation failure analysis.

title: Interactive Reward Agent: GUI Task Evaluation via Environment-State Verification
summary: Graphical user interface task evaluation aims to determine whether a GUI agent has successfully completed a user instruction. Automated GUI task evaluation has received increasing attention because the evaluation results can serve as reward signals for both test-time scaling and post-training. However, reliable GUI task evaluation remains challenging because the judgments often require access to environment states, such as system configurations, file data, and application settings, beyond the screenshots of execution trajectories. In this paper, we propose an interactive reward agent (IRA) based on a propose-then-verify framework to acquire and verify evidence from the post-execution environment. Given a task instruction and a GUI environment after the GUI agent execution, IRA first proposes the task completion conditions and then verifies them by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools. This design combines evidence from both visible interfaces and the environment state in an interactive process. We further introduce GUI-RewardBench, a benchmark of 321 GUI task trajectories spanning 10 Ubuntu desktop application categories. Experiments show that IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench, outperforming existing evaluator baselines. We further apply IRA to reinforcement learning of GUI agents, achieving a 34.0% OSWorld success rate, which demonstrates that IRA can provide effective reward signals for training GUI agents.

AI.tldr: IRA is an interactive reward agent using a propose-then-verify framework that acquires and verifies evidence from post-execution environment states (via system, application, and GUI tools) for automated GUI task evaluation, achieving 86.9% accuracy on the new GUI-RewardBench benchmark and demonstrating effectiveness for RL-based GUI agent training (34.0% OSWorld success rate).
AI.motivation: Automated GUI task evaluation is important for providing reward signals for test-time scaling and post-training of GUI agents, but reliable evaluation is challenging because judgments often require access to environment states (system configs, file data, app settings) beyond execution trajectory screenshots.
AI.method: Proposes an Interactive Reward Agent (IRA) based on a propose-then-verify framework: (1) propose task completion conditions from the instruction, then (2) verify them interactively by invoking system tools, application tools, and GUI tools to gather evidence from both visible interfaces and underlying environment states.
AI.result: IRA achieves 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench (321 GUI task trajectories across 10 Ubuntu desktop app categories), outperforming existing evaluator baselines. Applied to RL-based GUI agent training, IRA yields a 34.0% OSWorld success rate.
AI.conclusion: Interactive evidence gathering from environment states (beyond screenshots) significantly improves GUI task evaluation accuracy, and IRA can serve as an effective reward signal provider for training GUI agents via reinforcement learning.

title: Toward Standardized Cross-Vendor Agent Tool Trust Management in Autonomous Networks
summary: Autonomous Network Levels 4-5 require AI agents to invoke tools across vendor boundaries without human oversight, yet existing management standards lack a standardized mechanism for cross-vendor trust visibility. When a tool from Vendor B is compromised, agents from Vendor A continue invoking it -- unaware of the trust degradation -- causing cascading service impact. We present AgentToolMO, a proposed 3GPP NRM information model for agent tool trust management. The model comprises: a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement, damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence, cross-vendor trust notifications via existing Management Services (MnS) interfaces, and retroactive impact assessment through NRM dependency graph traversal. Simulation-based evaluation across multi-vendor topologies shows that standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery, with cascade convergence guaranteed in bounded iterations and sub-linear notification scaling across vendor domains. The framework operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

AI.tldr: AgentToolMO is a proposed 3GPP NRM information model enabling cross-vendor trust management for autonomous networks (Levels 4-5). It includes a formal trust state machine, damped cascade propagation, cross-vendor notifications via MnS interfaces, and dependency-based impact assessment. Simulations show it reduces blast radius from hours to near-real-time containment with bounded convergence.
AI.motivation: Autonomous network levels 4-5 require cross-vendor tool invocation without human oversight, but no standardized mechanism exists for cross-vendor trust visibility. Compromised tools from one vendor continue being invoked by agents from other vendors, leading to cascading service failures.
AI.method: Proposes AgentToolMO as a 3GPP NRM information model with: (1) a formally defined trust state machine with provable graduated enforcement; (2) damped cascade propagation with bounded convergence; (3) cross-vendor trust notifications via existing MnS interfaces; (4) retroactive impact assessment via NRM dependency graph traversal. Evaluated via simulation across multi-vendor topologies.
AI.result: Standardized cross-vendor notifications reduce blast radius from hours-scale undetected propagation to near-real-time containment bounded by MnS notification delivery. Cascade convergence is guaranteed in bounded iterations with sub-linear notification scaling across vendor domains.
AI.conclusion: AgentToolMO operates within existing 3GPP management infrastructure, leverages existing protocols, and provides a standardization pathway for trustworthy multi-vendor autonomous network management.

title: Penelope: Localized Latent Recurrence for Efficient Structured Reasoning
summary: Complex structured reasoning tasks often require additional computation, yet current language models obtain it mainly by increasing parameter scale or by serializing intermediate steps as chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens. The former raises training and deployment costs, while the latter ties reasoning computation to autoregressive output length. We introduce Penelope, an efficient latent-reasoning framework for pretrained decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval. The lower decoder prefix is evaluated once to construct a problem-conditioned boundary memory, which is then iteratively refined through time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states before answer generation. A progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum transfers visible reasoning into this internal recurrent path, allowing additional computation to be allocated in latent space without repeatedly executing the complete decoder or generating a long intermediate trace. Experiments on open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks show that, at validation-selected latent budgets, Penelope attains competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models while reducing measured inference latency. These results show that latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval, reducing repeated full-decoder execution without generating a long visible reasoning trace and providing a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

AI.tldr: Penelope introduces a latent-reasoning framework for pretrained decoder-only Transformers that localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval, using time-modulated GRU dynamics and a progressive CoT-to-latent curriculum to reduce inference latency while maintaining competitive accuracy on structured-reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current language models handle complex structured reasoning either by scaling up parameters (costly training/deployment) or by serializing intermediate steps as CoT tokens (tying reasoning computation to autoregressive output length). The paper aims to break this tradeoff by enabling additional computation in latent space without full-decoder execution or long visible traces.
AI.method: Penelope localizes recurrent computation to a selected decoder interval: the lower decoder prefix is evaluated once to build a problem-conditioned boundary memory, which is iteratively refined via time-modulated GRU dynamics and recurrent readout states before answer generation. A progressive curriculum transfers visible CoT reasoning into this internal recurrent path.
AI.result: On open-source structured-reasoning benchmarks, Penelope achieves competitive accuracy relative to established latent-reasoning models while reducing measured inference latency at validation-selected latent budgets.
AI.conclusion: Latent refinement can be localized to a narrow decoder interval, reducing repeated full-decoder execution and long visible reasoning traces, offering a practical accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for decoder-only Transformer models.

title: dtControl2+$\varepsilon$: Trading Optimality for Explainability in MDPs via Decision Trees
comment: This paper is accepted at FMCAD26
summary: Over the past decade, decision trees have been used to represent controllers (a.k.a. policies) in an explainable way, with dtControl2 as a current state-of-the-art tool. However, for systems that are large or have many corner cases, even such representations tend to be too complex and not human-comprehensible. Unfortunately, reducing the size of the decision tree is not straightforward, as missing just a single crucial case might result in an incorrect controller. We tackle this issue in the setting of Markov decision processes, extending dtControl2 by "$\varepsilon$" functionality: Given an allowed imprecision $\varepsilon \geq 0$, we construct a smaller decision tree, distilling the essence of the controller, while still guaranteeing its $\varepsilon$-optimality. This enables us to provide tunably simpler explanations, omitting a controllable amount of detail. Our tool constructs decision trees that are orders of magnitude smaller than the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper extends dtControl2 with ε-functionality to construct smaller decision trees for Markov decision process controllers, allowing users to trade precision for simplicity by omitting controllable detail while guaranteeing ε-optimality.
AI.motivation: Decision tree controllers for large systems become too complex for human comprehension. Reducing tree size without risking incorrectness is difficult, motivating a tunable approach that sacrifices bounded precision for simplicity.
AI.method: The authors extend dtControl2 by introducing an ε parameter that allows bounded imprecision, enabling construction of smaller decision trees that distill the essence of the controller while still guaranteeing ε-optimality in the Markov decision process setting.
AI.result: The constructed decision trees are orders of magnitude smaller than the state-of-the-art (dtControl2 without ε-functionality).
AI.conclusion: By allowing tunable imprecision, the approach provides simpler, more human-comprehensible explanations of controllers while maintaining formal guarantees on optimality, making it practical for large systems with many corner cases.

title: A Cost-Effective Multimodal LLM Reasoning Framework for Question Answering over Irregular Clinical Time Series
summary: Question answering (QA) over irregular clinical time series (ICTS) plays a pivotal role in a wide range of healthcare applications. Although recent multimodal time-series large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in general-purpose time-series QA, they remain poorly equipped to model the sparsity, asynchrony, and irregular sampling patterns of clinical observations. To fill this gap, we propose ClinPRISM, a cost-effective multimodal LLM reasoning framework for question answering over ICTS data. First, we devise an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder to capture sparse clinical evidence at diverse temporal scales. Then, we propose a temporal evidence distiller to integrate representations across these scales and compress them into a small number of LLM-compatible tokens. Moreover, we introduce a progressive alignment strategy that sequentially aligns the irregular trajectories with the LLM's textual embedding space. To facilitate training, we construct 30,000 clinical time series paired with multi-scale descriptions, together with 41,000 instruction-tuning instances spanning 11 tasks. Using a 4-billion-parameter LLM backbone, ClinPRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the held-out evaluation benchmark while using only 16 time-series tokens and achieving an average inference latency of 0.15 seconds per question.

AI.tldr: ClinPRISM is a cost-effective multimodal LLM framework for question answering over irregular clinical time series (ICTS), using an irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder, temporal evidence distiller, and progressive alignment strategy to achieve SOTA performance with only 16 tokens and 0.15s inference latency.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal time-series LLMs cannot handle the sparsity, asynchrony, and irregular sampling patterns of clinical observations, limiting their effectiveness for clinical QA over irregular time series.
AI.method: (1) Irregularity-aware multi-scale encoder to capture diverse temporal scale evidence; (2) Temporal evidence distiller to integrate and compress representations into LLM-compatible tokens; (3) Progressive alignment strategy for aligning irregular trajectories with LLM embedding space; trained on 30K clinical time series + 41K instruction instances across 11 tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on held-out benchmark using only 16 time-series tokens, 4B LLM backbone, and 0.15s average inference latency.
AI.conclusion: ClinPRISM effectively addresses irregular clinical time-series QA in a cost-effective manner, achieving superior efficiency and accuracy.

title: Large Language Model for Operations Research Formulation Selection in Multi-Warehouse Inventory Allocation
summary: Multi-warehouse inventory allocation is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) problem, yet no single formulation consistently matches heterogeneous instance-level regimes induced by demand concentration, inventory imbalance, replenishment scale, service constraints, and forecast volatility. We study this issue as instance-wise operations research (OR) formulation selection, where each allocation instance is assigned to a solver-executable formulation from a candidate OR expert library. We propose a solver-guided large language model (LLM) framework for OR formulation selection, in which each OR expert corresponds to a MIP formulation encoding a distinct allocation priority. To train the selector, the framework first constructs balanced expert-conditioned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) records for schema learning, and then uses MIP solver evaluation on historical instances to convert solver-evaluated allocation-quality gaps into margin-weighted identity preference optimization (IPO) preferences and per-instance expert-score metadata for reward lookup during group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to assign rewards to sampled responses. Experiments on multi-warehouse inventory allocation instances from JD$\mathord{.}$com, one of China's largest e-retailers, demonstrate that GRPO substantially improves expert-selection accuracy relative to the SFT+IPO selector and, more importantly, produces higher realized allocation quality than both the preference-trained selector and the best fixed formulation. With GRPO, Hit Ratio@1 and Hit Ratio@2 increase from 21.45% to 50.42% and from 70.47% to 82.31%. The resulting selector achieves an allocation accuracy gain of 12.57 percentage points over the incumbent baseline, outperforming both the SFT+IPO selector and the best fixed OR expert, and reduces the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a solver-guided LLM framework for selecting the best MIP formulation for multi-warehouse inventory allocation, using GRPO to train a selector that outperforms baselines and reduces the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points on JD.com instances.
AI.motivation: No single MIP formulation consistently matches heterogeneous instance-level regimes in multi-warehouse inventory allocation, motivating instance-wise OR formulation selection.
AI.method: A solver-guided LLM framework that constructs balanced SFT records for schema learning, then uses IPO for preference training, and finally applies GRPO with solver-evaluated allocation-quality gaps as reward signals to train the formulation selector.
AI.result: GRPO improves Hit Ratio@1 from 21.45% to 50.42% and Hit Ratio@2 from 70.47% to 82.31%; allocation accuracy gains 12.57 percentage points over baseline, reducing the gap to the ex-post oracle to 4.85 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The solver-guided LLM framework with GRPO substantially outperforms both SFT+IPO selectors and fixed formulations, demonstrating the effectiveness of using solver feedback as reward signals for formulation selection in OR.

title: CHARM: A Multimodal Graph Foundation Model with Hierarchical Context Modeling for Zero-Shot Transfer
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for transferring knowledge across graph domains and tasks. Real-world graphs associate nodes with text, images, and other modalities, making multimodal graphs essential for representing complex entities and relations. Moreover, collecting labels and adapting models for every new graph domain is costly and often infeasible, motivating zero-shot transfer. Unfortunately, zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs remains underexplored. Existing GNN-based graph foundation models typically require downstream adaptation, whereas LLM-based graph methods mainly address unimodal graphs or tasks within a single domain. This setting presents two key challenges. First, models must generalize knowledge from individual modalities while capturing transferable cross-modal relations. Second, without target-domain fine-tuning, node representations remain entangled with domain-specific structures and modality-specific characteristics, obscuring shared concepts in unseen domains. To address these challenges, we propose CHARM, a multimodal graph foundation model with hierarchical context modeling for zero-shot transfer. CHARM replaces isolated raw nodes with hierarchical graph contexts that capture multimodal semantics and cross-modal relations. These contexts map domain-specific node patterns to shared high-level concepts, reducing reliance on target-domain supervision or adaptation. A modality-aware graph context encoder integrates multimodal information with graph structure and converts the resulting representations into graph tokens for a large language model . Experiments show consistent improvements on zero-shot multimodal graph tasks.

AI.tldr: CHARM is a multimodal graph foundation model that uses hierarchical context modeling to achieve zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs by replacing raw nodes with graph contexts that capture multimodal semantics and cross-modal relations, then encoding them into tokens for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs remains underexplored. Existing GNN-based GFMs require downstream adaptation, and LLM-based methods mainly handle unimodal graphs or single-domain tasks. There is a need for models that can generalize across modalities and graph domains without target-domain fine-tuning.
AI.method: CHARM replaces isolated raw nodes with hierarchical graph contexts that capture multimodal semantics and cross-modal relations, mapping domain-specific patterns to shared high-level concepts. A modality-aware graph context encoder integrates multimodal information with graph structure and converts representations into graph tokens for a large language model.
AI.result: Consistent improvements on zero-shot multimodal graph tasks.
AI.conclusion: CHARM effectively enables zero-shot transfer on multimodal graphs by leveraging hierarchical context modeling to bridge domain-specific and shared concepts, reducing reliance on target-domain supervision.

title: Falling Behind Drives Unsafe Development in an Idealised AI Race Experiment
summary: Technological races create tension between speed and safety: actors may gain by moving faster than competitors, even when risky development is harmful. This is prominent in debates about artificial intelligence (AI), where competitive pressure is often argued to incentivise riskier, less safety-conscious development. We study this using a framed behavioural experiment based on an idealised AI race, in which paired participants repeatedly chose between Safe and Unsafe development under an uncertain time horizon. Unsafe development gave faster progress and higher immediate payoffs but accumulated private risk up to a treatment-specific maximum of 10\%, 60\%, or 90\%; the race's competitive structure was held constant, and only this maximum risk varied. Neither the pre-registered comparison between risk levels nor the role of elicited risk preferences was supported by the data. Instead, exploratory analyses motivated by the task's repeated structure show that Unsafe behaviour is shaped less by risk preferences than by the evolving strategic state of the race: participants are more likely to choose Unsafe after their opponent does so, being ahead reduces Unsafe play while falling behind increases it, and first-round choices predict later behaviour. To interpret these effects we introduce a reduced evolutionary model with four strategies -- Always Safe, Always Unsafe, Conditionally Safe, and Conditionally Antisocial Safe -- which reproduces the treatment effect and shows how conditional Unsafe behaviour can be favoured by competitive race dynamics. Together, the experiment and model show that unsafe development can emerge from early behavioural momentum, opponent behaviour, and fear of falling behind, rather than from risk preferences alone, suggesting policy should focus on reducing competitive pressure and promoting cooperation in AI development rather than only individual risk.

AI.tldr: A behavioral experiment and evolutionary model show that unsafe AI development in competitive races is driven more by strategic dynamics (opponent behavior, falling behind) than by individual risk preferences, suggesting policy should focus on reducing competitive pressure rather than just managing risk.
AI.motivation: Technological races, particularly in AI, create tension between speed and safety, with competitive pressure incentivizing riskier development. The paper aims to understand whether unsafe behavior is driven by risk preferences or strategic race dynamics.
AI.method: Framed behavioral experiment with paired participants repeatedly choosing Safe or Unsafe development under uncertain time horizons, with treatment-specific maximum risk levels (10%, 60%, 90%). Supplemented by a reduced evolutionary model with four strategies (Always Safe, Always Unsafe, Conditionally Safe, Conditionally Antisocial Safe).
AI.result: Neither pre-registered risk level comparisons nor elicited risk preferences predicted behavior. Instead, exploratory analyses revealed: participants copy opponent's Unsafe choices, being ahead reduces Unsafe play while falling behind increases it, and first-round choices predict later behavior. The evolutionary model reproduces treatment effects and shows conditional Unsafe behavior can be favored by competitive dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Unsafe development emerges from early behavioral momentum, opponent behavior, and fear of falling behind rather than risk preferences alone. Policy should focus on reducing competitive pressure and promoting cooperation in AI development.

title: Domain-Prior-Regularized Graph Modeling for Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems
comment: 12 pages, ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Anomaly detection on multivariate sensor time series is critical for industrial monitoring of cyber-physical systems (CPS), where even subtle deviations from normal behavior can indicate process disruption. Recent graph-based approaches have made significant progress, but they often struggle in small-scale physical systems with scarce labeled anomalies and limited normal data. In such settings, graph-based models tend to capture spurious correlations and produce unstable sensor topologies. We propose DPR-GM (Domain-Prior-Regularized Graph Modeling), a forecasting-based framework that incorporates system design knowledge into graph construction. DPR-GM leverages a large language model (LLM) to extract directed physical couplings between sensor pairs from system documentation, which are encoded as a binary domain adjacency matrix serving as a structural gate over sensor relations. This gate is then modulated by Pearson correlations estimated from normal training data. The anomaly score is further weighted by sensor-level reliability derived from the coefficient of variation. All graph and weighting components are fixed prior to training and add no learnable parameters. On the SKAB benchmark, DPR-GM outperforms graph-based, statistical, and deep learning baselines across F1, AUROC, and AUPRC, showing that domain-structured graph priors are a practical alternative to fully learned topologies in data-scarce CPS.

AI.tldr: DPR-GM is a forecasting-based anomaly detection framework for multivariate sensor time series that uses LLM-extracted physical couplings from system documentation as a structural prior (binary domain adjacency matrix) gated with Pearson correlations, plus sensor-level reliability weighting, achieving SOTA on SKAB benchmark without adding learnable parameters.
AI.motivation: Graph-based anomaly detection methods struggle in small-scale cyber-physical systems with scarce labeled anomalies and limited normal data, as they tend to capture spurious correlations and produce unstable sensor topologies.
AI.method: DPR-GM uses an LLM to extract directed physical couplings from system documentation, encodes them as a binary domain adjacency matrix serving as a structural gate, modulates it with Pearson correlations from normal training data, and weights anomaly scores by sensor-level reliability (coefficient of variation). All components are fixed pre-training with no learnable parameters.
AI.result: On the SKAB benchmark, DPR-GM outperforms graph-based, statistical, and deep learning baselines across F1, AUROC, and AUPRC metrics.
AI.conclusion: Domain-structured graph priors are a practical alternative to fully learned topologies in data-scarce CPS settings, eliminating the need for learnable graph parameters while improving robustness.
